II.
 
He’s the last one holding the fort; a tradition that is a remnant from a time belonging to an
entirely different house, and in many ways to an entirely different life as well – but one that
he still honours, strangely enough.
Lando’s in the kitchen of his parents’ new home in Bath. It’s not the one he grew up in, the
one in Somerset, with the chickens and the forest surrounding the house; the sprawling
property he used to trek through countless times as a teenager, coming home drunk as a
skunk from some party down in the village at dawn, sneaking through the front door before
stumbling upstairs and collapsing into bed, where he’d sleep until noon.
No, this house Lando barely knows. He’s only here at Christmas, if even.

Ever since Oliver got married and had two daughters, the Norrises no longer assemble in
their full glory every year – though Lando always makes an effort to be there. It’s one of the
few opportunities he gets to see his sisters without too much logistical gymnastics, and even
if he remains somewhat unfamiliar with this house, his mother has made it homely enough
that he likes being here.
Still, there is something strange about being the last one awake in a home where he feels a
little like a guest, despite the fact that his parents live here and he has a room somewhere on
the second floor that his mother refuses to touch, even if he only sleeps in it a handful of
times a year.
But Lando has always been the last one awake on Christmas Eve.
He likes to ghost through the house as the final man standing, watching the Christmas lights
twinkle in the windows, the tree visible through the open archway connecting the kitchen to
the living room.
It began as a childhood ambition. Back when he genuinely thought he might catch Father
Christmas in the act; distributing presents beneath the tree, filling stockings hanging from the
fireplace with sweets and little gifts.
And even when he got older, when he knew Father Christmas was entirely made up, he kept
the tradition anyway. At some point his parents simply gave up trying to send him to bed,
accepting that he was never going to sleep regardless.
And so, if nothing else, at least someone was there to watch the lights.
Lando’s tearing through his mother’s cookie jars; heaps of homemade Speculoos, his
favourite Belgian Christmas cookie that she still makes every year, as he leans over the
kitchen counter and once again finds himself scrolling through Grindr.
He enjoys the different selection of men here; the ones in and around Monaco he’s gotten a
little bored of already, even though he rarely indulges these days. No, the men he scrolls
through here remind him, in an almost nostalgic sort of way, of all the boys he used to have
crushes on growing up around here; run-of-the-mill English lads with their conviction that
the most romantic date imaginable is the pub down the road and that ideal conversation
consists of football or, if they’re feeling particularly brave, local council politics.
Lando knows a life like that would have paralysed him. Bored him to death, probably.
And still, as he scrolls through all the Colins and Nigels and Daniels and Joshs while absent-
mindedly demolishing his mother’s Christmas cookies, he finds himself wondering what his
life might have looked like if he hadn’t become a Formula One driver.
All in all, it would only have taken one thing. One different decision, or one wrong turn. Like
Oscar. Or perhaps he simply wouldn’t have been good enough. Like Max.
Would he be married already?

Oliver had already been married at his age, but then again he’d also been dating Sav for what
felt like most of his adult life. Lando rather doubts he would be married even if he wasn’t
famous; as he doubts one of the Colins or Nigels or Daniels of the world would have
managed to hold his attention for particularly long, pub dates or not.
None of the men on his screen manage to captivate him for more than a few seconds at a
time. He scrolls through them like he’s skimming an endless wine list while not actually
being in the mood to drink, vaguely aware that there are probably excellent options available
to him, but finding himself strangely uninterested all the same.
After a while he closes the app and switches back to Discord instead.
He scrolls upwards through his chat with Oscar and discovers that ever since yesterday
evening, when Oscar sent him the photo, they have somehow managed to exchange enough
messages that it takes him almost a full minute to find it again.
Lando balances the cookie jar under his arm as he slowly makes his way through the living
room and collapses onto the sofa, rereading their conversation from the bottom upwards;
lingering over messages that were entirely inconsequential at the time and somehow less so
now.
He’s halfway through one of Oscar’s increasingly impassioned rants about the MCSR
Ranked season he’s currently competing in when his phone freezes for a split second in his
hand, and for a brief moment he assumes Discord has crashed.
Then the screen changes. Incoming video call. From Oscar.
“Video call?” Lando asks incredulously, his voice much too loud for the serene atmosphere of
his parents’ living room.
He immediately sits up straighter, brushing at his face in an attempt to remove any lingering
Speculoos crumbs before running a hand through his curls, trying to coax them into looking
at least halfway presentable.
He doesn’t expect to see Oscar’s face when he accepts the call, but there is a part of him that
still desperately hopes he will.
Of course, he’s greeted by an entirely different sight instead; something that couldn’t seem
more surreal against the dim backdrop of his parents’ living room.
In front of him stretches the ocean. 
The sun shines golden and warm across its surface, turning the small ripples of the waves
into sheets of liquid light. It has already climbed high enough into the sky that the morning
feels properly awake, but remains low enough to cast everything in gold.
It takes Lando a moment to realise what he’s looking at. Oscar has called him from his
surfboard.

In the lower edge of the frame he can make out part of it; some yellow-green colour cutting
through the water, and from the angle of the camera it seems as though Oscar is straddling it.
“What the fuck?” Lando asks, feeling his heartbeat immediately jump into his throat.
“Shht,” Oscar says, his voice accompanied by the soft lapping of waves around him. “Look.
A bottlenose dolphin.”
Lando immediately stops breathing, as though that might somehow improve the viewing
experience, and focuses on the patch of ocean Oscar is pointing the camera towards, not even
three metres away from him.
In the middle of all that warm gold and blue, Lando finally sees it. A grey blur beneath the
surface. Then a head breaking through the water, the elegant curve of a body before it
disappears beneath the waves once more.
“Oh, my god,” Lando says, his voice barely emerging as more than a broken whisper.
It seems perfectly ephemeral, almost unreal; the sleek edge of a dolphin threading through the
water, keeping eye contact with Oscar for a fleeting moment before disappearing again
beneath the vastness of the ocean.
And then, quite unexpectedly, a strange, sick, twisted sort of jealousy rises inside him;
directed at the dolphin.
Sure, the freedom to swim every ocean on earth is already quite the privilege – but in contrast
to Lando, the dolphin had seen Oscar’s face, if only briefly.
For the moment Oscar had pointed the camera towards it and selected Lando’s contact in a
moment of instinctive wanting-to-share, the dolphin had seen the face of the man sitting on
the surfboard.
Lando finds himself trying to imagine what that must have looked like. Or worse: trying to
project himself into the body of the animal.
For a moment, he imagines himself suspended between the waves, the cold Australian water
pressing against his gummatous skin as he breaks through the surface, caught by the play of
sunlight on the ocean; rising from beneath the water just long enough to see a man sitting
astride a green surfboard and looking back at him.
And still, even in the supposed vastness of his own imagination, he finds himself unable to
conjure a face. 
All he sees is light. The sun directly behind Oscar, bright enough to turn him into little more
than a silhouette, every feature swallowed by gold before Lando can make it out properly.
The dolphin dives beneath the surface again, favouring the dark depths of the ocean over the
man on the surfboard, and suddenly Lando finds himself back on his parents' sofa, his own
reflection faintly visible in the screen; his face illuminated only by the Christmas lights on

the tree and the brightness of Oscar's Australian morning transmitted halfway across the
world through a video call.
“Is he coming back?” Lando asks, trying to follow the shadow of the animal beneath the
waves.
“Don't think so,” Oscar replies from somewhere behind the camera. “Very nice of him to wait
until I'd gotten my phone out and called you, though.”
“He wanted to meet a celebrity,” Lando quips. “You know what they say about a dolphin's
intelligence.”
Oscar snorts. “Sure. He's going to tell his entire school now that he came face to face with the
great Lando Norris today.”
“He better,” Lando grins. He stretches out on the sofa, shifting until he's comfortable and
angling his phone ever so slightly away from himself so that the Christmas lights catch him a
little more flatteringly. “Why the fuck do you have your phone with you while surfing?”
“I don't usually,” Oscar says.
Lando is still looking at the ocean stretched out before him; the sheer vastness of it, endless
blue and gold reaching towards the horizon. Oscar, predictably, is keeping the camera angled
away from the shoreline, smart enough not to give away where he lives through a stray
glimpse of the skyline alone.
Not that Lando would stand much of a chance figuring it out. He's currently training to
become a passable Minecraft speedrunner, not a Geoguessr champion.
“But these last few days I’ve been ruthlessly stalked by what I believe to be the same
dolphin, and I wanted to take a picture of it. I promised my sister. She believes I’m making it
up.”
Even without seeing his face, Lando can hear the fond eye-roll in Oscar’s voice.
“The same sister who cuts up sport jerseys and carries packages through the city for you?” he
asks, greedy for every little piece of personal information Oscar lets slip into their
conversations.
“No,” Oscar says. “Different one.”
The horizon tilts slightly sideways as Oscar appears to switch the phone from one hand to the
other. For a brief moment, Lando catches sight of a ghostly pale hand gripping the nose of the
surfboard, adjusting it slightly after a cluster of small waves seems to have nudged it off
course.
“Alright,” Oscar says after a moment. “I’m gonna hang up now. Sorry for the abrupt call
without warning.”

“No, please don’t hang up,” Lando says immediately, almost embarrassed by how whiny he
sounds. “You only just called.”
This, a voice says from somewhere in the back of his mind, sounding infuriatingly like Max,
is not normal. This cannot be measured in terms of friendship.
“I’m in the middle of the ocean, Lando,” Oscar says, almost gently.
“And?”
“What if I drown because I don’t see a wave coming because I’m busy trying to balance
myself on this board?”
“I’m pretty sure you know how to swim, Osc.”
“Oh, so you’d risk my untimely death rather than end this call?”
“You’re catastrophising.” Lando can’t help grinning. “Turn the camera around, Osc.”
“No.” The answer comes immediately, the old line in the sand being drawn with practiced
ease.
Lando pouts.
“Is your hair wet?” he asks, and doesn’t really know why. If he can’t see him, then he at least
wants as much information as possible.
“No,” Oscar replies. “Didn’t go in yet.”
“You think you look better with wet hair or dry hair?” The question escapes before Lando can
stop it.
Oscar goes quiet for a moment. “Uh,” he says eventually, sounding genuinely puzzled.
“Dunno. Neither.”
“Oh, come on,” Lando snorts. “I definitely look better with dry hair. The curls don’t take
water very well.”
“I have genuinely never thought about that.” There’s something in Oscar’s voice that makes
Lando smile; that slight edge that appears whenever he’s embarrassed by something.
“You’ve got straight hair?”
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “Boring, plain, straight hair.” A brief pause. “Unlike your curls.”
“Nawww,” Lando says, running his fingers through the mess on top of his head, and this time
he really can’t deny the slight flirtatious edge to his voice. Fuck. “You like my curls?”
Oscar doesn’t answer. And Lando immediately knows he’s gone too far.

He’s slightly tipsy from the port his father insisted on bringing up from the wine cellar after
dinner, and the fact that he’s spent the last three hours scrolling through Grindr has left him
craving a kind of language he hasn’t spoken in a while; a syntax that once came naturally to
him, all teasing and implication and coquettish little provocations.
Doing it with his Minecraft coach, however, is probably not advisable.
In a sudden bout of self-consciousness, Lando taps the screen and turns off his facecam,
allowing himself the luxury of blushing in private.
“Hey,” Oscar complains immediately, so quickly that it makes Lando smile despite himself.
“Why did you turn off your camera?”
“Because it’s unfair if you can see me but I can’t see you.”
“You’re looking at the Southern Ocean in the morning sun on Christmas Day,” Oscar
immediately retorts. “Trust me, you’re getting the better deal.”
“I really don’t think so,” Lando says. “I see that carpet of wet every year at Albert Park.”
“Carpet of wet,” Oscar scoffs. “You’re a snob.”
“Easy deal. Turn your facecam around and I’ll turn mine on again.”
“No, Lando,” Oscar says, and it sounds final.
He knows better than to keep pushing. Oscar has his boundaries, and while every single other
one seems willing to stretch beneath the pressure of their banter, that is the one line he never
relents on.
“Fine,” Lando scoffs, tapping his screen and enabling his front camera again. “Because you
showed me a dolphin.”
There’s a brief pause on the other end of the line. Then: “Attaboy.”
Lando nearly slides off the sofa.
There’s a strange pang low in his stomach as Oscar’s Australian accent wraps itself around
the phrase, and some deeply embarrassing part of him – the same part that perks up at praise
like a fucking dog whenever Oscar tells him he’s done something well – immediately feels
heat rush into his cheeks, accompanied by the dizzying sort of euphoria that comes from
knowing Oscar is pleased with him.
Hey, his inner Max immediately cuts in before he can get too carried away with himself.
Before you cream your pants over this, have you ever considered asking yourself why exactly
Oscar wants to see you so badly?
Lando nervously bites down on his thumbnail at that, the warmth still lingering stubbornly
beneath his skin.

“So,” Oscar says after a moment. “You’re at home then?”
During the trip to Bath – which had been arduous in the way that first the airport and then the
car service that brought Max to Birmingham and him to Bath had conspired to make the
journey as inconvenient as possible – Lando had texted Oscar constantly about every minor
inconvenience, much to the amusement of his best friend, whose eyebrows seemed to rise a
little higher every single time Lando grinned down at his phone.
“Well, not home,” Lando says. “But I’m at my parents’ house.”
Only after saying it does he realise that Oscar has never actually told him what he’s doing for
Christmas. As usual, he had been relentlessly inquisitive about Lando’s plans instead,
somehow managing to sidestep every counter-question with the same slippery ease he always
does.
“And you?”
“I’m in the middle of the ocean on a surfboard.”
Lando rolls his eyes. “Don’t be sassy with me, Mister.”
“My sisters are coming over later,” he says after a moment.
“You’re not celebrating with your parents? Friends?” Lando plucks up the courage. “A
girlfriend, maybe?”
“My parents are in Perth over the holidays,” Oscar says. “My youngest sister’s with them.
My friends largely live in the US, though Fein and I are planning on filming a video later.”
Lando waits anxiously.
“And, uh, girlfriend.” Oscar laughs awkwardly. “I’m afraid I’m severely lacking in that
department.”
He sounds faintly embarrassed. Lando has to actively remind himself that his facecam is still
on before he does something deeply humiliating, like pump his fist in celebration.
Not that it would make any difference. Not that he has any claim whatsoever over Oscar’s
romantic prospects.
But still. The idea of Oscar dating someone would have annoyed him immensely.
“Ah, no matter,” Lando says before he can stop himself. “I’ve got loads of attractive female
friends who are really into nerdy guys. I’m sure I could introduce you to a bunch of them
when we meet in Albert Park in March.”
The second the words leave his mouth, he wants to physically grab them and stuff them back
in.

Why the fuck is he doing this? Why is he overcorrecting so aggressively? Why is he
suggesting something that he does not, under any circumstances, want to happen?
The mere thought of Oscar hitting it off with one of his friends makes something unpleasant
twist low in his stomach. He would genuinely rather gouge his own eyes out. He’s such a
fucking idiot.
There had been approximately ten million other directions this conversation could have
taken, but of course the deeply ingrained instincts of his straight fuckboy persona had seized
control of the wheel and steered them back towards territory that felt familiar; somewhere he
could stand without immediately setting himself on fire.
The camera shakes slightly. Lando hears water splash against the board as Oscar adjusts his
position again.
“You’re such a fucking cliché of a well-travelled athlete,” he says after a moment, and Lando
genuinely can’t tell whether he sounds amused or annoyed. “Having a roster in every city that
you just hit up whenever you’re there.”
Well. To be fair, Oscar isn’t entirely wrong. It’s just that the roster generally isn't women.
“I’m just saying, I’m willing to share,” Lando says, reliably making everything worse almost
immediately.
This is exactly why he has the arrangement with Magui.
Whenever he attempts to act straight, something invariably goes catastrophically wrong and
he turns into the most insufferable cliché of a straight fuckboy imaginable. That probably
stems from the frankly absurd amount of looksmaxxing content he watches late at night,
laughing himself sick over it at three in the morning; his only real point of contact with
people attempting to perform heterosexuality with just as little success as him.
“Well, that’s very generous of you,” Oscar says, and suddenly something about his voice
sounds off to Lando.
A little colder. Perhaps he doesn’t appreciate the way Lando talks about his supposed female
friends. Which, considering he has three sisters, would be entirely fair.
“But no thank you.” A brief pause. “And I’m not coming to Albert Park.”
“Oh, you are,” Lando says, immediately grateful for the change of topic. “Did you forget I
pulled off a zero cycle?”
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “One single zero cycle. And I rewatched the footage. It was sloppy. You
fucked up the last bed and got lucky enough to crit the dragon twice before she could fly
away again.”
“Hey,” Lando protests. “There was a time when I also pulled off my first divebomb overtake.
I only got better with every subsequent one.”

“Fine,” Oscar says, sounding faintly amused now. “Then that was your first zero cycle of
many.” A short pause. “I know I take the piss out of you constantly, but I am proud.”
Lando beams. He catches sight of himself in the little preview window at the bottom of the
screen; his face softly illuminated by the Christmas lights in the living room, a gummy,
unabashed grin stretching across it that makes him look strangely young – a little like he did
back then. Back when he was a fresh-faced rookie stumbling into a Formula One paddock for
the first time with all of his closest friends alongside him.
“Thank you, coach,” he says. “The credit belongs to you.”
Oscar scoffs. “It doesn’t. You’ve been working really hard.” Lando hears more water lapping
against the board as Oscar adjusts his position again. “I’m genuinely impressed. You’re
spending a lot of time on this. More than I would ever have expected.”
“What can I say?” Lando replies, already aware of the flirtatious edge creeping back into his
voice before he can stop it. “I just really, really like it when my coach praises me.”
“Ha,” Oscar snorts. “Does Zak not give you enough attention?”
“Plenty of it,” Lando says. “He treats me like the sun shines out of my ass. It’s great when
your boss is a fan of yours. But it’s different with you.”
“How so?”
Because I fucking love the way your voice sounds when praise creeps into it. Zak’s an old
man. He’s nice enough, but he doesn’t get me going like that.
“Dunno,” Lando deflects. “I know I’m good at racing. I’ve been good at it for a long time.
Every improvement I make is just a tiny course correction. But I genuinely suck so, so badly
at Minecraft that every improvement still feels like a milestone. And you’re so remarkably
stingy with praise that every time you do pay me a compliment, it feels like I’ve conquered a
mountain.”
“Stingy with praise,” Oscar snorts. “I think I’ve given you more compliments and words of
encouragement than I’ve given anyone else in my entire life up to this point.”
“What a pair we are,” Lando says, propping his chin onto his fist, elbow sinking into the
cushion beside him.
“Truly.” The camera shifts again and for a moment Lando sees more surfboard than ocean.
“Hold on for a second. I need to–”
Then the entire image jolts violently.
For an instant, Lando is convinced Oscar has dropped his phone into the ocean as blue
suddenly floods the screen, followed by the greenish-yellow of the surfboard, a flash of sky,
and then–
Thighs. 

Encased in a wetsuit, spread on either side of the board where Oscar is balancing himself,
firmly anchored against the movement of the water.
Big thighs, too. Strong thighs. The sort that fit the broad shoulders and powerful build Lando
already knows about.
For one brief, deeply unfortunate moment, his imagination supplies an image entirely
unprompted: he imagines those thighs on either side of his own legs, pushing in on him,
folding in around him.
The thought arrives so suddenly that it almost steals the air from his lungs. The only reason
he doesn't immediately turn his facecam off again is because he knows he has to overplay it.
Pretend everything is normal.
“Wave got you?” he asks eventually, once he trusts his voice to emerge sounding remotely
human.
Unfortunately, Oscar chooses that exact moment to turn the camera off. Lando follows suit
almost immediately, finally allowing himself to bury his face in one of the sofa cushions
while he attempts to recover what little remains of his dignity.
It is objectively embarrassing to lose his composure over something so utterly mundane. He
feels like a Victorian gentleman who has just caught sight of a lady’s ankles.
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “Saw it too late because I was too transfixed by, uh...” He trails off. “My
hair’s wet now, by the way.”
“Proof?”
He laughs softly. “You’re gonna have to take my word for it.”
There are splashes on the other end of the line. “And I can’t help but notice you’ve turned
your camera off again.”
“As did you.”
“Yeah,” Oscar replies. “Too risky. Another wave like that could’ve doxed me.”
“I’ve got the ocean on my side, it seems,” Lando says lazily. He stretches out further across
the sofa. “Osc, you know what? I really don’t want to be held responsible for your drowning,
so I’m going to let you get back to surfing.” A pause. “Under one condition.”
“Yeah?”
“You call me once you’re back at shore.”
Oscar laughs, properly this time; not the quiet chuckle he usually lets out when Lando says
something mildly amusing, but a full laugh. “You serious?”

“We’ve barely talked today,” Lando says, before he can stop himself. “And we didn’t talk
yesterday either because you were streaming for ages and I had to pack for the trip.”
The words leave his mouth and immediately sound worse and much more whiny than they
had in his head. God, he hates himself when he sounds like that.
Needy as hell. And for what? His Minecraft coach?
“You should go to bed,” Oscar says, gently but firmly. “It’s late for you, is it not?”
“I’m always up late on Christmas Eve.”
Lando turns his camera back on, and immediately becomes aware of the heat still lingering in
his cheeks. It feels much too treacherous, much too revealing; but Oscar doesn’t comment on
it. He probably can’t even see it. The only illumination comes from the Christmas lights on
the tree and his mother’s careful arrangement of candles and fairy lights along the
windowsills, casting the room in a glow too soft to expose the full extent of Lando’s
embarrassment.
“You’d just be keeping me company.”
“Why?” Oscar asks. “Are you always awake this late?”
“You’ll have to call me once you’re back on shore to find out,” Lando says, grinning into the
camera.
“Fine,” Oscar sighs after a moment. “Expect my call in twenty minutes.”
“Hey, don’t cut your surf short because of me.”
“Lando,” Oscar sighs, and there’s something almost defeated about it. “Talking to you is kind
of the highlight of my day. You’ve got to have realised that by now.”
And then the line disconnects. Just like that, leaving Lando staring at the screen, at the chat
he had been scrolling through before the call came in, Oscar’s words lingering long after the
connection itself has vanished.
His heartbeat picks up almost immediately. It’s a very Oscar thing to do, actually. To say
something like that and then disappear before Lando has the opportunity to respond; either
mortified by his own honesty, or smug enough to toss the ball into Lando’s court and leave
him standing there with it.
Lando is still sitting perfectly motionless on the sofa, phone loose in his hand, rereading the
last line of their call in his head for perhaps the fifteenth time when–
“Huh.” The voice comes from directly behind him. Lando nearly launches himself through
the ceiling. “Who’s the guy and why is he in love with you?”
It’s Cisca.

His sister is standing in the doorway to the kitchen in her pyjamas and a hoodie, a glass of
water in her hand. Apparently she’d come downstairs to quench some nocturnal thirst and
had been standing there for a while considering her glass is already half empty.
She leans against the frame with a mischievous sparkle in her eyes, as though she knows
exactly how embarrassed he immediately is by whatever she has heard.
“No one,” Lando blurts out at once, before realising that this is perhaps not the strongest
opening defence. “My, uh, Minecraft coach. Strategy meeting. He’s not in love with me.”
“No?” Cisca asks lazily, still propped against the doorway, running a finger around the rim of
her glass. “I mean, I’m not one of the boys. Maybe this is how you lot always talk to each
other behind closed doors when you’re gaming. So tenderly. So affectionately.”
“It was a perfectly mundane conversation.”
She raises an eyebrow. “You’re delusional.”
Pushing herself away from the doorway, she crosses the room and folds herself onto the edge
of the sofa opposite him, their legs touching as she takes another sip from her glass.
“I listened to you for a solid few minutes because apparently you were far too entranced by
your ‘perfectly mundane conversation’ to hear me stomping downstairs, clinking glasses,
turning on the tap or nearly dropping this thing.”
“I swear to God, I didn’t hear shit.”
“Yeah,” Cisca says. “Proving my point.”
“You were eavesdropping.”
“Was not.” She sounds genuinely offended by the allegation and immediately starts trying to
wedge her foot underneath his leg to annoy him. “Trust me, I was actually trying very hard to
make myself known because I was terrified you were about to start purring some smooth shit
into his ear that would’ve made me want to walk directly into a frozen river.”
Lando schools his face into what he hopes is neutrality. “Your fault for jumping to
conclusions.”
“He literally said talking to you is the highlight of his day, Lando.” She snorts as though she
genuinely cannot believe he is attempting this defence. Then she grins. “He sounds hot. Is he
hot?”
“No idea,” Lando says, immediately returning to chewing at his thumbnail.
Cisca furrows her brow and pokes him in the shin with her foot after successfully escaping
the confines of her side of the sofa. “What do you mean no idea? Show me a picture.”
“I ain’t got a picture, dumbass. I don’t know what he looks like.”

She stares at him. “You’re in love with him and you don’t know what he looks like?” A
pause. “Who are you and what have you done to my incredibly shallow brother?”
“I take strong exception to that insinuation.”
“What?” Cisca grins. “The shallowness?”
“That I’m in love with him.” Lando rolls his eyes. “I am fully aware that I’m shallow. But
I’m also an athlete. Supposedly there’s not much in my brain.”
“Yeah,” she says, tilting her head as she studies him. “You massive airhead. You are prosaic
and dumb, but you've never been delusional.” A beat. “Or oblivious.”
Lando worries at his lip. “Okay,” he says. “I’ll indulge you. Why do you think I’m in love
with him?”
Cisca raises her eyebrows. “Well, for one, you’re up at stupid o’clock talking to him in a soft
voice. You’re flushed. And you’ve spent the last ten minutes whining about the fact that you
want to talk to him more.”
“I’m an affectionate person.”
“You are,” she concedes. “But you’re not usually the kind of guy who lets himself get fobbed
off with weirdly charged-up phone calls when he could have the real deal.”
“Yeah, because we’re friends.” Lando clears his throat. “And I cannot be in love with him
because I don’t know what he looks like.”
“Mmh.” Cisca doesn't sound convinced. “You have absolutely no plan?”
“I’ve got a picture of his upper body,” Lando admits after a moment. “Wait.”
He starts scrolling through Discord again before switching to the media tab to find it quicker.
The picture appears on his screen.
Even now, looking at it again, he remembers how disproportionately affected he'd been when
it first arrived.
For a moment he hesitates. He hasn't forwarded it to Max. Something about sending it around
feels like too much of a violation of Oscar's privacy. Showing it to Cisca for a moment feels
different somehow; temporary enough to satisfy his conscience.
So he turns the phone towards her. Cisca leans forward.
He watches her face as she takes it in. “Kinda built,” she says. “Didn't you tell me he was
your Minecraft coach?”
“Yeah.” Lando carefully keeps his voice neutral. “He surfs.”

He turns the phone back around and looks at the picture again. Now that he's seen the
glimpse of Oscar's legs on the surfboard, he finds himself unconsciously fitting more and
more pieces together.
“I've got to be honest,” Cisca says. “It's a good picture, but it's not exactly earth-shattering.”
She points at the phone. “The fact that you're keeping it this close to your heart like a
Victorian widow carrying a photograph in a locket is doing much more for your case than the
picture itself.”
“Fuck you,” Lando says automatically. Mostly because she's his sister, and because she's
annoyingly right.
“I think it's cute,” Cisca yawns, her head slumping against the side of the sofa as she
struggles to keep her eyes open. “I think it humbles you.”
“What humbles me?”
“That he's not an easy nut to crack.” Cisca points vaguely at the phone. “He makes you work
for every single picture, doesn't he?”
“What do you mean?”
She shrugs. “I know exactly what he's doing. I've been on his side of this before.”
Lando groans. “Please don't say that.”
“Talking to someone I had a massive crush on and breadcrumbing myself,” she continues,
entirely undeterred. “Giving them little things. Making them wait. Stretching it out because
the anticipation is half the fun.”
“That is not what's happening here.”
“It absolutely is.”
“He genuinely wants to remain faceless. It's part of his whole thing.”
Cisca laughs. “Oh, Lando.” She reaches over and taps the edge of the phone. “If he genuinely
wanted to remain faceless, he'd never have sent this in the first place. He could very easily
not have done it.” A pause. “But he knows he's hot.”
Lando immediately feels heat crawl up his neck.
She tilts her head. “Please tell me you appropriately freaked out about it.”
“I didn't react at all,” Lando admits after a moment.
“Ugh, oh my God.” Cisca drops her head back dramatically. “You're fucking terrible at this.
You've got to freak out a little. Give him something to work with.”

“If I freaked out about it, I would've freaked him out,” Lando says, feeling that familiar
uneasy sensation return as he realises that Cisca has somehow arrived at almost exactly the
same conclusion as Max. “And he's incredibly jumpy. Every time I brush up against a
boundary, he shuts down.”
“Then you're doing it wrong.” Cisca sounds completely confident. “You've got to compliment
him.”
She gestures at the phone again. “Not privately stare at the pictures he sends you and then
pretend they never happened.” A beat. “I genuinely cannot believe how bad you are at this.”
“What the fuck would you advise me to do then?”
“I genuinely cannot believe that my fuckboy big brother is coming to little old me for
romantic advice.” Cisca laughs.
“Don’t make this harder than it needs to be.”
“Fine,” she sighs. “You start dropping hints.”
“Hints about what?”
“That you want him.”
Lando stares at her. “But I don’t want him.”
“Oh, come on.” She smacks him lightly on the side of the head. “I saw the way you looked at
that photo. And I heard you talking to him. You want that mysterious Australian surfer boy
bad.”
“I am not that kind of guy.”
“What? One to yearn?” Cisca grins. “Right. You’re not.”
She shifts on the sofa, pulling her knees up against her chest. “Because you’ve never actually
had to do it before. Your entire life has basically been engineered to prevent you from
developing that particular character trait.”
“What the fuck does that mean?”
“It means that, while I personally would very much not subscribe to this sort of assessment,
objectively speaking you’re handsome, famous, rich – outright charming when you feel like
it – and you’ve spent most of your adult life existing in environments where people already
know who you are before you’ve even opened your mouth.”
Lando groans. “Oh, come on.”
“No, seriously.” Cisca points at him with her glass. “Yearning requires resistance. It requires
uncertainty. It requires not knowing where you stand. And you’ve simply never had to deal
with any of those things for very long.”

Lando frowns as his sister sizes him up, looking at him with the kind of merciless clarity only
siblings seem capable of mustering.
“But unfortunately for you, fate, or the universe, or whatever cosmic force enjoys making fun
of people, appears to have paired you up with an absurdly secretive Minecraft nerd who is
humbling you on a level I have honestly never witnessed before.”
Lando bites his lip. “But what if I misinterpret things? What if I come on too strong? I have
no reason to believe he isn’t straight – and I’m not necessarily looking to expose myself in
front of someone who hasn’t even told me their last name.”
Cisca squints at him. “I’m absolutely awe-struck. This boy did a number on you. I’ve never
seen you so incredibly unsure about anything before. Usually, Max has to hold you by the
reins so that you don’t make a fool of yourself.”
“It’s a valid concern.”
“It would be,” Cisca agrees. “It absolutely would be, if he weren’t as obsessed with you as
you are with him.”
“You cannot read that into the three minutes of a phone call you heard,” Lando laments. “If
he really were interested in me, then he wouldn’t hide away.”
“Maybe he’s got his reasons,” Cisca says with a shrug. “Maybe he wants to tell you
everything about himself, but there’s something holding him back. If you ask me, the fact that
he sent you that picture – even though he has this strict policy of anonymity – is the part of
him that’s obsessed with you and wants you to see him, fighting against the careful, reserved,
guarded part.”
She tilts her head.
“Most of the time, the latter seems to be winning, marginally. But if that picture is any
indication, then sometimes his need to be seen by you wins.” She puts her hand on his knee.
“And you have to feed that part. Give him an incentive to show more of himself. Not reacting
is the worst thing you could do.”
Of course, she’s making sense. This makes perfect sense. The more she talks, the more a low-
grade panic starts to build in him as he realises that perhaps he has already catastrophically
mishandled the situation; neither really reacting to the jersey photo nor the thumbs-up picture
from earlier today.
Then again, Oscar never reacts to his pictures either. Only subliminally, in ways he probably
doesn’t even know he betrays.
Cisca pats his knee. “It’s going to be fine, Lando. Has there ever been a guy you haven’t
gotten? You’re like the universe’s favourite golden boy.”
“I can’t even win a championship,” he snorts. “And there have been plenty of times I’ve
gotten my heart fucking destroyed.”

“Yeah,” she grins. “Because you keep going for straight guys.”
“Which is a concern here as well.”
“Not really,” she yawns. Before she can add anything, the phone in Lando’s hand starts
ringing again, coming to life with the Discord icon on the screen.
Cisca laughs. “Those weren’t twenty minutes. Never. He immediately went to shore to talk to
you.” He sees her bite her lip. “Oh, Lando. How do you do it?”
He shoos her away. “Go to bed, you annoying gnome.”
She smacks his knee but gets up without protest, shuffling out of the room and throwing him
a kiss from the doorway. He flips her off before accepting Oscar’s call.
It’s only a voice call, sadly enough, but that does at least allow him to sink further into the
sofa, phone resting on his chest exactly the way it usually does.
“That was fast,” Lando says in lieu of a greeting.
He hears Oscar snort. “I speedran the fuck out of those waves.”
“That’s so hot of you,” Lando says, anxiously chewing at his thumbnail as he decides to risk
it and turn up the temperature of their conversation just a little. “I have got to know: do you
speedrun everything in your life? Force of habit?”
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “Who has time for doing things the normal way? I love cutting corners.”
“Me too,” Lando grins. “Unfortunately, in my profession you get track limits called on you
and your lap time deleted.”
He’s pretty sure he can hear voices in the background of Oscar’s call; the waves still crashing
somewhere nearby. 
“Where are you? I can hear people.”
“Still at the beach, you nosy fuck.” Oscar sounds fond, though. “Where, unfortunately, there
sometimes happen to be people. Especially when I’m running late like this. Which is why
I’m getting the fuck out of here. Just trying to peel this sticky suit off me.”
“Not a fan of people?”
“Oh, I love them,” Oscar says dryly. “That’s why I became a Minecraft speedrunner,
actually.”
Lando tries not to think about Oscar peeling himself out of the wetsuit, his surfboard propped
up beside him against some beach shack he imagines there, or maybe a palm tree. Are there
palm trees in Australia?
“Do you ever meet your real-life friends?” Lando asks. “Go to the beach together?”

He tries to picture Oscar around a beach bonfire, sitting on a log in a t-shirt and shorts, a beer
bottle dangling loosely from one hand as he absent-mindedly peels at the label, listening to
friends speaking over one another in absurdly Australian accents.
“No, not really,” Oscar says. “I don’t like going to the beach.”
“You are literally at the beach.”
“Without a valid reason,” he adds. “Which I believe surfing is.”
“Meeting friends is a valid reason as well.” Lando can’t help grinning. “And the beach is
such a romantic spot, too. For dates, I mean.”
He waits anxiously. Oscar merely scoffs. “Is it? Sand’s pretty annoying, no?”
“It’s not about the sand. It’s about the whole... scenery. Feeling small in the scope of how
large and awe-inspiring nature around you is.”
“That’s not very romantic, though, is it? Being plagued by existential thoughts?”
“It’s certainly a bonding moment.”
That makes Oscar snort. “Well, sounds like people have a great time on dates with you.”
Lando bites his lip, his pulse immediately spiking even though Oscar is clearly just bantering
with him. “So what’s your ideal date, then?”
“Don’t know,” Oscar says. “I don’t think I have an answer to that.”
“Well, think of one.”
And it seems like he does, because for almost ten seconds Lando hears nothing except distant
laughter, voices, waves crashing against the shore, the squeak of a surfboard being picked up,
and the faint rustle of fabric.
Then Oscar speaks again. “I thought about it.” A pause. “And I still don’t know.”
Lando groans. “Oh, come on. You’ve got to be able to think of something. What kind of dates
do you go on?”
“Uh,” Oscar says. “Dinner, I guess.”
Lando immediately hates that he asked. Hates that he pushed far enough to get an answer –
 because now he has one. And now he feels sick with it; sick with the thin, sticky threads of
jealousy winding themselves through him.
He crosses his arms over his chest and presses his chin deeper into the pillow beside him.
“Yeah?”

“Not that I’d really know anymore.” There’s a faint thread of embarrassment in Oscar’s
voice. “It’s been a long time since I went on a date.”
“When was your last date?”
“Over a year ago, I think,” Oscar says. “My sister set me up with one of her friends. She was
sick and tired of me playing Minecraft all day. Said I was ruining our family’s aura.”
“The sister who loves dolphins or the sister who picks up packages for you?”
“A different one. The third one.” He laughs fondly. “She’s got a lot of friends.”
“Was it a good date?”
Lando asks the question and immediately dreads the answer, though the fact that the date
happened over a year ago and apparently never led anywhere probably speaks for itself.
“I don’t like those staged date situations,” Oscar says after a moment, and Lando notices the
voices in the background are getting quieter as he moves away from the beach. “I don’t like
how upfront you have to be about your intentions.”
“What do you mean?”
“Everyone knows why you're there.” Oscar sounds faintly pained by the very concept. “You
know, they know, the person who set you up knows, the waiter knows. Everyone knows the
whole point is to eventually crack, and I think that’s incredibly embarrassing.”
Lando genuinely laughs at that. “Well, what do you prefer?”
“Falling in love with your best friend,” Oscar says immediately. Then, after a brief pause:
“Completely organically.”
He sounds remarkably certain about it.
“I think a good relationship needs a foundation that comes from something further removed
from romantic intention. Otherwise it just feels like confirmation bias.”
“What do you mean?”
“I mean if you start seeing someone with the explicit goal of getting with them romantically,
you immediately skew the whole thing.” Oscar pauses. “You start interpreting everything
through that lens. And then, at some point, you don't even know whether you genuinely like
the person or whether you've just convinced yourself that you do.”
Lando hums. “And friendship fixes that?”
“I think so.” Oscar sounds thoughtful now. “If you build a genuine friendship first and
romantic feelings happen afterward, then at least you already know you liked each other
before any of that entered the equation.”

“Interesting theory,” Lando says, worrying at his lip. “But what about overwhelming
attraction?”
“What about it?”
“The kind where you look at someone once and immediately know you're fucked. Would you
really give that up just because you didn't get the chance to be friends first?”
“Well, I don’t know.”
“It’s like that for me,” Lando admits, and he feels the pulse in his throat hammering painfully.
“I fear I’m exactly the kind of person you just described. I date, and I like dating. I don’t care
that it reveals my intentions. I’m not ashamed of them. I like physical intimacy.”
Oscar doesn’t reply immediately, and with every passing second Lando feels more self-
conscious; like he’s revealing himself to be shallow in front of an audience. A one-man
audience, admittedly, but one whose opinion he would kill to know more of.
Now he knows. And he disagrees with it.
“That’s fine,” Oscar says finally, his voice carefully neutral. “I think most people think like
you.”
“Did you ever have a friend you fell in love with?”
“No,” Oscar says, and Lando’s heart feels a little lighter at that. “Maybe my theory is bullshit
anyway. Maybe I have absolutely no idea what I’m talking about.”
He laughs then, and it sounds genuinely self-deprecating. 
“I mean, you’re the world-famous athlete. I’m a Minecraft streamer. I don’t think we should
be putting much weight on my opinions.”
“No, actually,” Lando says quickly. “I like what you say. It seems like you’re very cautious
with your love, and I think that’s admirable.”
“So you’re saying I’m idealistic and real life doesn’t work like that.”
A brief silence stretches between them. Then Lando asks: “Did you ever have a partner?”
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “I had a girlfriend in school. And in uni I dated one of my lab partners
for a while.”
Girlfriend. Well. He’s had a good run, then. Time to return to the real world.
“But I think we were mostly just bored and overwhelmed by how fucking harrowing lab was,
and somehow convinced ourselves that making out behind our advisor’s back would
magically improve the situation.”
“And did it?”

Oscar snorts. “No. Lab was still the worst experience of my life.”
“Chemistry, then?”
“No,” Oscar laughs. “There are other kinds of labs.”
“This excludes mathematics, though.”
“Right,” Oscar says, sounding amused. “I didn’t study maths.”
“But you did a lot of it during your studies, right?”
Lando is almost relieved that the conversation has drifted back to something more mundane;
even though there’s a part of him that still wants to keep probing, to find out more about the
way Oscar loves, dates, navigates all of that romantic shebang.
“A fair amount.”
“Physics, then.”
“I’m not going to tell you.” 
“I would find you if I knew, wouldn’t I?” He grins. “You did leave a trail, Oscar. Did you
not?”
“I will neither confirm nor deny.”
Lando laughs. “Let me guess. You graduated with honours, pulled off something insane
during your degree, and your university’s website still keeps an embarrassing reminder of it
tethered to your name.”
“You’re quite perceptive, Lando Norris.”
“Well,” Lando says, grinning smugly to himself. “I have my moments.”
“I have got to say, that’s what surprised me most.”
“What?” Lando snorts. “You thought I was dumb as balls, didn’t you?”
Oscar laughs, and it’s the softest, darndest sound. Lando wants to punch a wall. “No, not
dumb as balls. I always had the feeling you played it up a little for the cameras. But I didn’t
think you were... well...” He trails off.
“I hear a compliment coming,” Lando teases. “Don’t get shy now. Hand it over, Osc.”
“You’re remarkably easy to talk to,” Oscar says, veering away from whatever he'd originally
intended to say. “In fact, I could talk to you for twenty-four fucking hours a day. And if you
knew me, you’d know how insane that is.”
He breaks off for a moment, and Lando thinks he can hear traffic through the speakers. 

“You’re not known for talking much?”
“I’m not above it. I’m a streamer, after all. But...” He pauses. “I don’t have a lot of
experience actually wanting to talk to someone all the time.” He breaks off again, but this
time Lando lets him find his train of thought on his own. “I said it before. Talking to you is
the highlight of my days. I feel like...”
“We understand each other very well,” Lando finishes for him. “I think so too, Osc.”
And I don’t understand why you don’t want to meet me. Why I first have to prove that I could
pull off a zero cycle before you’d allow me anywhere near you.
“In fact,” Lando says after a moment, “I love talking to you as well.”
He doesn’t even expect Oscar to reply. He knows this has been too much, even if Oscar had
been the first one to brush up against the subject; the fact that they get along so well, to the
point that time seems to speed up whenever they find themselves in the throes of a
conversation with one another.
“You should go to bed,” Oscar says – entirely predictably. He always does this whenever he
feels their conversations becoming a little too self-indulgent. “You don’t want to sleep
through Christmas Day.”
“I’m going to bed soon,” Lando promises. “You still haven’t told me about your Christmas
plans.”
“Yes, I did. Film a video with Fein, and then H is coming over.”
“Who’s H?”
“My sister.” He sighs. “I’ve decided to refer to them by their initials so you don’t get
confused and have to ask which sister I’m talking about every five minutes.”
“So H is the sister with the alternative clothing style?”
“Yes,” Oscar says. “M is the one who’s in Perth with my parents and loves every animal
known to mankind, and E is the one who tried to set me up with her friend once.”
“I see,” Lando grins. “Well, they sound delightful.”
“They aren’t.” Oscar scoffs. “They’re my biggest opps. H keeps telling me to–” He cuts
himself off. “Whatever.”
“What?”
“Nothing,” Oscar says a little too quickly. “Tangerine’s sitting on the steps again and won’t
let me past.”
“Who’s Tangerine?”

“My neighbour’s obese fucking cat. She keeps blocking the only path upstairs, and ever since
the elevator broke, the fuckass beast has become incredibly despotic.”
Lando snorts.
“I’m serious. I genuinely didn’t know cats could be that opportunistic. Her reign of terror
affects us all.”
Lando closes his eyes, trying to transport himself into Oscar’s world. “You live in an
apartment complex near the ocean then?”
Oscar sighs. “Fuck. I gave away too much again.”
“I’m not going to find you from that,” Lando assures him. “Besides, I’m not going to look.
It’s not what you want, and I respect that.”
There’s a brief pause. “Thank you, Lando.”
“Course.”
Absent-mindedly, he chews at the string of his hoodie. For a while they are both silent, and
Lando feels himself sinking deeper into a sort of leaden fatigue that he knows he ought to
remedy by actually going to bed.
“Happy Christmas, Oscar.”
He hears him exhale, faintly amused. “Merry Christmas, Lando.”
“Not yet,” Lando yawns. “Just Christmas Eve for me.”
“Are you at least getting some snow?”
Lando honestly has no idea. He hasn’t looked out of the window in what feels like hours. So
he unfolds himself from the sofa, squeezes past the sprawling branches of the Christmas tree,
and wanders over to the window.
“No,” he says regretfully. “No snow for us.”
“Not here either,” Oscar says.
Lando snorts. “You’re an idiot.” He’s fairly sure he hears purring on the other end of the line. 
“Osc, are you seriously petting the dictatorial cat?” Leaning against the window, he looks out
at the garden, at the silhouettes of bare trees illuminated only faintly by the light spilling from
the house. “You’ve got no backbone.”
“She won’t let me past otherwise,” Oscar insists.
“Oh, come on.” Lando grins. “You can admit you’ve got a soft side.”
“What do you mean?” Oscar sounds faintly offended. “You don’t think I’m generally soft?”

“You’re one of the most reserved people I’ve ever interacted with.”
Silence. “Ouch.”
“What?”
“God.” Oscar laughs, though there’s very little humour in it. “I’m going out on a limb every
time I talk to you. I feel like I’m already pushing against everything I’m used to. I’ve
practically changed my entire communication style for you.”
Lando straightens. “What do you mean?”
“Forget it.” The warmth is gone from his voice. Not entirely, but enough that Lando notices it
immediately – enough that it reminds him of earlier, when he’d offered to set him up with
one of his friends. “I have to go.”
“No, Osc,” Lando says immediately, feeling a genuine pang of panic in his chest. “Don’t be
like that. Tell me how I upset you. Let me make it right.”
Otherwise I’m probably not going to sleep at all.
“You haven’t upset me,” Oscar says after a moment. “You couldn’t.” He breaks off. “I guess I
just...” Another pause. “I guess H is right.”
“About what?”
“Not important.” His voice is soft again – soft enough that relief immediately washes through
Lando. “I’m sorry. It’s a weird day for me.”
“Because it’s Christmas?”
“A combination of a lot of things,” Oscar says. “But I genuinely have to go. I’m covered in
sand and cat hair, and H is coming over in an hour. She already thinks I’m enough of a sorry
sight as it is. No need to give her more ammunition.”
“Okay,” Lando says, absent-mindedly plucking at one of the branches of the Christmas tree
he’s half leaning against by the window.
“I hope you have a great Christmas. Tell H I said hi.”
“I will,” Oscar promises, and Lando is almost certain he’ll do no such thing. “You go to
sleep.”
“I will,” Lando promises too.
For a moment, neither of them speaks, and Lando can sense the silence between them
growing thicker and thicker, pregnant with all the things neither of them seems capable of
saying.

For a moment, he closes his eyes, and he feels it. The strangely grating feeling in his chest;
the realisation that this isn’t just friendship anymore.
This is yearning, exactly as Cisca prophesied; something Lando genuinely has never
experienced before in his life.
It feels like a slow unraveling, like a part of himself dissolving like an ice cube in water much
too warm for it; wearing away at his essence, until he feels as though he is slowly withering
from the inside out.
He hates it. Lando isn’t supposed to feel this way.
He’s supposed to come, see and conquer.
He’s supposed to spot a silhouette through the haze of bodies and lock onto it with purpose.
He’s meant to feel the warmth of skin against his own skin, to allow himself to dissolve in the
arms of another, to come apart, to be taken apart.
He isn’t supposed to feel like this. So far removed from his nature; to have the whole thing
turned back on him.
To find himself standing wedged between a Christmas tree and a window because an
Australian halfway across the world asked whether it was snowing outside.
He isn’t supposed to feel the unwelcome maelstrom of want churning inside him when want,
in Lando Norris’ world, has always come with immediate relief.
Desire and release are a dyad for him, and they are not supposed to be separated from one
another. They are not supposed to haunt him with longing without offering any possibility of
alleviation. He isn’t supposed to feel this way for someone whose face he doesn’t even know.
Because usually, for Lando, the face comes first.
He knows the silence is becoming too long. He knows that if there is one thing even more
charged than flirting, it is the moment when the flirting fails.
When there are no words left. And Lando wonders if Oscar feels it too.
“Sleep well,” Oscar says after almost a minute in which neither of them has spoken. It’s a
lifeline he throws between them. “Next time we talk will be during the pre-game briefing on
tournament day one.”
Lando feels the familiar pang of nerves low in his gut. “Talk to you then,” he replies as
neutrally as possible. “Can’t wait.”


III. 
 

Lando hasn’t gone live yet, but he’s already sitting in front of his PC, cross-legged on his
chair, munching on a dry granola bar while he watches the official Midoffs stream.
On screen, Tubbo is conducting quick interviews with the coaches, inquiring about their
experiences with their protégés over the past two weeks as they made it their utmost priority
to turn them into passable speedrunners.
Right now it’s Couriway’s turn, and he’s talking about Max, speaking positively about the
amount of effort he put into training.
“He’s taken a giant leap in these two weeks,” Couri says. “He shows up when he needs to,
and he hasn’t shown nerves once. You can really tell he comes from competitive karting by
the way he stays calm under pressure.”
On his desk, Lando’s phone lights up.  He sets down his granola bar and picks it up. It’s Max.

 
Max
he’s so kind to me here but i’m telling u that man did not let me breathe these past few
weeks

 
Lando snorts as he types up a reply.
 

Lando
hey, i mean he got u to a sub-15

 
Something Lando still hasn’t managed himself. He’s consistent, yes – but he’s desperately
missing that one personal-best run that would give him the feeling that he’s actually ready to
enter a tournament full of people who have spent years developing an almost intuitive
understanding of the game.
He’s a fish out of water. He knows it. 
On screen, Tubbo wraps up the interview with Couriway and moves on to Oscar. Lando
immediately feels a strange tension pool low in his stomach as the collective attention shifts
towards him.
“OP,” Tubbo says, a grin tugging at the corners of his mouth. “You have unwittingly
bestowed the tournament’s favourite storyline upon us when you caused a major upset during
the draft and wagered a frankly obscene amount of points on Lando Norris.” Lando watches
him lean forward in his chair, propping his chin on his hands. “I guess what we all want to

know is whether that gamble paid off. Did you make a speedrunner out of Formula One
runner-up Lando Norris?”
Oscar laughs softly, his Discord icon lighting up. “Well, I know some of my fellow coaches
have publicly and privately expressed their… concern regarding my large investment early
on, but Lando has surpassed even my greatest expectations.”
“Is that so?” Tubbo raises both eyebrows. “How?”
“Well, for starters, he’s extremely coachable. During the early stages of training, I was
worried he might not listen to me, because he is, in every sense of the word, one of the most
impressive athletes out there.”
Lando feels himself grin despite himself.
“He should have been World Champion this year if it hadn’t been for a technical
disagreement with his teammate, so I was briefly concerned that he simply wouldn’t take on
my coaching – just by circumstance of being incredibly impressive at everything he does.”
“But he did, right?”
“Yes. Very much so,” Oscar says, and Lando can hear the smile in his voice. “And he’s
genuinely been a joy to coach as well. He’s dexterous, a quick learner, and he’s got the
stamina to work through snags when they arise. He takes criticism very well and gives great
feedback, which I think comes from his day job and the fact that he’s in constant
communication with his engineers.”
Lando’s phone lights up again. Without taking his eyes off the screen – or wiping the frankly
ridiculous smile off his face – he picks it up.
 

Max
wow. that’s a LOT of praise from one OP81

 
Lando
what can i say… I taught him well

 
On stream, Tubbo grins just as broadly. “As you probably know by now, we’ve just closed
the poll on the viewers’ favourite coach-mentee duos, and you and Lando absolutely smashed
the competition with, I think, almost forty percent of all votes.” He shakes his head in mock
disbelief. “It seems the training streams have revealed to your collective audiences that you
two get along very well. What would you say to that?”

There’s a brief pause. Then Oscar says, “I’d agree with them. Of course, I’ve always been a
fan of him, so there’s no surprise on my end – but he’s handled being forced to spend an
alarming amount of time with an annoying fanboy remarkably well.”
Tubbo laughs. “I’d say more than well. You’ve become friends, it seems. At least if we look
at your respective social media accounts, where you two have been shouting each other out
quite a bit over the past few weeks.”
Oscar laughs too – one of those soft, almost embarrassed laughs that Lando loves so much.
“Yeah.”
“Do you think you’ll stay in touch after the tournament?” Tubbo asks. “Considering he leads
a very busy life and will soon have to start preparing for the new season, which kicks off in
March, while you’ve got the MCSR Ranked playoffs coming up.”
Lando bites his lip and leans forward slightly, unwilling to miss a single word of the reply.
“I should hope so,” Oscar finally says.
Tubbo immediately pounces. “And the question we’ve all been asking: will you meet in real
life? Considering the first stop of the new Formula One season is Australia – which just so
happens to be where you live.”
Immediately, Lando’s pulse jumps. He starts worrying at his lip, feeling his brow crease as he
waits for the answer he wants.
“Let’s see about that,” Oscar says, neatly sidestepping the question. The familiar
disappointment settles in Lando’s chest almost immediately. 
“If you do, please let us know,” Tubbo says, clearly recognising Oscar’s unwillingness to
elaborate. “I don’t think there’s a single person watching today who isn’t deeply invested in
this unexpected partnership.”
He grins. 
“After all, you kind of live the dream. Befriending your childhood hero. I think we could all
use some of that energy in our lives.”
After that, Tubbo moves on to Lily, asking Oscar how coaching her has been for him, and
almost immediately, some of the euphoria drains out of Lando.
He listens as Oscar is just as fair and kind to Lily as he was to him, praising her consistency,
her intuitive understanding of the game, and her ability to recognise risks that simply aren’t
worth taking.
Lando knows that last part is directed at him: their biggest coaching disagreement, by far, has
always been the fact that Lando insists on risking perfectly salvageable runs for manoeuvres
that are objectively risky. Things like attempting a zero cycle when a one-cycle would do, or
scaling alongside a wall with awkward parkour when he could simply pillar up, lose a few
seconds, and look considerably less impressive while doing it.

He knows it’s entirely asinine. Oscar coaches both of them, and praise for Lando does not
diminish simply because Oscar extends it to Lily as well. And yet there is a part of him – a
jealous, ugly, insecure part – that wants Oscar to gloss over her achievements and talents
simply because Lando cannot stand hearing him heap praise onto someone else.
Maybe because, foolishly enough, Lando has started to think of this as their achievement: the
praise and encouragement. The reassurance. As though it belongs to the strange little
ecosystem the two of them have built over the past weeks.
As though it had been Lando slowly teaching Oscar that compliments don’t have to be
rationed out like emergency supplies; that praise can simply be given when someone has
done something well.
And now Oscar has thawed generally. Now he finds kind words for Lily, too.
No, Lando thinks selfishly. They should all belong to me.
His thoughts drift back to their call on Christmas, to the moment Oscar had sounded almost
desperate when he'd admitted between gritted teeth that he'd changed his entire
communication style for him, only to be met with Lando calling him reserved.
He understands now why it hurt, and he feels genuinely awful about it.
Oscar has changed. Lando can see that now. And maybe he’s giving himself too much credit,
but he cannot shake the feeling that he has something to do with it.
It seems as though Oscar is constantly unhinging his own boundaries for him; sending him
pictures, divulging details about himself he’s never told anyone else, reshaping the way he
communicates so that it fits more naturally against Lando's.
And all Lando does is ask for more. He barely reacts to the pictures. He keeps pushing to
meet. He keeps reaching for the next thing, and the next thing after that, without ever
properly stopping to acknowledge how much Oscar has already given him.
Maybe Oscar sees that too. Maybe that’s why he keeps dodging every conversation about
meeting in person: because from his perspective, Lando’s wants are endless.
First he wants the name. Then the face. Then to meet him in real life. And after that? 
Lando feels vaguely sick.
Maybe Oscar genuinely believes that the moment Lando finally solves the mystery of him,
finally manages to crack open the secretive Minecraft speedrunner who briefly brushed
against his life, the fascination will evaporate. That he’ll lose interest, move on and discard
him.
Lando doesn’t know how to tell him that this couldn’t be further from the truth.
Tubbo wraps up his interview with Oscar after that, and Lando sits there for a moment,
feeling strangely vulnerable and raw.

He doesn’t know how to tell Oscar this – that he wants to meet him not because he wants to
be the one who shatters his final boundary, who takes and takes, selfishly and ravenously; not
because he sees the life Oscar has built for himself as an enigma to solve, but because he has
never had a conversation that has excavated him so deeply and thoroughly, and he simply has
to know the person behind it.
Lando knows he’s pushy, and clingy, and that even his best friend occasionally gets tired of
him; of the way he is – just a little too much, a little too intense.
And yet Oscar has never made him feel that way. Not once.
Instead, he has always met him exactly where he is; calls him, texts him, answers him, and
only ever ends their conversations out of genuine concern for Lando's wellbeing, because he
thinks he ought to sleep, or eat, or do something other than spend another hour talking to him.
He’s met the person he’s been looking for all along, Lando realises. The person whose face
he has been searching for in every room he walks into.
The person he has been trying to find in every conversation that left him strangely
dissatisfied afterward, hungrier than before for a kind of understanding and intimacy he had
never known, but had always suspected himself capable of feeling one day.
He has been anticipating him. 
Maybe that is why his personality has become unbearable for everyone who isn’t Oscar.
Because Oscar is the first person who seems to understand exactly what to do with all of it.
All of him.
But Oscar is never going to agree to meet him. And worse than that, Lando suspects he is
never going to tell him why.
He can feel the disappointment – the grief of it, almost – burning behind his eyes, and he
knows this is perhaps the worst possible moment to be having revelations of this magnitude.
So he does what he always does when Oscar occupies too much of his head.
He reaches for his phone. His thumb hovers over their Discord chat for a moment.
For a moment he thinks about what to send him, then settles for superficial banter when all he
really wants is to turn himself inside out and send the whole thing over to Oscar, lay it at his
feet and let him sort through it.

before my first match

 

Of course Oscar replies immediately. For a moment, Lando closes his eyes and tries to
separate himself from the maelstrom in his chest that has him running so hot he has to tug
open the collar of his shirt.

For a moment longer, he sees the typing indicator appear underneath Oscar’s last message.
Then it disappears again. No follow-up.
Lando leans back in his chair. He should probably start his own stream soon so that he can
live-react to the first few matches before it becomes his turn to play against someone he
knows almost nothing about beyond the fact that she is almost certainly going to destroy him.
His first opponent is an American content creator called Jojosolos. According to the cursory
amount of research he conducted while vetting the other participants, she is exceptionally
good at the game.
Lando has already made peace with the possibility that this tournament might be a very short
experience for him. Or at least he is trying to – trying to prepare himself for the very real
possibility that he spent two weeks training only to get knocked out in the first round.
Jojo’s personal best sits comfortably below fourteen minutes. Lando’s best run is still above
twenty-two.
Realistically, she would have to die three separate times for him to have a chance of catching
up.
And she is coached by Feinberg – Oscar’s best friend and a deeply sarcastic man with a
bizarre sense of humour who intimidates Lando far more than he would ever willingly admit.
Fein has spent the last two weeks relentlessly making fun of him in a manner Oscar insists is
friendly.

Lando remains unconvinced. If he crashes out in the first round, then Fein will be right, and
Oscar will have to endure the consequences of having believed in him.
Max’s first opponent is considerably easier to beat – a massive content creator who is even
worse at the game than Max was two weeks ago and who has spent the last fortnight running
an event of his own, meaning he barely found any time to train at all.
Max is almost certainly making it through to round two. He deserves it, Lando decides.
All things considered, Max has been every bit as invested in this stupid block game as he has,
and he has trained tirelessly over the past two weeks in a way that undoubtedly showcases his
best friend’s ability to achieve whatever he sets his mind to.
Lando is going to root for him, too, once he inevitably crashes out of the tournament and is
forced to watch the rest of it from the sidelines.
Lily is up first, and she’s facing someone she apparently already knows from one of the
servers they both play on. According to the endless discussions on Twitter, it’s going to be a
battle for the ages.
Lando cannot wait to watch it – to see how Oscar coaches her through it, even if he’s going to
be malding the entire time.
The tournament is double elimination, which means that if he loses his first match, he’ll drop
into the lower bracket and be given another chance to redeem himself. Lose the first round,
and he plays again today. Win it, and he only has to survive a single game.
His own match is the final game of the upper bracket today, while Max is second-to-last, so
the two of them will stream together and watch the earlier rounds before Max eventually has
to leave for his own run.
Not even five minutes after going live – and with the first match still a few minutes away –
 Lando has already shattered his all-time viewer record.
He knows why. A mainstream outlet published an article about the tournament this morning,
focusing heavily on the fact that an active Formula One driver is participating, and Lando
assumes a sizeable chunk of casual viewers have tuned in purely to witness him attempt to
speedrun.
George certainly seems to be very invested in this, because Lando had woken up to a
message from him that morning – with a link to the article, and then: Going through a
quarter-life crisis? I wish you all the best though, mate. Just pretend your opponent is
Verstappen.
The message had made him laugh. Mostly because George and he are probably the only
people on the grid who genuinely cannot stand Max Verstappen – or, at the very least, have
an exceedingly complicated relationship with him.

Chat trickles in as usual, though it moves considerably faster now that so many new viewers
have tuned in to see what exactly Lando Norris gets up to during the off-season.

It is strange – and strangely endearing – to see Oscar’s viewers in his chat. To see that they
seem to have adopted him almost as enthusiastically as his own audience has embraced
Oscar.

It truly feels as though the two communities have grown together over the course of the past
few weeks and Lando is probably going to find traces of Oscar’s fans among his own for the
rest of his career.
The strange mood that has lingered ever since his epiphany about Oscar eases a little once
Max finally joins the call. As always, the presence of his best friend does exactly what it is
supposed to do: it clears his head, blows away some of the gloom and replaces it with the
familiar buzz of excitement for whatever ridiculous thing they are about to do together.
“Chat,” Max asks, “who’s making it farther? Lando or me?”
Their audience appears split almost directly down the middle. There are genuinely people in
chat claiming that Lando is going to “win this ez”, and while he appreciates the enthusiasm,
he is mildly concerned about their ability to accurately assess reality. 
If they think he can win this thing, perhaps they are generally somewhat delusional. And
perhaps he is actually much, much further away from a championship than his droves of
supporters have led him to believe.
At the same time, there are plenty of people reminding him that while his improvement over
the last two weeks has been genuinely astonishing – and while it is still surreal that he can
now speedrun this game after barely being able to kill a sheep a fortnight ago – he simply is
not fast enough to make a deep run.
“How are your nerves?” Max asks him, and Lando snorts.
“Mate, I’m an F1 driver. I can handle this.”
Of course, that’s objectively true. This tournament doesn’t matter in the grand scheme of his
life; the only reason he’s here is to raise money for charity, which is steadily ticking upward
in the background, and to have a little fun. This is not his day job, not his legacy, not the
thing he has spent his entire life pursuing – and still, he feels a sort of anxiety at the idea of
dropping out on the first day that he can’t quite rationalise.
He knows it’s because of Oscar.
He knows that even though Oscar would never judge him for it, would never be disappointed
in him – as he has already assured Lando approximately half a billion times – he still doesn’t
want to fail. 
He doesn’t want all of this training Oscar has poured into him to go to waste. And more than
that, he knows that the second he drops out of the tournament, there is no longer any practical
reason for the two of them to keep up their calls.
And he’s terrified of that.
Terrified of losing a reason – or at the very least an excuse – to keep talking to him. 
Terrified that their relationship will simply run its course, and that all he’ll see of Oscar from
then on is the pink halo around his Instagram profile picture whenever he posts one of his

rare stories; a familiar fixture sitting at the top of his feed.
He can practically feel Max sizing him up – especially once Lily’s match finally begins and
she loads into her race against her friend.
Lily strongly dislikes shipwrecks, so she vetoes them immediately, while her opponent,
Hannah Rose, vetoes desert temple. They end up starting on ruined portal.
The stream Lando and Max are watching together is the official broadcast, where Tubbo and
another creator are doing commentary, but Lando finds himself much more interested in
Oscar’s stream. Eventually he switches over to his audio entirely so he can listen to him
coach Lily through the run.
She’s doing great.
For some reason she’s wearing a cosplay Lando doesn’t recognise – a consequence of some
subgoal, apparently – and despite the wig constantly falling into her eyes, she is astonishingly
locked in. She clears the overworld in barely three minutes, while Hannah gets stuck looking
for a way to light her portal after failing to find flint and steel.
Lando worries at his lip as he listens to Oscar’s voice. He is calm and careful, giving Lily as
much room as she needs, but reeling her back in whenever she becomes momentarily
uncertain about what to do next – or whenever she’s genuinely on the verge of throwing the
run.
“You’re doing great, Lily,” he tells her after she lets out a high-pitched scream when an
unexpected Hoglin barrels towards her and nearly knocks her off the path. “Don’t worry
about it. Hannah’s way behind.”
“Please don’t be lava housing, please, please, please,” she pleads as she makes her way to the
bastion.
“It’s not going to be,” Oscar assures her. “They wouldn’t pull that for the tournament.”
And he’s right – she gets a perfectly nice treasure bastion, and her trades are so good that
she’s done in three minutes; while she has already prepared a pearl hang to return to the Blaze
spawner and collect her rods.
“Can’t believe she can pearl hang,” Max comments in his other ear. “I never got the hang of
it. Haha, get it?”
“It’s not that hard, Osc taught me too,” Lando says absent-mindedly.
He doesn’t catch it. Not immediately. Not until chat suddenly accelerates beside him and
Max goes very still on camera, staring at him as though he’s just watched him step in front of
a moving train.
Fuck, Lando thinks. Oh, fuck.

certainty that he is entirely undeserving of Oscar’s friendship; undeserving of the trust he has
placed in him over these past weeks, of every little concession he has made, every boundary

clipping it, already posting it, already connecting dots that were never theirs to connect in the
first place.
