Lando stays out there for another minute, scrolling through Twitter while the panic settles
lower and lower in his stomach, curdling slowly into a kind of self-loathing so sharp and
overwhelming that it makes him nauseous.
But he can’t hide in the hallway forever. His thumb hovers over Oscar’s Discord chat. Does
he try to warn him? Give him a heads-up? But how would he even begin to phrase it?
There is no Discord message in the world that adequately communicates I am so sorry I
could crawl out of my own skin.
At this point, he feels like he ought to throw himself at Oscar’s feet and beg for forgiveness.
And yet the thought of meeting him on stream in an hour – of hearing his voice in his
headphones while knowing Oscar has already seen the clips, already knows what happened –
 fills him with equal dread.
Eventually, he returns to his streaming room and schools his face into something resembling
neutrality: Lily has reached the stronghold by now, locating it with ease, Oscar’s voice low
and reassuring in her ear.
“God, OP, I wouldn’t know what to do without you,” she says, laughing shakily as she portals
directly into the stronghold and uses the pie chart to locate the portal room. “You are the best
coach of all time. You’ve made an excellent player out of me. And of Lando, too. You should
be doing this more.”
Oscar laughs softly. Lando feels something inside him shrivel up.
“That’s kind of you, Lily,” Oscar says. “But we’re not out of the woods yet.”
That’s true. But she wins anyway. 
She advances to the next round and secures her place on day two, while Lando sits at his desk
and obsessively scrolls Twitter, all the while half-convinced that at any moment a new
message from Oscar is going to appear on his screen and tear him to shreds.
He texts one of his mods on Discord to ban the words Oscar and Osc, so that at the very least
newcomers don’t immediately stumble across what happened the second they enter chat –
which feels like the absolute bare minimum of damage control.
Now that he knows Oscar is off duty, having successfully coached his first pick through the
day, he waits anxiously for a message. He has got to have seen it by now. 
Nothing comes, though.
Lando knows he should be the one to send a message, knows that he ought to pick up his
phone and own up to it before Oscar has to hear about it from someone else, but he genuinely
cannot bring himself to do it; cannot bring himself to type out an apology and press send
when he is so overwhelmingly afraid of the reply that might come back.

Because what if it confirms everything he’s been terrified of all morning? What if this is it?
What if Oscar never forgives him for this?
So he spends the next hour in a state of low-level agony, replying to chat messages whenever
the buzz in his head grows too loud, while Max does the lion’s share of the crowd work as he
usually does. Lando loves him for it.
Then, eventually, Max has to leave as well to prepare for his own match, to talk to Couriway
one last time before he goes live, and Lando is left alone with his thoughts again.
Which is a terrible place to be. He scrolls Twitter once more, chewing relentlessly at his lip.
People are still talking about it – especially the corner of the audience where Oscar’s and his
fanbases have fused together over the course of the tournament.
The reactions seem to oscillate between sympathy and delight. Some feel sorry for him,
realising that he clearly never intended to say Oscar’s name out loud in front of ninety
thousand people.
Others seem almost giddy about it, as though this accidental slip-up somehow confirms what
they have been saying for weeks – that whatever exists between Lando and Oscar on stream
is real, and that they genuinely do mean more to one another than either of them is willing to
admit.
The clips are already everywhere. Lando sees himself in them too: slouched in his chair,
hands on his head, watching Lily’s stream through hooded eyes; the treacherous syllable
slipping past his defences before he can stop it.
The immediate freeze afterward, the way all the colour drains from his face. The dawning
horror.
It’s strange, watching himself realise in real time exactly how badly he has fucked up.
He can barely focus on Max’s game; but he makes it through as well. By the skin of his teeth
his best friend scrapes by with a beautiful one-cycle, getting an early perch almost the second
he makes it to the End.
Lando is euphoric for him – though even that can’t quite break through the dread settled low
in his stomach.
Because now it’s his turn, and he logs into the MCSR Ranked server and joins the live
Discord channel with Oscar.
“Hi,” he says, seeing that Oscar’s name is already sitting there.
“Hello,” Oscar replies, his voice perfectly neutral. “Any last-minute questions? Pointers?”
Lando frowns. Has he not seen it yet? That can’t be possible. His chat is full of it. Twitter is
full of it. Half the internet seems to be discussing it.

“No,” Lando says. “I just hope I don’t get village.”
“Oh, you’re good at village,” Oscar says, sounding as warm as ever. “Don’t worry about it.”
A minute later he’s dropped into the game. Jojo vetoed shipwreck, which leaves them with
desert temple – and Lando has trained that route more than any other.
Well. That’s the first thing that has gone to plan today.
He can only thank years of Formula One for the fact that he is capable of locking in so
completely even while everything inside his head is churning.
His fingers work flawlessly and he doesn’t misclick, not even once. He flies through the
temple, triggers the explosion, finds the lava pool in under a minute.
He hears Oscar suck in a breath. Lando has never – not once – been this fast through the
overworld. He clears the split in under two minutes.
“You’re flying through this, Lando,” Oscar says. “You’re doing so well I’m starting to feel
redundant. I should just log off.”
Lando laughs shakily. “No, please. I need you. Just in case. If I get lava housing.”
“You don’t have to be afraid of that,” Oscar reassures him.
Lando spots the bastion. Treasure – and at one end sits a huge lump of gold.
He pillars up immediately, creating himself a little safe zone where he can mine uninterrupted
while the piglins glare at him helplessly from below. Honestly, he’s a little surprised by how
quickly everything is coming together.
The RNG is incredible. Within minutes the piglins in his trading hole have dropped almost
two stacks of pearls, and before long he’s already moving on to the fortress and collecting
blaze rods with a precision that surprises even him.
“I don’t even want to say anything,” Oscar admits in his ear. “You absolutely do not need any
help. At this point I’m more worried about interrupting your steely focus. I think we’re
seeing Formula One Lando right now.”
Lando laughs. “Yeah,” he says. “And you’re my race engineer.”
He crafts his Eyes of Ender, builds a portal back to the Overworld and throws his pearl. He
doesn’t fuck up the jump either, and when he looks over to the side-view, he sees Jojo’s
position: she’s still in the Bastion, collecting Blaze rods.
Oscar immediately confirms it. “You’re ahead. No need for heroics.”
“Wasn’t planning on any.”
“Don’t try to zero cycle,” he warns him. “You have more than enough time for a one-cycle.”

“Yes,” Lando reassures him, as he locates the stronghold. Oscar affirms that he’s right as
well, before he jumps back into the Nether to travel to the correct coordinates in the
Overworld – and lo and behold, he lands almost directly on top of it, finding the portal room
just down the staircase and past the library.
It’s a two-eye again. He’s really lucky today, it seems. He enters the End at under seventeen
minutes.
This will be a personal best. Easily.
Especially as he sees Jojo only beginning to search for the Stronghold the moment he is
already standing beneath the obsidian pillars. He doesn’t need to force anything here. Doesn’t
need to attempt any dangerous heroics in an effort to claw back time. He’s genuinely on track
to make it out of day one and into round two.
The dragon perches barely a minute into his End split. Lando shoots the crystals atop the
pillars to accelerate the cycle and then manages a clean one-cycle, not fumbling a single bed
placement, all of them pre-crafted while he waited for her perch.
“Wow,” Oscar says as the dragon’s death animation blooms across the sky above him and the
End fountain transforms into the portal.
Lando hears something in his voice that he hasn’t heard very often before. Awe. “You’re
incredible.”

Lando leans back in his chair and feels all the tension leave him at once, exactly the same

The smile falters almost immediately afterwards. It’s impossible not to think about it now.
The slip-up, the name. The look on Max’s face. The panic.
It doesn’t help that Oscar leaves the voice channel shortly afterwards, offering one last

moment before he drops back into the one with Max, who immediately begins to glaze him

Lando sits there and takes the praise. Lets chat celebrate him. Lets Max tell him how

Oscar is simply too kind a person to ever sabotage him over something like this. Too kind to
withhold praise, too kind to leave him hanging during the most important run of the

Since he’s been the last match, and only the losers today will have to play a second one,
Lando decides to end stream after half an hour of idly interacting with chat, sending a raid

As soon as he’s turned off OBS and closed Minecraft, he just sits there, unmoving in the
sudden darkness of his room, staring at his PC background.
After a minute spent trying to gather his courage, he finally dares to do it. He switches back
to Discord and types a message into his chat with Oscar.

Lando’s fingers shake as he taps the call icon next to Oscar’s name. He immediately
abandons the kitchen again and retreats to his bedroom, closing the door behind him without
really knowing why.
“Hi,” Lando says the second he hears Oscar pick up.
“Hi,” Oscar replies.
Lando sits down on the edge of his bed, propping his forehead against one hand braced on his
knee, his phone clutched in the other.

“Oscar,” Lando breathes. “I’m so, so fucking sorry. You have no idea how much I hate
myself for this. I was so careless. You trusted me with this, you were worried this was going
to happen, and I assured you it wouldn’t. And it still did. One moment of negligence and I’ve
managed to fuck up the one thing you’ve been trying so hard to keep intact. I don’t know how
to ever put this right again. I can completely understand if–”
“It’s fine, Lando,” Oscar says, and his voice genuinely sounds soft. “I’m not mad at you.”
Lando breaks off. “What?” he asks. “Are you fucking with me?”
“No,” Oscar laughs. “I’m not fucking with you. I’m not mad at you.”
“But I–”
“Said my name on stream,” Oscar says. “Yes, you did.” Lando hears him breathe out slowly.
“But you didn’t do it on purpose. It slipped out.”
“But that’s exactly what you’ve been afraid of,” Lando says. “That’s why you held it back
from me for so long. You only told me because I promised it wouldn’t happen.”
“Lando,” Oscar says. “The second I told you my name, I was prepared for this exact
outcome. I wouldn’t have told you otherwise.”
Somehow, that feels even worse. “So you knew I’d fuck up.”
“It was inevitable,” Oscar says. “I broke containment on... everything about me the second I
let you in, even a little. I knew that.”
“But this just means–”
“I wanted you to know,” Oscar says after a moment.
Lando can’t help but sink back against his mattress, lowering himself into his rumpled sheets
as he presses his fingers against his eyes, trying to push back against the pressure building
behind them. 
“I wanted you to know more than I was scared of it getting out.”
“Why?”
Oscar is silent for a moment.
“I don’t know,” he says. “I wanted to be known by you under my real name.”
“But you won’t show me your face.” Lando swallows. “You want to be known by me, but
you also don’t.”
“Lando.” Oscar sighs. “This is not the moment.”
“I’m sorry,” he says quickly. “I am so, so sorry.”

“Stop apologising.” Lando can hear the smile in his voice. And somehow, that is what pushes
him over the edge. “I am not mad at you.”
“Why not?” Lando asks. “Why are you so kind to me? Why are you so patient and sweet and
understanding? Why do you care so much about me?”
He feels it then – the fact that he can’t hold it back any longer, the tears springing to his eyes
and wetting the side of his face. 
God, he’s fucking pathetic. He’s lying in the darkness of his own messy room, twenty-six
years old, and he’s crying. Why the fuck is he crying?
“Well,” Oscar says quietly, “why are you attentive and inquisitive and warm and funny and
effervescent?”
Lando closes his eyes in a last-ditch effort to keep the tears at bay.
“Why are you a Formula One driver I spent the better part of a decade idolising, and yet you
call me, listen to me, ask about me? Why do you know my routine? Why can you tell from
my voice when I’ve pulled an all-nighter? Why do you ask about my sisters, or the fucking
cat that lives in my building?” His voice softens. “Why do you remember everything?”
“Because I care about you, Osc. Because you’re my friend.”
“Right,” Oscar says, as though he’s just guided Lando toward the obvious conclusion. “And
you’re my friend.”
Lando bunches the fabric of his sheets between his fingers and pulls it over his face to hide
the treacherous tears. It shouldn’t hurt like this – hearing himself called a friend leaves
behind an ache he cannot put into words.
“So you forgive me?”
“There’s nothing to forgive, Lando,” Oscar replies. “It was an honest mistake.”
“But now they know.”
“Now they know,” he confirms. “And I can finally stop being known by two letters. People
can call me Oscar.” He pauses. “That does feel a little bit like a win, actually.”
Lando presses his sheets against his face.
“Especially,” Oscar continues, “because I’ve realised I don’t fully mind. Maybe I’ve just
become addicted to the way you call me Oscar, and I’m okay with the rest of the world
following suit.”
Lando worries at his lip. “You have no idea how happy I am to hear that.”
Are his boundaries loosening? Is this the first glimpse Lando gets of that great, gradual
thawing; of Oscar slowly reconsidering the arm’s length at which he keeps him?

For a moment neither of them says anything. Then: “I was really, really impressed with you
today, Lando.”
Heat immediately rushes into his face. “Oh, come on.”
“No, genuinely. You played exceptionally.” Oscar laughs softly. “Fein called me afterwards
and asked if I’d secretly been training you off-stream, or if you’d always been this good and
I’d known it when I drafted you. I think he was genuinely annoyed. He thought Jojo was
going to beat your ass. Now she has to play a second match.”
“No, I really just had a good coach.”
“This is not my achievement,” Oscar disagrees. “Though I’ll admit I had a bit of a head start
when it came to recruiting you. I’d been a fan of yours for such a long time. I already knew
how good you are at everything you do. How uniquely talented you are at pushing yourself
right to the limit, whether that’s in a fucking race car or while playing a block game.”
“Seriously, stop.”
“Wow.” Oscar laughs. “Lando Norris refusing a compliment?”
It is unusual, Lando has to admit that himself. But maybe it is because it feels genuinely
sincere, and because it connects to something much larger than a momentary appraisal of his
performance. It connects to the thread between them, to the decade Oscar spent watching him
from afar, learning him in fragments, collecting impressions and memories, while Lando had
no idea he existed at all.
“The ease with which you pay it makes me choke on it,” Lando says, in an attempt at banter.
Oscar laughs. “Trust me, it’s anything but easy.”
“Then thank you,” Lando says. “I hope I can continue to make you proud.”
For a moment, the line between them falls quiet, the two of them sitting in front of their
respective devices, neither quite sure how to continue from there.
“You should go to sleep,” Oscar says after a moment. “I know you’re tired and you need to
conserve your energy for tomorrow.”
“I will, soon.” Lando pushes himself upright. “But I don’t want to hang up yet.”
“Me neither,” Oscar admits, and the way he says it – almost grudgingly – makes something
deeply triumphant coil low in Lando’s stomach.
He gets up from his bed and wanders down the hall to the bathroom, where he begins
washing his face.
“Have you checked Twitter?”
“What about it?”

“Apart from, uh, name-gate, people are incredibly endeared by the fact that I call you Osc.”
Oscar laughs. “Yeah, well. I am too.” He pauses for a moment. “I think my fans are
incredibly surprised by the fact that you seem to like me so much. They genuinely believed
me to be some parasocial loser who manipulated the game to get close to his hero.”
Lando snorts, squeezing some cleanser onto his wet fingers, his phone propped up against the
mirror above the sink. He can’t shake how incredibly domestic it feels, almost as though
Oscar is sitting on the edge of the bathtub behind him, watching him go through his evening
routine.
“Well,” Lando says, rubbing the cleanser into his skin. “You kinda are.”
“Then I’m the luckiest parasocial loser of all time, because for some reason my idol loves
talking to me.”
“Yeah,” Lando grins. “Unfortunately, you are kind of the most interesting person I’ve ever
met.”
Oscar snorts. “I don’t believe that. More interesting than, say, Lewis Hamilton?”
“Most definitely,” Lando replies, already half-covered in cleanser. “He’s far too old to be
interesting to me. The only thing that intrigues me is his relationship with his former
teammate Nico Rosberg.”
“Oh, yeah.” Oscar snorts. “Do you actually have any insight into that? What happened
between them? That’s something I’ve wondered about for ages.”
“It was before my time, unfortunately,” Lando says regretfully. “But if you ask me, there
were some feelings there. There’s no way it turns that bitter otherwise.”
“You think so?” Oscar sounds genuinely surprised.
“Yeah.” Lando takes a fresh towel from the pile in his cabinet and wets it under the warm
water. “They still can’t look at one another. Nico works for Sky now, and sometimes he’s in
the paddock. Lewis always seems to scoot past him like he doesn’t see him.”
“You’d think they would’ve managed to talk it out by now. Nico hasn’t been racing for
almost a decade.”
“Right?” Lando grins. He has to admit, he quite enjoys gossip – but he never would’ve taken
Oscar for a gossip himself. “I think there are some slights you can’t forgive. Ever.”
“So you think there was more going on there?”
Lando stills for a moment. “I wouldn’t immediately put it past anyone. There are some, uh,
drivers on the grid who lean the other way.”
For a moment, the line goes quiet. “Really?”

“Yeah,” Lando says.
Oscar doesn’t ask. And for a moment, Lando feels strangely suspended there in the soft glow
of the bathroom light.
If he had asked, Lando wonders, would he have told him?
Would he have come out to him like this – with cleanser on his face and a towel in his hand
after a Minecraft tournament?
“Well,” Oscar says eventually, “I hope they can look each other in the eye again one day.”
Lando laughs as he wipes the cleanser from his face. “They probably won’t. They’re not the
people they were back then. I think they’ve both moved on. It doesn’t really pertain to their
lives anymore.”
“But that’s sad. They were best friends, weren’t they? By their own admission?”
“Yeah,” Lando says. “But there are some things a friendship cannot survive.”
“Like falling in love with your friend?” Oscar asks after a moment. “And having it be one-
sided?”
Lando feels a lump form in his throat. “Yeah. Or a title fight. I think a title fight does the
same thing to you.”
“Fair.” Oscar snorts. “Well, if you ever happen to find out what actually went on between
them, please tell me. I promise I won’t tell another soul. But I’ve always been intrigued by
them.”
Lando is done cleaning his face now, and he tosses the towel into the laundry basket beside
him. He can’t help but grin. “Oh, absolutely. You’d be the first person I told. Though I’m
really not close enough with Lewis to have any meaningful insight into his life.”
They change the subject after that, and the issue with Oscar’s name doesn’t come up again.
Instead, Oscar tells him about his short call with Feinberg while Lando brushes his teeth,
making the occasional sound of disapproval whenever Oscar recounts some outrageous thing
Fein has apparently said.
“All I’m hearing is that he’s butthurt,” Lando says as he takes his phone and returns to bed,
slipping underneath the covers.
“Yeah.” Oscar laughs. “I think he’s a little jealous.”
“That you still have both your candidates in the race?”
“No, actually.” Oscar clears his throat. “That I spend so much time with you. It does cut into
the time I can spend hanging out with him.”
Lando rummages for his charger in the drawer beside his bed and stills. “Oh, really?”

“Yeah,” Oscar replies. “I think he’s getting worried I might replace him.”
“Max is also a little jealous,” Lando says after a moment, finally finding the charger and
plugging his phone in before turning off the light.
“We do spend an awful lot of time together.”
“Yeah,” Lando says. “Next logical step is meeting up when I’m in Australia.”
“You really want it that badly, do you?”
It isn't an outright no. For the first time, it isn't an outright no. And that despite the fact that
Lando has royally fucked up today.
“Yes, Oscar.” Lando takes a deep breath, pulling the sheets up to his chin and settling onto his
side, his face turned toward the phone. “I really, really want to meet you.”
There is a long silence on the other end. And then, naturally, Oscar changes the subject. “Go
to sleep, Lando.”
Lando knows it isn't normal in any sense of the word. He knows that, especially this late at
night, he takes both hands and gleefully smudges whatever boundary still exists between
them.
“Can you stay on call?” he asks. “Tell me something?”
It's not the first time he's fallen asleep with Oscar on the line, but he still feels his heartbeat
pick up as he realises how difficult that habit is to interpret any other way.
“Yeah,” Oscar says after only the briefest hesitation. “Fine.”
“Thank you, Osc.”
“What do you want me to tell you?” 
Lando buries his face deeper into his pillow, turning toward the phone so he can hear Oscar's
voice clearly. “Tell me about your favourite memory.”
“Wow,” Oscar says. “Intense, Norris.”
“Fork it over.”
His own voice sounds tired already, lower than usual, the edges softened by exhaustion. He
knows Oscar can hear it too.
“I think my favourite memory is getting Basil.”
“Who's Basil?”
“My dog. He lives with my parents because I don't really have the apartment or the lifestyle
for a dog, but I think the happiest day of my life was the day we drove to the shelter and

picked him out.”
“You always wanted a dog?” Lando asks, no longer entirely sure whether he's speaking
coherently or whether exhaustion has started to make his syllables bleed together.
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “I know it sounds counterintuitive because I'm not exactly the most open
person in the world, but I do like... the idea of taking care of someone. Someone I love.”
Lando stares into the darkness. Is he still talking about the dog?
“That's also why I don't really like dating,” Oscar says after a moment, and Lando suddenly
wishes he were more awake for this conversation. “I can't connect with people like that.”
“How do you connect?” Lando asks, fighting to keep his eyes open.
“Dunno,” Oscar says, sounding faintly embarrassed. “I'm not particularly well versed. How
do you connect to people?”
“Sex, Oscar,” Lando replies. “As awful and wanton as that sounds.”
There is a brief silence on the other end of the line. Then: “Oh, wow.”
“You asked.”
“I guess I did.” Oscar sighs softly. “Well. Good for you.”
“That's why physicality is the most important thing to me,” Lando says, pressing his face
further into the pillow.
“I see,” Oscar says.
And then there is such a long pause that Lando falls asleep somewhere inside it. Maybe
Oscar says something else. Maybe he doesn't.
Lando never hears it.


IV.
 
Lando jumps off his morning Zoom-call marathon feeling faintly antsy, as he always does
whenever he's forced to sit through business matters for too long.
He knows it's a natural part of the sport he's given his heart to; discussing new sponsors,
negotiating media obligations split between Gabriel and himself, and trying to make their
increasingly impossible schedules fit together in a way that doesn't leave anyone completely
miserable.

The entire time during the call, Gabi had occupied the corner of his screen like some
malicious presence, constantly munching on something. First what looked suspiciously like
leftover pizza from the night before, then half a peach cobbler, before washing it all down
with a can of soda.
Lando had spent most of the meeting staring at him and his impromptu mukbang in the
corner of the screen instead of paying attention to Louise's presentation or Zak's endless
commentary.
Gabriel possesses the deeply enviable quality of being so tall and lanky that he can seemingly
eat whatever he wants without consequence, while Lando gets periodically placed on diets by
his trainer, and Jon enforces those diets with a draconic precision that Lando knows he
probably needs.
In the end, during the last five minutes of the call, Louise, Zak, Gabriel and Lando drifted
onto personal matters for a while, trying to wash the dry taste of business from their mouths.
And then Zak had said, sounding faintly amused: “Good luck for your tournament today.”
Lando had frozen. Just for a moment, but long enough for a wave of self-consciousness to
sweep through him.
Zak knows everything. He's his boss; keeping track of Lando is practically in the job
description. Still, he hadn't expected him to know about Midoffs.
Lando had laughed awkwardly, thanked him, and immediately dropped out of the Zoom call,
leaving Gabriel's openly delighted expression frozen on screen for a fraction of a second
before it disappeared.
Now, back in the quiet of his apartment, he picks up his phone almost without thinking.

Oscar doesn't reply. Lando guesses he's asleep for once – which, honestly, good for him. Ever
since Jon started lecturing him about the importance of sleep, Lando has become increasingly
concerned by Oscar's habit of pulling thirty-hour benders like they're a perfectly reasonable
way for a twenty-something to live his life. 
On that happy note, Lando decides to go for a run along the marina – something he usually
avoids, as he doesn't particularly enjoy being out in public when he can help it, even though
the autochthonous population of Monte Carlo tends not to care much about the number of
Formula One drivers moving through their midst. They've all grown up with drivers of the
past building their lives in the city-state; seeing one out on the street is hardly cause for
excitement.

Halfway down to the marina, he runs into Charles, who is out walking his sausage dog, and
Lando pauses long enough to awkwardly pet it and exchange a few words with his gridmate
before moving on.
Once he's finally able to break into a jog, he immediately feels the familiar sting in his sides –
 a reminder that he has more than slacked on his regimen over the last three weeks, during
which he'd done little besides play Minecraft and spend an objectively unreasonable amount
of time talking to, and increasingly flirting with, his Minecraft coach on Discord.
He needs to get back into shape before the new season – Jon has already sent over the
preliminary training programme that will become his life the second the new year rolls
around, and when Lando dug out last year's plan for comparison, he'd discovered that Jon had
somehow increased every single item on it by roughly fifty percent.
This had annoyed him. Does Jon genuinely think he lost the title because Max Verstappen
happened to do more pull-ups? More curls?
Because Lando knows for a fact that isn't true. He's never once seen the World Champion
willingly engage in cardio.
Still, it's Jon's job, and if Lando is ever going to reach for the championship again, it's going
to have to be this year. The disappointment of last season remains fresh enough that he can
still feel it when he thinks too hard about it, a bruise that hasn't quite faded beneath the skin.
As he pushes himself harder than he probably should, to the point where there's a metallic
taste at the back of his throat, rounding the marina with its absurdly expensive yachts wedged
into impossibly prestigious parking spots, his thoughts drift back to Oscar with the same
inevitability they always seem to.
To the way he reacted when Lando accidentally leaked his name. He'd told Max about it
when he woke up, because Max had immediately asked how Oscar had taken it, and when
Lando admitted that Oscar didn't seem to care nearly as much as he'd expected, Max had
simply replied: I don't think he's physically capable of being mad at you.
This thing that Lando had briefly thought might shatter the easy familiarity between them
forever, that had seemed capable of fundamentally changing the shape of their friendship, has
instead given him something he never thought he'd get out of it: hope.
Hope that Oscar is genuinely reconsidering his position. 
If he seems halfway okay with his name being out there now, then who's to say he won't
reconsider his stance on meeting Lando when he's in Melbourne for the Grand Prix?
Lando cannot even begin to articulate how direly he wants to meet him. Every single time his
mind brushes against the possibility that there might come a day in March when he is
standing in front of Oscar in the flesh, taking him in with his own two eyes, something inside
him immediately folds in on itself, as though the thought alone is enough to make him
capitulate.

He doesn't know why he reacts so strongly to the idea of adding physical presence to
whatever exists between them.
Well. That’s not entirely true. He has a suspicion.
He is already more taken with Oscar than he has ever been with another person in his life. He
feels a feverish sort of craving to talk to him at every hour of the day, to know what he thinks
about everything, to have his attention fixed on him and not on anyone else, and he knows
that this is highly unusual for him – considering he doesn’t even know his face.
He doesn't know how he would react if Oscar suddenly became more than a voice carried
through a Discord call. The mere thought of it makes him short-circuit, and crave it all the
same.
He returns to his apartment an hour later and takes an obscenely long shower, trying to
meditate himself into a different headspace – one that isn't occupied by Oscar at every turn.
It's a losing battle. Oscar lives there now. And Lando can feel it worsening by the day; the
way Oscar has gradually colonised every corner of his thoughts, every spare moment of his
attention, every inch of emotional bandwidth he has available to give.
Pathetically, he wonders whether Oscar feels the same – whether Lando's presence, the idea
of meeting him, has become a permanent fixture in his life too, or whether Lando is simply a
passing acquaintance; someone Oscar talks to the same way he talks to Fein or any of his
other internet friends.
And yet, maybe Lando is conceited enough to give himself too much importance, but he can't
quite shake the feeling that Oscar cares for him deeply.
That for Oscar, this might have started as a fun challenge, an experiment, the utterly batshit
idea of coaching his favourite athlete in something he happened to be good at, but somewhere
along the way it became something else too. Because if yesterday's heart-to-heart is proof of
anything, it's that Oscar seems every bit as bewildered by the closeness between them, by the
suddenness of it all, as Lando is.
It's strange, Lando thinks as he changes into sweats and his favourite black hoodie, that less
than three weeks ago he didn't even know Oscar existed.
And now there's a part of his brain permanently occupied with him, quietly turning him over
and over in the background like a process he can't shut down, a sizeable portion of his mental
bandwidth diverted toward nothing but Oscar, Oscar, Oscar.
Oscar wakes at around one in the afternoon, Lando's time, and eventually replies to his
message about Zak.

Lando grins to himself as he heads out for lunch, meeting Magui and Pietra at a nearby
brasserie.
Max is busy with something else, and as much as Lando enjoys his best friend's company, he
also deeply revels in the attention his two female friends give him whenever they can finally
yap about the things they want to talk about without Max weighing the conversation down
with snarky comments and his constant need to position himself as both the straight man and
the voice of reason.
Even so, Magui bans the word Minecraft before lunch has properly begun.
Pietra, meanwhile, immediately asks about Oscar – having apparently heard one thing or
another through the grapevine, most likely through her boyfriend.
Lando tries to play it cool, but his friends are far too observant to be fobbed off that easily,
and they haven't even made it through the appetisers before Magui is already convinced that
Lando has developed the largest crush in recorded history.
“I'm your wingwoman,” she says, sounding personally offended. “Why didn't you tell me
about this? I'll bag you the little nerd.”
Lando groans. “Stop. It's not like that.”
“Oh, come on.” Magui rolls her eyes. “Now you're just being deliberately obtuse.”
“He won't even show me his face, Margarida. It's not like that.”
She shrugs and takes a sip of her red wine. “Oh, it's absolutely like that. I'm coming with you
to Australia. We're doing this.”
“No,” Lando says, shaking his head. “Please. It's not like that. I'm not even sure I want–”
He doesn't finish the sentence, but he catches the look Pietra and Magui exchange across the
table; long and knowing and deeply unsettling in the way it seems to communicate an entire
volume he isn't privy to.
“Oh,” Magui says eventually. “So you're, like, in love with him. Got it.”
She's trying and failing to hide a shit-eating grin. 
“It's that serious. You don't even want me in his general vicinity because you want him all to
yourself, you lovesick little freak.”
“I'm going to leave you two here,” Lando threatens, viciously attacking the caramelised
butter with a butter knife as a familiar sense of dejection settles somewhere beneath his ribs.
“It's absolutely not like that. He's a good friend and also incredibly straight, and there's no
reason to turn this into something it isn't.”

Pietra pouts. “Oh, Lando.”
“What?”
“You've got approximately a billion hot men lined up for you at any given moment, but the
one you want is the straight guy who's giving you a little too much attention because he finds
the cars sexy that you drive.” She sighs, tearing apart a piece of white bread between her
fingers. “Does this count as self-sabotage already?”
“I don't know what Max told you, but he's genuinely just a friend.”
“He hasn't told me anything,” Pietra says. “I've just noticed that you're not permanently
attached to Max's hip anymore whenever you're bored. You've got someone else to talk to
now.”
“Is he, uh, upset about that?”
Pietra shrugs. “I don't know. I think he secretly hopes Oscar is in love with you, because I
know he viscerally hates the idea of you finding another best friend. You know how he is.”
“I could never replace him,” Lando says, sounding genuinely offended by the suggestion.
“Max has been with me through everything.”
“But do you see Oscar as your best friend?”
“No,” Lando says immediately. “I've known him for three weeks. We're probably going to
drift apart the second the tournament is over.” He bites at his lip. “In fact, every time he refers
to me as his friend, there's something inside me that dies a little.”
The joking atmosphere around the table evaporates instantly. Magui reaches across the table
without hesitation, takes his hand and leans her head against his shoulder. “Oh, chuchu.”
“It’s fine,” Lando says, trying to school his face into neutrality. “I’ll get over it. I got over
everything else eventually. Even my incredibly long-standing crush on Carlos.”
She stays wrapped around him for another moment, and over Pietra’s shoulder Lando catches
sight of someone discreetly taking a photo of them.
He already knows he’s going to find it on Twitter within a few hours, and the thought of
Oscar stumbling across it – seeing him with Magui curled against his side, her head on his
chest while he absent-mindedly plays with her hair – makes something unpleasant twist low
in his stomach. But he can’t tell him, can he?
Can’t tell him that Magui is just his friend; that despite being one of the most beautiful
women Lando has ever laid eyes on, her beauty barely registers to him in that way. Because
the second he starts explaining that, he has to explain so much more about himself too, and
there are still very few people he's actually out to.
And coming out to someone whose face he’s never seen and whose last name he doesn’t even
know feels like an objectively terrible idea.

Two hours later, Lando is back in front of his desktop, live again and reading through chat as
the first matches of the day flicker across his screen.
Unfortunately, Max loses his first match and drops into the lower bracket, where he'll get one
last chance to claw his way back through. Lily loses too, and not even Lando can blame her
for it. She gets absolutely horrendous luck, while her opponent somehow pulls off a sub-
fifteen.
If that happens to him, he’s fucked. He knows it.
Lando listens closely as Oscar coaches her through the slow-motion disaster of her run, and
despite himself he's deeply impressed by how deftly he steers her through the panic that
begins to settle in the moment she notices her opponent is an entire split ahead.
“Hey, Lily, you're good,” Oscar says softly, in a tone that makes Lando want to repeatedly
slam his forehead into his desk. “Don’t look at the sidebar. Don’t think about that. Focus on
your own run. You can’t control what’s happening on the other screen. You can only control
what you do next.”
She manages to claw back a little time after that. Not enough, though. The match ends with
Lily still in the Stronghold.
“Oh, OP, I’m so sorry,” she says, sounding genuinely devastated. “I really tried, but I–”
“You did all you could,” Oscar interrupts gently. “You played really well. I’m incredibly
proud of you.”
At this point, Lando is actively grinding his teeth.
Unfortunately, chat notices too.
