That is almost certainly true. But for the five minutes Oscar spends in the call, he seems more
amused than anything else by Max's determination to establish that Oscar and Lando might
get along brilliantly, but he'll still have to settle for second place.
An hour later, Lily loses her second match too and is now officially out of the tournament.
Lando immediately opens Twitter again – he needs the distraction, because chat had been
right earlier: his face has subtitles.
And if he keeps watching the stream, everyone is going to realise that he's not nearly as
devastated by Oscar's second candidate being eliminated as he probably ought to be –
 especially after the entire tournament spent weeks insisting that Oscar was insane for
choosing Lando over literally anyone else.
At some point, Tubbo drops into their call. “Hey, you guys. We’ve got a slight scheduling
issue with your opponent, Max, which means we’re changing who you have to play against.”
Max doesn’t sound bothered in the slightest. “Oh, sure.”
“It would be Lando.” Tubbo sounds incredibly apologetic. “I hope that’s okay with you two.”
Max snorts. “Yeah, it’s fine. We’ve been competing against each other since we were eight.”
“Thank you. Seriously, thank you.” Tubbo sounds visibly relieved. “Which means you’re up
next, by the way.”

He leaves the channel, and for a moment both Max and Lando are quiet.
“Well,” Lando says eventually. “I’m afraid you’re getting knocked out now.”
“Oh, sure.” Max rolls his eyes. “As if I’m not consistently faster than you. Sorry, Lando, but I
brought you into this tournament and I’m kicking you out of it as well.”
“You might be consistently faster than me, but my personal best absolutely shits on yours.
And I know how to pearl hang.”
They’re bantering, as always, but Lando knows there’s the thinnest layer beneath it all that
lends the exchange a seriousness neither of them would ever openly acknowledge: the old
rivalry. It has never really left their relationship, even after their lives diverged so completely
from one another.
Not that this match is going to change anything. Lando knows that. Part of him even hopes
Max wins.
Because he knows how much this means to him; how far he’s come, farther than anyone
expected him to, including himself. Winning this tournament, proving wrong everyone who
passed on him during the draft – that is something Lando genuinely wants for him.
But he also has to think about himself. About the fact that he wants this just as badly.
Not because he needs to prove that he can beat everyone – this is Minecraft, not racing, and
Lando knows the difference – but because a part of him has become convinced that he has to
do this for Oscar.
To impress him. He wants Oscar to call him tonight too and tell him how well he did.
There was an undeniable shift in their conversation yesterday. They have edged closer and
closer to something unspoken, a strange, shapeless thing that has been growing between them
almost from the beginning – quietly weaving itself through the foundations of their friendship
until it became a structure in its own right.
They feed it every time Oscar sidesteps a question about meeting him. Every time he changes
the subject when Magui comes up. 
It grows quietly in the background, like mistletoe high in the crown of a tree, drawing
sustenance from the friendship beneath it while becoming something separate from it all the
same.
And whenever the conversation turns momentarily charged, whenever a risky remark lands
and neither of them speaks for a second too long, Lando can almost feel it stirring.
Whatever exists between them is impossible to examine directly. The moment he tries to look
at it head-on, it disappears. It can only ever be glimpsed obliquely, in the silences, in the
evasions, in the things left unsaid.

But that somehow makes it feel more tangible, not less. Lando knows it has taken hold of
their entire relationship. 
And whatever it is, it keeps drawing them toward the edge of something. An edge they both
seem strangely fascinated by, and an edge neither of them is willing to cross.
His thoughts are still heavy with all of this half an hour later when he logs into MCSR
Ranked and hears Oscar’s voice in his ear.
“You ready?”
“Yeah,” Lando says.
“I’m sorry it’s against Max.”
“I’m not,” Lando replies laconically. “Let’s wipe the floor with him.”
The upside of playing against your best friend – the person you've spent the last three weeks
debriefing every session with, the person you've spent an entire holiday talking shop with – is
that you know their weaknesses extremely well. The downside is that they know yours.
Lando vetoes desert temple and Max vetoes shipwreck, leaving them with ruined portal once
again.
The second Lando reaches the portal, he knows he's on a good run. He gathers everything he
needs with barely a moment wasted before jumping into the Nether at a little over two
minutes – a very, very respectable split for him.
From there, everything seems to fall into place.
The same strange confidence settles over him, the one that occasionally takes hold during
races as well; the feeling that his brain has stepped aside and handed control over to
something more efficient, something capable of moving through the task without second-
guessing itself or making mistakes.
It helps that Oscar's voice is in his ear the entire time. Low. Steady. Constantly reassuring
him. Constantly praising him.
“You’re doing so, so good,” he says, and Lando immediately digs his teeth into his lip.
God. The way Oscar's voice bleeds into his headphones while adrenaline courses through
him, sharpening every thought to a razor's edge, is becoming a genuine problem.
By now, Lando feels as though he's running hotter with every passing minute. Maybe he's
imagining it. Maybe he's hearing what he wants to hear – but there is something different
about Oscar's voice today. Something he hasn't heard before. The familiar layer of irony
seems to have disappeared.
Usually, even when Oscar is being kind, there's a trace of amusement underneath it all, as
though he finds the entire world faintly ridiculous.

Not today. Today he sounds sincere – as though he's genuinely sitting there, watching Lando
play, and finding himself impressed by what he sees.
Lando knows he's winning the moment he leaves the Nether to triangulate in the Overworld.
He pulls off both sprint jumps cleanly.
“Three hundred and ten blocks east,” he tells Oscar.
“Yes,” Oscar replies immediately. A beat passes. “Excellent.”
The word settles somewhere deep beneath Lando's ribs, and he jumps back into the Nether,
pearls toward the correct coordinates and finds the Stronghold within seconds.
A minute later he's standing in the End at under fourteen minutes.
“Don’t do it,” Oscar warns immediately. “Max is still in the Nether. He died to a Blaze. You
do not need to prove anything.”
But Lando does. Or at least it feels that way.
“Well,” he says, unable to keep the grin out of his voice, “you promised, didn't you?”
“Lando,” Oscar says again, and there is something almost desperate in the warning this time.
“No.”
“You promised.”
Lando is fully aware that there are probably more than three hundred thousand people
watching across the various streams, and he is equally aware that he is alluding to things
nobody else should be privy to. But what is he supposed to do?
“You do not need to zero cycle,” Oscar tells him. “Don't risk the run. If the dragon pushes
you off and you die, you lose everything.”
Lando knows he's right. He can win this with a one-cycle. Hell, he could probably win it by
playing completely normally and shooting out the crystals one by one.
But he's a Formula One driver – he didn't get this far by always choosing the safest option
available to him, the path of least resistance.
Oscar exhales sharply into his headset as Lando ignores the End Fountain entirely and instead
pillars up to the correct height, placing his beds.
“You’re going to waste them if you mess this up,” Oscar warns, and there is a genuine edge
to his voice now. “And without beds you can't one-cycle. You'll have to kill the dragon the
hard way.”
“I can do this,” Lando says. “I can.”
“You've done it once in practice,” Oscar shoots back. “This is not the moment to test it.”

Unfortunately, Lando can already see the shape of the future unfolding ahead of him. This is
probably his last chance.
If he wins this match, he'll make the semifinals, and there is no universe in which he's beating
Jojo a second time. She has already clawed her way back through the losers' bracket, and
chances are he won't even make it to the End in their rematch.
He won't get another opportunity. Won't get another chance to prove that he can do it.
And Oscar promised, didn't he? He wouldn't take that promise back now.
Thankfully, the dragon spots him on top of the pillar and immediately starts drifting toward
him. Lando's fingers feel slippery against the keys as he detonates the first bed.
The explosion tears through the dragon's health bar. The second one lands as well. Another
huge chunk disappears.
God. Is he actually pulling this off?
Oscar has gone completely silent.
And then the inevitable happens: the force of the previous explosions has nudged Lando
closer and closer to the edge of the pillar.
His fingers are moving too quickly, and for one fatal moment, they slip from the shift key.
Suddenly there is nothing beneath him, the world drops away. For a split second, Lando is
falling.
Only years of Formula One – of operating on instinct, of reacting before conscious thought
can catch up – save him.
In one fluid motion, he switches his off-hand, flicks downward, and places the water bucket.
The clutch lands. And three hundred thousand people watch Lando Norris cheat death by a
fraction of a second.
For a moment, he just stands there on the pale yellow endstone, staring up at the dragon
circling overhead.
“Great job,” Oscar says, dripping with sarcasm. “Now you don't have any beds left and the
dragon is regenerating her health.”
Lando ignores him. He immediately sprints back to the fountain, pulls out his bow and starts
shooting at the crystals. He has to admit, this part isn't exactly his specialty. Usually he only
shoots the crystals to force a quicker perch for a one-cycle; actually having to clear all of
them is unfamiliar territory.
To make matters worse, he can see Max leave the Nether in the sidebar and begin searching
for the Stronghold.

Lando still has enough pearls to scale the pillars, intercepting his falls with hastily placed
blocks beneath his feet as he tears through the crystals one by one, preventing the dragon
from regenerating any more health.
It takes him a little over two minutes. His hopes for a personal best are long gone, and Max is
already in the Stronghold.
Lando returns to the fountain and waits for the dragon to perch, peppering her with arrows in
the meantime, though his supply is running dangerously low.
When she finally swoops down, he switches to his iron axe and throws himself at her with
everything he has. Somewhere else, Max is probably setting up a one-cycle. He almost
certainly has enough beds.
The relief that crashes through Lando when the final blow lands is so immense it feels as
though an entire mountain has been lifted from his shoulders.
The dragon dies promptly and the sky above him fractures.

MATCH WINNER: landonorris – 19:24:93
For a moment, nobody says anything. Lando leans back in his chair, too exhausted to
celebrate properly.
“You know you're genuinely loved by the universe, right?” Oscar says eventually.
Lando clears his throat. “I’m sorry, OP.”
“You pulled it off,” Oscar replies. There is a pause. “You actually pulled it off.”
He sounds relieved. And maybe a little annoyed.
“Congrats. You're in the semifinals.”
Before Lando can respond, Tubbo drops into the channel to whisk him away for a quick
winner's interview: he's officially qualified for the final day of the tournament now.
First he'll have to face Jojo again, and if by some miracle he beats her, he'll have to play the
winner of the upper bracket in the final.
The interview is thankfully short. Lando has spent half his life giving interviews, so he slips
into familiar territory immediately, doing his best to downplay the catastrophe that had nearly
unfolded in the End.
Thankfully, Tubbo doesn't dwell on the failed zero-cycle attempt for very long. The second
he's free, he drops into Max's voice channel.
“Pietra texted me,” Max says instead of a greeting. “She says she's buying you lunch
tomorrow for knocking me out prematurely.”

“You're welcome,” Lando grins. “Sorry, by the way.”
“No, you're good.” Max snorts. “What the hell happened in the End, though? You were in
there for like seven minutes.”
“Uh.” Lando scratches the back of his neck. “I attempted a zero-cycle.”
“You fucking show-off.” His best friend sounds genuinely delighted. “Can't believe you
almost handed me the win because you were too busy trying to be the hero.”
“Yeah, well.”
Max knows exactly why he did it. Thankfully, he isn't about to say it on stream. 
Half an hour later, Lando ends stream and immediately opens Discord.
 

landonorris
call?

 
Oscar doesn't reply for several minutes. During that time, Lando wanders into the kitchen in
search of food while absent-mindedly scrolling Twitter.
His fans are ecstatic: most of the speedrunning community had spent weeks criticising every
aspect of his gameplay and questioning Oscar's decision to draft him in the first place, and
now he's one of the last four players standing. Lando finds himself oddly touched by their
excitement. 
Some viewers, however, seem much more interested in a different detail.

did you catch that? he said "you promised" when OP told him not to attempt the zero
cycle. what exactly did he promise him? UGH i’m going insane i need to know

They are alarmingly perceptive – Lando is going to have to be more careful. Because
apparently even the smallest slip of the tongue is enough to keep the internet occupied for
days.
Lando chews on his lower lip as he stares at the chat between him and Oscar. This might be
the longest Oscar has ever gone without replying while Lando knew he was awake.
He tries not to read into it – Oscar's probably busy. Likely talking to Feinberg, whose
candidate Lando is going to have to face again tomorrow. Maybe he's debriefing with Lily. Or
maybe he's just finally taking a break from staring at Minecraft for sixteen hours straight.
There are a hundred perfectly reasonable explanations. Unfortunately, Lando only seems
interested in the unreasonable ones.

Eventually, he decides to go to bed, trying very hard not to dwell on the fact that Oscar still
hasn't answered him.
It shouldn't bother him this much. And yet it does.
It's strange, really. Oscar seems more upset about Lando ignoring his coaching than he was
about having his name leaked in front of ninety thousand people.
Lando understands it, too.
Objectively, Oscar has every right to be annoyed. He'd spent weeks drilling risk management
into him, only for Lando to throw a perfectly safe win into jeopardy because he couldn't resist
showing off. Because he'd wanted to pull off a zero cycle. Because he'd wanted to impress
him.
But there is another thought that keeps circling back – one Lando can't quite get rid of.
Maybe Oscar isn't only annoyed because Lando ignored his advice – maybe he's annoyed
because Lando came far closer than either of them had expected. 
Because a week ago, when Oscar had agreed to meet him if he managed a zero cycle, it had
felt hypothetical. A ridiculous challenge. Something safely impossible.
And then, today, Lando had almost done it. Almost. The thought settles heavily in his chest.
He checks his phone one last time before bed: nothing. No reply.
Lando switches his phone to Do Not Disturb, plugs it in and buries himself beneath the
covers.
For the first time in a long while, sleep doesn't come easily. And when it finally does, it is
restless.
 


V.
 
Pietra comes through on that promised lunch. They return to the same brasserie the next day,
this time with Max in tow, who seems remarkably relaxed about the fact that he's out of the
tournament now.
“I'm just so fucking glad I can think about something other than endgame strategies again,”
he says when Lando meets him outside the restaurant. He immediately pulls him into one of
those one-sided hugs that have become common between them. Lando briefly rests his chin
on his shoulder, for which Max gives him a strange look.

After lunch, Lando returns to his apartment for his pre-semifinal debrief with Oscar.
His coach hasn't really spoken to him since yesterday. There had been a message at three in
the morning, Lando's time, explaining that he had in fact been talking to Feinberg and simply
hadn't been able to call him afterwards.
Lando hadn't replied.
Now, sitting in the call half an hour before the semifinal, he immediately feels how strangely
stilted everything is. 
Oscar doesn't mention yesterday's End split once – instead, he replays Lando's sloppiest
moments from the run, something he has never really done before. 
Lando can take it. He's spent most of his life having mistakes dissected for him in real time,
videotaped and cut together for his convenience. So he listens, taking Oscar's criticism
without complaint. When they finally reach the End split, Oscar still doesn't bring up the fact
that he'd very strongly advised against the entire ordeal.
Instead, he points out the positioning error on the pillar that had sent Lando plummeting off
it.
“I'd advise putting a safety rail behind you,” Oscar says. “Just another block. Then even if
you let go of the shift key for a second, you're not immediately dead.”
Lando blinks. He can't help wondering whether this is some kind of peace offering. After all,
Oscar is actively giving him advice on how to pull off another zero cycle – which isn't
something he has to do.
“Okay,” Lando says quietly. “Thanks.”
“You feel ready?” Oscar asks after a moment.
“Uh.” Lando hesitates.
He doesn't really know why he's struggling to thaw around him – it's not as though Oscar has
actually done anything wrong. 
He didn't ignore him. He replied five hours later – that's a perfectly normal amount of time.
It's just that Oscar's usual response time sits somewhere around twenty seconds, and
apparently Lando has become catastrophically accustomed to that.
“As ready as I can be,” he finally says.
When he starts streaming half an hour later, he smashes one hundred thousand viewers
almost immediately. The second the starting screen disappears, the number keeps climbing –
making the semifinals has apparently elevated this whole thing beyond the confines of
Minecraft.

The official Formula One accounts have posted about it. Lando Norris advances to Minecraft
Speedrunning Championship semifinals.
Naturally, Tubbo is ecstatic about the additional coverage, and Lando is happy for him. And,
if he's being honest, happy for Oscar too. Because Oscar is tied to this run now.
Every article about Lando's unlikely tournament performance mentions the anonymous
Minecraft speedrunner who drafted him, coached him and somehow turned him into a
semifinalist in the span of three weeks.
Oscar is getting attention from all of it. Attention he absolutely never wanted – but attention
Lando knows he deserves, for the incredible amount of work he's put into him.
Half an hour later, Lando is strapped in for the semifinals, facing Jojo again. He knows this is
where it's supposed to end.
He's not going to beat her a second time. The first victory had already felt impossible enough,
and even then he'd gotten lucky. She's still the better player. Lando knows that.
He just has these occasional flashes of brilliance now. Moments where something clicks into
place and he suddenly looks miles ahead of the other casual players – and, if he’s honest,
those flashes are probably the only reason he's still in the tournament.
They settle on shipwreck, which he knows she's weaker at than he is, so at least he'll have a
slight head start. The second the countdown disappears and he's dropped into the world,
Oscar's voice in his ear, he feels it return.
That steely focus. That ice-cold, razor-sharp concentration that strips everything else away
until all he can see is the racing line of the run ahead of him – almost as clearly as the one he
sees on track. The line that instinct alone is enough to follow.
When he slips into that mode, he barely needs Oscar's commentary. Except Oscar seems to
understand that. He seems to understand him.
Whenever Lando falls into that strange state, Oscar offers exactly the information he needs
and nothing more – keeping unnecessary chatter and over-explanations to himself, voicing
merely the next thing that matters.
It's a thought that honestly freaks Lando out a little. Oscar would make the perfect race
engineer.
The kind he can only dream about. A sort of GP Lambiase to his Max Verstappen.
Not that he doesn't get along with Will. He does. But this feels different – this strange sort of
symbiosis. The way Oscar seems able to slip directly into his head and know precisely what
he needs before Lando even realises he needs it himself.
“Careful,” Lando hears in his ear. “There's a gap in the ground on the way back to the
Fortress. I don't think you noticed it on the way here. It might prove fatal.”

And, of course, he's right. As Lando doubles back to kill more Blazes, his inventory already
full of pearls and obsidian, he realises Oscar is absolutely right.
He hadn't seen it – on the way over he'd drifted slightly farther left and avoided it entirely,
never registering the danger in the first place.
But Oscar had. Oscar had noticed the gap. And he'd noticed that Lando hadn't.
“Thank you,” he says, feeling the relief bleed into his voice. “That truly would've proven
fatal.”
“You're exceedingly welcome.”
For the briefest moment, he sounds like the old Oscar again – just a touch sarcastic in a way
that makes Lando's heart kick painfully against his ribs.
“Gap to Jojo?” Lando asks.
Oscar laughs. “You're not in a car, Lando.” He pauses. “But she's approximately thirty
seconds behind.”
“Okay.”
He needs to lock in. He cannot start bantering with Oscar now just because the adrenaline
flooding his bloodstream has filled him with a strange sort of giddiness.
He does the triangulation. “Portal's at four hundred blocks south-east.”
“As always, you’re correct.”
Lando slips back into the Nether, covering the remaining distance through the hell dimension
before building a new portal and lighting it. 
The Stronghold comes easily. The portal room even more so.
But he sees Jojo's status switch to Stronghold the exact moment he enters the End and spawns
on the obsidian platform beyond the island. She enters roughly twenty seconds after him.
“One-cycle,” Oscar commends immediately.
“What if she doesn't perch?”
“She will.” Oscar sounds completely certain. “Shoot the crystals. It'll accelerate the perch.
Craft your beds while you wait.”
Lando obeys. There isn't time to hesitate, time to think. Unlike his earlier runs, he cannot
afford mistakes.
He hates the fact that Oscar is forcing him into a one-cycle, but he also knows he's right. A
failed zero-cycle, even if he somehow pulled it off, would cost precious seconds. Seconds he

no longer has.
“Let's go,” Oscar says the moment the dragon begins to descend. “Show me what you're
capable of.”
Lando doesn't need to be told twice. He bites down so hard on his lip that he tastes blood.
Bed after bed detonates against the dragon's hitbox. He's perfect.
Or close enough to it. One explosion catches him slightly, shaving off a bit of health, but
that's it.
Ten seconds later, the dragon dies.
Lando launches himself from the pillar and dives into the fountain the instant it transforms
into a portal.

MATCH WINNER: landonorris – 13:55:43
“Personal best,” Lando says. The words come out almost disbelieving.
“Yeah.” Oscar is quiet for a moment. “Congrats, Lando. That was...” He breaks off. “That
was really fucking great.”
Lando can't help smiling at that. He doesn't even care what happens next. He's in the final.
He has a sub-fourteen. He beat Feinberg's candidate, one of the favourites to win the entire
tournament – and he didn't even need the zero-cycle.
“Thank you,” he says eventually. “For, uh... your guidance.”
But Oscar immediately brushes it aside. “That was all you.” A pause. “You're exceptional.”
For a moment, Lando just sits there. The adrenaline slowly drains from his bloodstream,
leaving him shaky and breathless, his throat burning. 
“I’m taking five,” he tells no one in particular before getting up. His fingers are still shaking
as he grabs his phone from the desk and leaves the room, pulling the door shut behind him.
He has the phone pressed to his ear before he even reaches the kitchen.
“Mate, congrats,” Max says immediately, the second he picks up, sounding genuinely
ecstatic. “I just saw it and you were so, so fucking good. I couldn’t–”
“I think I’m in love with Oscar.”
Silence. A heavy kind of silence. For a moment it hangs between them, and then Max replies,
carefully, with a note of concern creeping into his voice: “Tell me more.”
Lando slides down the side of the cabinet until he's sitting on the kitchen floor, burying his
forehead in his hands as he drags in a shaky breath.

“I don’t know,” he manages eventually, and he can hear the desperation in his own voice. “It
just... hit me.”
“Well.” Max is quiet for a moment. “If it’s any consolation, I could tell.”
Lando lets out a miserable laugh. That isn't any consolation. If anything, it makes him panic
harder.
He can feel it tightening around his chest, that familiar corset of metal clamping around his
ribs whenever an emotion gets too big, too overwhelming. The first warning signs of a panic
attack. Or maybe just self-loathing.
“Why do you sound so distraught about it?” Max asks after a moment.
“I can’t be in love with him,” Lando breathes. The words feel ridiculous even as he says
them. “I don’t even know what he looks like. I’ve known him for three weeks. He doesn’t
want to meet me. I’m losing my fucking mind on my kitchen floor and he doesn’t give half a
shit.”
“I don't think that's the right read on the situation,” Max says immediately. In fact, he sounds
almost offended on Oscar's behalf. “I think the man's in agony over you.”
“He doesn’t care. He doesn’t want to meet me.”
“Oh, Lando.” Max sighs. “I think he does. I think he really fucking does.”
Lando closes his eyes. “Then why won't he?”
“Because I think he's spent years getting comfortable inside his anonymity,” Max replies.
“And that's not something you just give up overnight. Especially because it gives him
control.”
He pauses.
“Control over what people know. Control over what parts of himself exist out there in the
world.”
Lando doesn't say anything.
“And you fuck with that control,” Max continues. “That's your whole thing. You make people
want to tell you everything. You make them want to hand over pieces of themselves. But he's
also a guy with insanely strong self-preservation instincts. So now you've got two parts of
him fighting each other.”
“But–”
“I can practically guarantee it,” Max cuts in. “He's as in love with you as you are with him.”
“You're delusional.”

Max snorts. “Fine. Suit yourself.” A beat. “May I ask what triggered your epiphany?”
“I couldn’t tell you,” Lando says, breathing shakily. “I just... I just suddenly felt so fucking
nauseous. I heard his voice in my ear and I realised that I cannot have this end. I don’t ever
want to suffer through a day where I don’t... where I cannot...”
“Oh, Lando.” Max sounds genuinely sad now. “You've got to tell him. Please promise me
you'll tell him.”
“What would it change?” Lando asks bitterly. “It wouldn't change a fucking thing about the
fact that he's keeping me at arm's length. That every attempt on my part to get to know him is
met with this sort of insulting indifference.”
“I'm sure that's not–”
“I'll get over it,” Lando says. He always does. Or at least that's what he tells himself. 
He scrambles back to his feet, hauling himself upright with the handle of one of the kitchen
cabinets. “I've got to go back to stream. Finals are in half an hour.”
“Do you want me to come over?” Max asks. “I can be there in forty-five minutes. We can
order dinner. Invite the girls too. Forget about this whole sorry affair for a while.” He pauses.
“And then tomorrow you can still decide what you're going to do. Whether you're going to
tell him.”
Lando already knows he isn't going to. He might be experiencing the most overwhelming
combination of emotions he has ever felt for another person, but he's not pathetic. He's not
going to confess to a man who has made it abundantly clear that meeting him is not a
priority. 
He is Lando Norris, after all – and if there's one thing he's exceptionally good at, it's suffering
in silence. That's practically his defining character trait.
“It'd be great if you came over,” he says. “And bring the girls. But don't tell them anything.”
He rubs a hand over his face. “About what I just told you.”
“Of course.”
God. Lando genuinely doesn't know what he'd do without him. There's a reason Max sits at
the top of his call list and probably always will.
When he returns to stream, chat welcomes him back as though he's already won the entire
tournament: and with some shock, he notices that his viewer count has climbed beyond two
hundred thousand.
He never would've expected this many people to care about his bizarre off-season side quest,
but apparently there's something entertaining about watching a Formula One driver become
strangely goated at an absurdly niche block game.

He spends the next twenty minutes interacting with chat – then, ten minutes before the final
begins, the bracket is confirmed.
He's up against a British creator called Jonnaay, whom he's never heard of before, coached by
Infume – which makes the match doubly interesting, considering Oscar's long-standing
rivalry with him.
In contrast to the other games, the final is a best-of-three – so Lando doesn't just have to play
one game, but at minimum two, until either he or his opponent takes two wins. And that
means he has to stay focused for the better part of an hour. That's fine. He's used to that from
racing.
Oscar drops into the call five minutes before the first match starts.
“Hey.”
“Hi.”
“How are you feeling?” Oscar asks, his voice warm.
“Locked in,” Lando replies.
He hears Oscar laugh softly. “Yeah. I know you are.” A brief pause follows. “I just wanted to
tell you that no matter what happens now, you've already won.”
Lando leans back in his chair. “Have I?”
“Yes,” Oscar says, and he sounds so sincere that a part of Lando immediately wants to shrivel
up and die. “You made the finals. Three weeks ago you hadn't even finished the game once.”
He pauses. “The way you're playing now goes beyond anything I taught you.”
“That's not–”
“It is,” Oscar interrupts. “I've watched you for years, Lando. I know what you're like when
you decide to put your mind to something.” His voice softens slightly. “You don't really do
things halfway. I always thought we'd end up here.”
“You're so–”
“What can I say?” Oscar laughs. “I'm a fanboy. I've done the research.”
“Well,” Lando says after a moment, his voice coming out rougher than intended, “you've
been the best coach I could've asked for.”
He swallows. “So thank you. For believing in me. For spending an absurd number of draft
points on me that first day.”
Oscar groans. “I really did overshoot.”

“A little.”
“A lot,” Oscar corrects. “Nobody else was going to take you from me.” The words settle
warmly somewhere beneath Lando's ribs. “But I needed to make sure.”
Lando knows they probably shouldn't be having this conversation on stream. This feels like
the sort of thing that belongs in one of their late-night calls instead; something traded in the
darkness when neither of them can see the other.
And yet maybe having it here makes it safer – sterilises it, turns it into something public and
harmless.
Mutual admiration. Friendship. Something that can be broadcast to hundreds of thousands of
people because there is supposedly nothing dangerous about it.
“Well,” Lando says after a moment. “I'm glad. Glad you overshot.”
Chat is cooing and emoting in a way Lando has never seen before. Of course, nerves are
running high before the final stretch, and suddenly he's very, very glad he doesn't have a live
feed of his fans' voices piped into the cockpit of his car. That would honestly derail him in a
way he cannot even begin to describe. Oscar is incredibly tenacious for dealing with that all
the time.
Lando waits in front of the loading screen, and he sees his phone light up. Max. 
 

Max
I've timed our arrival so you should be done when we get there.

 
Lando reacts with a thumbs-up before turning his attention back to the game. 
The second he's dropped into the world, he's back there again: in that strange state of
concentration that's taken hold of him every single time over the last few days whenever he's
realised that this is where he actually has to lock in.
Yet again, he tears through the overworld split – his opponent isn't far behind, though.
Some splits Jonnaay finishes faster than him, some slower. The gap between them never
seems to widen beyond a few seconds. 
Oscar barely says a word until the triangulation thirteen minutes into the run, only confirming
Lando's reading of the angle. Lando is grateful for it.
He's silent too, there are no questions to ask. He wins the first game with a one-cycle – by
roughly ten seconds, close enough that Jonnaay's dragon is already dying by the time Lando's
portal opens, ending the race.

The second game goes the other way. Lando loses by almost exactly the same margin,
proving more or less that they are operating at the same level.
Which means it all comes down to game three. The decider.
They roll a buried treasure seed, one Lando isn't particularly comfortable on, but he gets
lucky with the locate and is gathering wood in under a minute.
Oscar talks him through the underwater portal in the ravine, something they haven't practiced
much, and although Lando doesn't misplace a single block, Jonnaay still enters the Nether
first.
“Don't worry about it,” Oscar tells him. “You can make that time back.”
And he does. He finds a fortress closer than the one Jonnaay is searching for – or so Oscar
tells him, keeping him informed just enough to know where he stands without overwhelming
him.
Lando gets unlucky with trades, though – as his piglins take approximately half a millennium
to fork over the obsidian he needs. At least it gives him time to pearl back toward the fortress
and farm enough blaze rods to finish the run.
While he's still waiting on the final pieces of obsidian, he sees Jonnaay's status switch to
Locating Stronghold.
“Oh, for fuck’s sake,” he curses under his breath.
“Don't look at that,” Oscar says immediately. “He can fumble just as easily. You're right
behind.”
And, in fact, Oscar is right. Even though Jonnaay starts locating much earlier, something
seems to go wrong because they enter the End almost simultaneously.
“He's going for a one-cycle,” Oscar informs him the moment Lando pillars onto the main
island.
And in that instant, Lando knows. He just knows.
This time Oscar doesn't say it. He doesn't tell him not to do it. In fact, he says nothing at all.
Maybe because he knows this is the only way to still win this. Jonnaay has the head start, and
if Lando goes for a one-cycle and waits for a perch, he will almost certainly lose.
And in that moment, Lando realises that for all of his supposed chillness, all of his feigned
stoicism, Oscar wants this.
He wants them to win this.
Not because he gives a shit about the points it awards him, or what it does for his ranking, but
because he wants to do this together. He wants them to triumph together. To be tied together

in victory.
And Lando knows Oscar cannot tell him to do it. Not after everything he put him through
yesterday. Not after what this stupid promise has come to mean in private.
But he also knows that Oscar hopes he does it anyway. That he still goes for it.
So instead of rushing toward the End Fountain like he would for a one-cycle, Lando abruptly
changes direction and throws an ender pearl against the obsidian pillar beside him, already
switching to his netherrack as he begins to tower toward the correct position.
“Safety railing,” is all Oscar says the moment Lando starts building the platform, just as the
dragon banks sharply and comes hurtling towards him. Lando has to bite the inside of his
cheek to stop himself from grinning.
Oh. He so wants him to do it.
Lando places the extra block behind him exactly the way Oscar showed him during the
debrief, then drops the first bed onto the obsidian platform.
The first explosion lands. Then the second. Then the third.
A perfect two-plus-two, with no single misclicks – all the while he holds shift as though his
life depends on it.
And then, just like that, the dragon's health bar disappears.
“It’s not over,” Oscar warns immediately. “Pearl down.”
The one weakness of a zero-cycle is that the dragon has to die over the End Fountain. It
means waiting through ten agonising seconds while she returns to the centre of the island
before the game will actually register the kill.
Ten seconds. An eternity.
Lando pearls down exactly as instructed, managing not to throw himself into the void on the
final stretch. He keeps his eyes trained on the ground so he doesn't accidentally aggro an
enderman and lose the entire thing to something stupid now of all moments.
Then he runs. As fast as he can. 
There still is no banner, no announcement, no declaration that Jonnaay has won.
Lando throws himself into the fountain and waits. Waits, waits, waits.
Above him, the dragon finally leaves the place where Lando struck the killing blow and
glides back toward the centre of the island, descending slowly onto the End Fountain.
The sky cracks pink.

And–
EVENT WINNER: landonorris – 14:34:45

For a moment neither of them speaks, and Lando can see chat accelerating in the corner of
his eye at a speed he's never witnessed before. The entire thing is little more than a blur now;
a grey streak of emotes and euphoric screaming racing past while the game throws him back
into the menu.
He fidgets with his headset, suddenly unsure whether he should be the first to speak, or if
Oscar will.
“That's...” Oscar finally starts, only to trail off.
“Your doing,” Lando finishes for him immediately. “You're simply the best fucking coach to
ever do it.”
Oscar laughs. But it's different from his usual laugh. Less amused, almost strained. Like the
sound is being pulled out of him against his will.
“No, Lando,” he says. “You did all of that yourself.” A pause. “And you zero cycled.”
“Yeah,” Lando says, grinning despite himself. “After you told me to put that idea out of my
head.”
“I should've known better than to try and withhold from you anything that presented an
opportunity to show off.”
Oscar still sounds strange. Lando realises he can't quite read him right now.
“We really won this, huh?”
That earns another laugh. “Oh,” Oscar says, “I think we did.”
“I swear, after the second game I was starting to doubt we would–”
The door behind him flies open with a bang. Max, Pietra and Magui burst into the room like a
tsunami wave, all three of them are yelling at the top of their lungs.
Apparently they'd already been lurking in the living room, watching the final moments on
stream, and now that Lando's free they've decided to descend upon him.
Well. Magui and Pietra have. Max follows a few steps behind them with an expression of
outright horror on his face, as though he'd made a genuine attempt to hold them back and
failed spectacularly.
Magui immediately loops her arms around Lando from behind and litters the side of his face
with kisses, making him laugh despite himself. “Oh, my brilliant, talented, nerdy little
chuchu.”

As always, she smells overwhelmingly of vanilla. Her hair tickles against his cheek as he
attempts to pry her off, but she manages to plant one final kiss on the side of his face before
he can escape. Then she cackles triumphantly and disappears from the room again.
Max, meanwhile, is the only one who seems to grasp the full extent of what just happened.
“Sorry, chat,” he says dryly. “Didn't mean to interrupt. Carry on.”
Of course, chat immediately begs Max to stay. They've always cared significantly less about
Magui and Pietra.
Lando clears his throat and turns back to the screen, back to the call.
“Sorry,” he says. “I didn't know they were waiting outside.”
“No worries,” Oscar replies. And immediately Lando hears it: the distance. That same
distance that always leaves something painfully exposed inside his chest. “You did win the
whole thing, after all.”
“We did,” Lando corrects him, but Oscar only laughs weakly.
It takes almost another hour before he's finally able to end stream: first Tubbo pulls him aside
for an interview, ecstatic about the upset victory and promising to get the trophy shipped to
Monaco as quickly as possible. Lando tells him to send it to Woking instead – that's where
he'll be in a few days anyway. Back at the MTC and back to preparing for a season that
suddenly feels much closer than it did this morning.
Lando hasn’t had the chance to talk to Oscar about any of it yet. To properly debrief. To hear
his unfiltered thoughts on the last three games.
The moment the tournament ended, Lando had been whisked away by Tubbo and the event
organisers, while Oscar had his own interviews to get through. And when Lando finally
switched over to Oscar's stream tab afterwards, he'd found him in a call with Feinberg and
Infume.
Lando hadn't dared drop in. So he'd ended stream instead.
Chat is begging him to stay, begging him not to disappear for another six months now that
he's won the thing, now that he no longer has any obligation to stream.
Lando makes vague promises about coming back soon – but he doesn't know whether he'll be
able to keep them.
Because deep down, he knows it's probably going to be up to Oscar – if Twitch ends up being
the only thing keeping their friendship alive, if this is the space where they get to continue
being whatever they are to one another, then he'll be there. He'll stream like it's 2020 again.
Magui and Pietra keep taking turns barging into his room, each appearance more dramatic
than the last, demanding to know when he's finally going to get off stream so they can
celebrate properly.

Eventually Lando gives in. After all, he's been live for almost six hours, a new personal
record.
As he finally turns off stream, closes OBS and switches off his camera, he finds himself
wondering whether this is it. Whether this was a strange little detour in his life that's now
over. Or whether he'll be live again next week. He genuinely doesn't know.
When he emerges into the living room, his friends erupt – it turns out they hadn't just shown
up empty-handed either.
His dining table is absolutely covered in food, containers of Indian takeaway spread across
the entire surface, and judging by the way Magui and Pietra are giggling at absolutely
everything, they've already made a serious dent in the alcohol – something they immediately
set out to rectify for him as well, pressing a glass of champagne into his hand before he can
even sit down.
They celebrate him as though he'd just won the Formula One World Championship  – and
Lando has to admit that, eventually, he starts enjoying himself.
It's over now. Done. He won. Not only did he avoid making a fool of himself, he proved – to
himself more than anyone else – that he can become good at almost anything if he commits
to it fully. If that isn’t a great omen for the new season.
And Oscar won too.
Lily made it to day two, which means Oscar picked up points for her as well, enough to put
him at the top of the coach rankings overall.
The entire time, Lando's fingers itch for his phone, for the Discord chat. To send a message.
Anything. Just something to break the awful silence from Oscar's side, because he's gone
quiet too.
Across the table, over the steadily diminishing tubs of takeaway, Lando catches Max
throwing him long, searching looks. It's obvious what he wants to talk about.
The little breakdown before the final. The confession Lando hadn't been able to hold back in
a moment of weakness. One he regrets now.
Or maybe not regrets. Just feels differently about, now that everything has settled inside him.
Now that the tournament is over. Now that he's a little drunk and sprawled across the sofa,
Magui half draped over his chest with a bottle of wine in hand.
Pietra takes countless photos of them, immediately uploading them to her story, where she
naturally finds a way to brag about the fact that Lando is now officially a Minecraft
speedrunner. A sub-fourteen isn't a joke either.
It's a surreal evening all around. The official Formula One account tweets about it too,
posting the clip of Lando's final victory: the last desperate moments of his zero cycle, the

dragon exploding overhead, his celebration with Oscar. The nosy bastards running the social
media account have somehow even managed to find Oscar's account and tag him.
Lando watches his follower count climb by the minute. He refreshes Oscar's profile more
times than he'd ever admit to.
No halo around the profile picture. No story. No post. Nothing.
Max never gets a chance to corner him that night, because every time he tries, Lando slips
away. On the walk to the bathroom. Out onto the balcony when he needs air. Standing at the
railing and looking out toward the dark ocean while the cool night breeze tries and fails to
clear his head.
Eventually, around one in the morning, his friends leave, abandoning him with the aftermath
of their impromptu celebration.
Lando immediately starts cleaning – not because he particularly cares about the mess, but
because he needs something to do.
Something to occupy his hands and his thoughts before he ends up opening his chat with
Oscar and doing something stupid.
No matter. Because a few minutes into his cleaning spree, his phone lights up.
 

OP81
call?

 
Lando hits the call button before the message has even fully loaded. Oscar picks up just as
quickly.
For a moment, neither of them says anything. Then Oscar clears his throat. "Hi."
"Hi," Lando replies, leaning against the kitchen island, his phone pressed close to his face. He
doesn't allow himself more than that. Not until he figures out what kind of conversation this
is going to be. 
"Your friends still there?"
"No," Lando says. "I'm alone now."
"Good." Oscar sounds strange again. Or maybe Lando's the strange one. Maybe there's
enough alcohol in his bloodstream by now to make him imagine things.
"I guess, uh..." Oscar trails off for a moment. "I just wanted to call you. Wanted to tell you in
person."

Lando frowns. "What?"
"That I'm keeping my promise."
He's still confused. "You're keeping your promise?" He doesn't even understand what Oscar
means, simply because it never occurs to him – not even for a second – that he actually
might… that he might–
Oscar snorts. "Seems like you've forgotten about it entirely. How much did you have to
drink?"
"Not much," Lando says, running a hand through his hair. "Wait, wait, wait. Are you saying –
 are you actually saying–"
"Yes," Oscar says. Just that. "Yes."
It can't be. He's got to be dreaming. Hallucinating. It's one in the morning, he's slightly drunk,
standing barefoot in his kitchen, and he's hallucinating.
"Are you serious?"
"I mean, I promised you," Oscar says. "Didn't I?"
"I didn't think–"
"I'd hold up my end of the deal?" he asks, and there's a faint thread of amusement in his
voice. "To be honest, I never thought you were actually going to pull it off. I made that
promise because I considered it physically impossible." He laughs softly. "But I should've
known better. I should've known not to stand between Lando Norris and doing the
impossible."
Lando bites his lip. "Oscar, you don't have to do this, you know that, right? As much as I
appreciate that you want to keep your word, the last thing I want is to disrespect your
boundaries. And you clearly don't–"
"Lando." Oscar says his name so seriously, so intensely, that Lando immediately falls silent.
"I want to."
The words land heavily between them.
"I want to meet you."
"But that would mean..."
"That I'd show you my face," Oscar says. "Yeah. I know."
"And you'd be okay with that?"
"Yes." This time there's no amusement in his voice. “I’d be okay with that."

Lando feels something in his chest want to burst free violently, something that has been
carving out its miserable existence in there for weeks now; his stupid, lovesick fucking heart
that still dares to hope.
“Osc.”
“What?”
He doesn’t know what to say.
“Thank you,” he says after almost five seconds of silence. “For, uh, agreeing to this.”
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “I am getting a paddock pass out of this, right?”
Lando genuinely laughs, and he sounds a little teary even to himself. “Oh my God. Yes. A
hundred if you want. One for your sisters each. Your parents. Whatever you need.”
“That’s good then,” Oscar says after a moment, and his voice sounds soft again – the exact
softness Lando has been missing over the past two days. “I guess this means… we’re meeting
in Albert Park then.”
“Yes,” Lando says, and suddenly everything seems steeped in golden light. The mess on his
dinner table. The sterile kitchen. The Monaco skyline glittering beyond his window. Inside
him, a maelstrom of euphoria and anxiety surges so violently it almost hurts.
Two months. The Melbourne race is in two months.
He has two months to deal with this. Two months to come to terms with the fact that this is
actually happening.
“Good,” Oscar says finally. “I have to go now. I have a date with a dolphin.”
Lando laughs shakily. “Okay. Have fun. Send me a picture if you see it again.”
“I will,” he promises. For a moment, he seems to hesitate. “Bye, Lando.”
“Bye, Oscar.”
Neither of them ends the call and for a moment, Lando can hear his breathing. It’s shallow
and quicker than Lando expected, and he almost thinks he hears something else in the
accelerated rhythm of this. 
He’s scared, Lando realises. This isn’t easy for him at all. 
But he’s doing it anyway.

Chapter 4: Aftermath/End
Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

 
I.

 
Back in the death throes of December, the mere idea of March had seemed like an
impossibility to him. A phantasmagoria of sorts; an ever-shifting faraway land he’d never
truly believed he would one day set foot in.
It always feels that way. Every year, December stretches out around him like a strange little
pocket universe, disconnected from the rest of his bustling life. The season reduced to
debriefs and statistics and caustic what-ifs; the next one still trapped in the realm of suit
fittings and sponsor obligations, of endless photoshoots and factory visits and the first
tentative laps of a car that does not yet properly exist.
But this year, March had carried an additional weight: not just anxiety, but also anticipation.
The gnawing awareness that every passing day brought him closer not merely to the season
opener, but to something else entirely. Something he found himself looking forward to with
an intensity that occasionally bordered on unbecoming.
Every night that dissolved into the early hours with Oscar’s voice filtering through his
headphones, every morning that began with a message waiting on his phone, every Discord
call that stretched far beyond the point where either of them should’ve gone to sleep: all of it
carrying him inexorably toward Melbourne.
Lando had spent those two months in a state of near-constant frenzy.
The off-season, supposedly designed for rest and recovery, had somehow become busier than
the season itself. His obligations as not only a Formula One driver but one of McLaren’s
most recognisable ambassadors had him ricocheting relentlessly between Monaco and
Woking, then briefly across the Atlantic for sponsor obligations in the United States,
followed by an even shorter stint in the Middle East before being flung straight back again.
In between it all, he talks to Oscar.
He calls him from sterile hotel rooms, sprawled across crisp white sheets with his shoes still
on. He calls him from the gym between sets, much to Jon’s growing irritation. He calls him
while waiting for coffee. On the drive to the golf course. From airport lounges. From the back
seats of cars weaving through cities he barely has time to properly see.
He texts him underneath conference tables during sponsor meetings. 

He accidentally leaks part of the new race suit because he sends Oscar a mirror selfie from a
fitting before remembering that the launch hasn’t happened yet.
He confuses Alex and George during a dinner in SoHo because he spends half the evening
staring at his phone with a grin he apparently cannot control.
And Oscar, somehow, picks up the phone every time. He replies to messages that are
objectively ridiculous. Sends photographs of the dolphin that has apparently decided they’re
buddies now, ambushing him whenever he takes his board out. Types entire paragraphs
analysing Australia’s cricket season despite the fact that Lando understands approximately
none of it.
And yet he downloads the official cricket app anyway, checking scores that mean absolutely
nothing to him just to see how Australia is doing.
Oscar is busy himself during January. The MCSR season has ended, meaning the playoffs
have begun, where the highest-ranked players compete against one another in something
vaguely similar to the Midoffs, only considerably more serious.
Lando doesn’t miss a single one of Oscar’s games. And if he does – because Zak is making
him sit through a McLaren retrospective or some interminable sponsor obligation – he
follows an update account on Twitter that keeps everyone informed about every split.
Oscar plays magnificently. If anything, watching him compete only worsens whatever
unfortunate condition Lando appears to have developed. 
Oscar has always been impressive. Lando knew that. But there is something uniquely
captivating about watching him operate at the absolute limit of his abilities; watching him
carve through a run with impossible precision, making decisions so quickly that Lando barely
understands what’s happening before Oscar is already thirty seconds further ahead.
Twitter pundits spend days pontificating about it afterwards; about how Oscar seems to be
playing better than ever, about how they’re surprised he found the time to improve this much
while simultaneously coaching in the Midoffs.
And for some reason, seeing people praise him like that makes something coil low and hot in
Lando’s gut. Because they’re right, Oscar is extraordinary.
Lando engages with the playoffs openly. He tweets about them, retweets Oscar whenever he
advances another round, and for the final he even posts a picture of himself watching from
his hotel room, tagging him.

look at my coach @op81. he’s even better when he gets to play the game himself
The MCSR community is, by all accounts, delighted. Delighted that he’s putting this many
eyes on a niche, deeply geeky corner of the internet; delighted that one of the biggest athletes
in the world has somehow become emotionally invested in Minecraft speedrunning.

Every day when he logs on, he finds hundreds of tweets steeped in unbridled joy over the fact
that Lando Norris and OP81 apparently remain very close friends.
Sometimes Lando wonders what they would say if they knew just how close they actually
are.
That there is no innocent explanation for this anymore, for this feverish obsession they seem
to have developed for one another.
The fact that his mind is constantly on Oscar; contemplating him, wondering what he’s doing.
And if Oscar is kind enough to tell him, then Lando simply spends the next several hours
imagining it instead.
He is uniquely distracted by him. A part of his mind is always elsewhere, always occupied,
and with every second that passes, he comes relentlessly closer to the moment when he will
finally be standing in front of him. When he will no longer have to imagine.
Much to the delight of his own fans, Lando has somehow managed to maintain a halfway
consistent streaming schedule even after the Midoffs ended and he’d been crowned the
surprising champion of halfway-average Minecraft speedrunners.
And he streams with Oscar all the time.
Sometimes they’re joined by Max and some of Oscar’s friends as well – Feinberg, edcr and
Hax – exploring different modes of the game together. Oscar and Fein introduce Lando to
AA, another subgenre of Minecraft speedrunning where the goal is to obtain every
achievement in the game; something Lando is catastrophically bad at and which, to his
immense satisfaction, Fein also manages to beat Oscar at.
But mostly, Lando and Oscar stream alone.
They’ve even started a Minecraft world, where they spend most of their time doing
absolutely nothing productive. They wander around. Begin projects. Get distracted. End up
bantering instead of actually playing.
The fans eat it up.
At some point, Lando has clearly been absorbed into the wider Minecraft ecosystem entirely;
elevated to the status of honorary Minecraft streamer and becoming a fixture of Oscar’s
online presence almost as much as he is of Formula One.
The frenzy surrounding them during the Midoffs had been one thing, these two months
leading up to Melbourne are another entirely.
Because their friendship doesn’t just deepen in private – evolving from something exciting
and novel and almost dizzying in its intensity into an indispensable part of his daily routine –
the public perception of it changes too.
Lando scrolls through it every evening. Obsessively. 

they’re in love. they are actually in love
they make me lose my fucking mind. i literally can’t sleep or eat. i only think about them.
what they’re doing. what giggly conversation they’re probably having right now
PUT ME IN THE CUCK CHAIR IMMEDIATELY
if they randomly stop speaking one day we all know exactly what happened. i’ve been
hurt before
PLEASE DON’T EVER BECOME A STRANGER WHOSE LAUGH I COULD
RECOGNISE ANYWHERE

Ever since Oscar started going more openly by his real name – part of his audience slowly
adjusting to it, while half his fandom stubbornly continues calling him OP – they have
become Landoscar.
Lando and Oscar. A single unit, and something that freaks Lando out considerably more than
it delights him.
Do they have any idea what’s actually happening behind the scenes? Do they know that
Lando is failing – absolutely and spectacularly failing – at bagging the man?
Do they have even the faintest understanding of how difficult it is to walk the line between
wanting to crawl directly through the screen and into Oscar’s personal space, and desperately
trying not to push too hard?
Trying not to ask for too much, to want too much. Trying not to do anything that might make
Oscar retreat back behind the walls Lando’d spent months painstakingly dismantling.
Anything that might make him reconsider. Anything that might make him rescind his promise
to meet him in Albert Park.
Lando genuinely wonders how he does it. How he manages to pretend that being Oscar’s
friend is enough. To refer to him as such in front of everyone who isn’t Max – including
Oscar himself – while feeling vaguely sick at the thought that this might be the optimum of
their relationship.
That he’ll see him in Melbourne and Oscar will simply be a good friend. Will still hold him at
arm’s length. Will greet him with one of those awkward bro-hugs Lando himself hands out
far too freely, a clap on the back and a grin, entirely unaware that Lando has spent the last
two months slowly losing his sanity.
Over those two months, Lando’s feelings – realised during a moment of weakness and
promptly confessed to Max, his ever-patient priest on the other side of the confessional booth
– have unfortunately only intensified.
They’ve begun to engrain themselves into the very fabric of his thinking; an undercurrent
running beneath his internal monologue, a subtext lurking underneath almost every
conversation he has.

Oscar has, on occasion, sent more glimpses of himself. 
He seems to have realised that excessive gatekeeping is ultimately futile anyway, considering
Lando is going to see him in March.
Still, the photographs remain fragments. And Lando realises, with increasing alarm, that he is
starting to fall in love even with those fragments in an almost obsessive way.
Here, a glimpse of his hair when Oscar sends him a picture of the morning sun spilling across
his pillow as proof of life after sleeping for almost twenty-four hours following one of his
characteristic fifty-hour benders.
There, a photograph of Tangerine, the despotic groundskeeper cat, where Lando can just
make out Oscar’s shadow reflected faintly against the pavement.
A picture of his laptop screen; the one time Oscar works from his balcony while editing a
video, the sunlight bright enough that Lando can see the reflection of part of his neck in the
display. Pale, mole-riddled and sturdy.
Lando collects all of these fragments of him – these scattered glimpses into the body of the
man who lays his soul bare to him night after night on their calls – like a complete maniac,
obsessively, hungrily.
He revisits them during stretches of boredom. During meetings. In moments of
understimulation. Or simply when he misses Oscar’s voice too much and needs something to
tide him over until the next call.
He’s got them all saved in a folder on his phone. Seven photographs. And a handful of
clandestine screenshots from rare video calls.
Sometimes Lando wonders if Oscar has a folder like the one he keeps on his own phone; a
folder which, Lando suspects, has to be considerably fuller, because Lando sends him a lot of
pictures of himself. Partly because he doesn’t have to gatekeep himself from Oscar, but also
because he’s shamefully addicted to the way Oscar still reacts to them.
Especially when Lando cranks the risk up and sends him a shirtless picture from the gym
under the pretense of wanting to show him a bruise he’d acquired from falling over a chair in
his hotel room the night before. 
The bruise sits there beneath his costal arch, dark and faintly misshapen, but Lando has taken
enough thirst traps in his life to choose the angle with ulterior motives.
Or when he sends him a picture right after having jerked off, his thoughts full of Oscar,
sometimes even propping his phone up against his knee so he can stare at one of his elusive
seven pictures while he goes at it.
Of course, he doesn’t tell Oscar under what circumstances those pictures come into being.
But he gets a kick out of making it as obvious as possible anyway, the insinuation woven into
the picture itself.

In his flushed cheeks. The enraptured look in his eyes. The state of his hair.
And he gets an even greater kick out of inventing perfectly innocuous explanations for his
appearance. Just had a near-death experience changing a lightbulb. Hopped out of the sim.
The new car is great.
He imagines Oscar catching his drift every single time despite the accompanying explanation,
and there’s a part of him that hopes Oscar saves those pictures as well; that he zooms in on
Lando’s lips, or his cheeks, the line of his jaw, the tiny beads of sweat gathered at the side of
his throat, visible only if you stare long enough.
He hopes that Oscar’s hand cramps into the bedsheets, his other hand holding his phone,
Lando’s image glowing on the screen while he wrestles with the urgent desire to dishonour
the picture; to sully the purity of their friendship.
You cannot use pictures of your friends as wank material.
And while Lando violates this particular unspoken rule on a near-daily basis, he hopes that
Oscar does too. That he feels just as guilty when he can’t control himself, when his breathing
grows shallow and the dim glow of his phone illuminates the shameful act of going too far.
The thought finishes Lando off every time. Oscar being just as desperate, just as consumed
by guilt. Just as incapable of resisting the temptation to step across the boundary of a
friendship they both claim to honour so much.
Maybe he’s projecting. Maybe this is simply what keeps him sane during those strange,
elusive months between December and March; the impossible hope that he isn’t the only
loser in this friendship constantly stepping over the boundaries and rules they’ve so carefully
established.
But sometimes Oscar’s voice sounds just a little rougher after Lando sends him a picture
several hours into a call. Sometimes he changes the subject whenever Lando so much as
brushes against the topic of Magui. Sometimes he asks questions that seem almost impossibly
subtle in hindsight. Questions about love. About dating. About what Lando wants from a
relationship.
And Lando, incapable of keeping his mouth shut, promptly spills his guts: about how badly
he needs physical affection, about how important intimacy is to him. About how he can’t help
draping himself all over his friends, especially after a few drinks.
And afterwards, Oscar starts talking about Melbourne again.
That’s the thing: Oscar almost never brings Melbourne up himself. It’s usually Lando talking
about the race, about logistics, about contingencies, about where they’re meeting and when
and how they’ll find each other.
From Oscar’s side, it all remains frustratingly vague. Almost as though he’s still quietly
searching for reasons not to show up.

And yet, whenever Lando starts talking about touch, about affection, about how much
physical closeness matters to him, Oscar suddenly becomes aware of his own corporeality.
Suddenly he enters the conversation. Suddenly he inserts himself into the imagined
geography of their first meeting somewhere in the McLaren hospitality suite at Albert Park.
It cannot be a coincidence: it has to be some sort of knee-jerk reaction. An attempt to remind
Lando that he may be a voice now, but one day soon he’ll be a body too.
A body Lando will be able to stand beside, a body Lando will be able to touch. A body
capable of returning the gesture.
Lando thinks about their first hug more often than he should: imagines being swallowed up
by him, Oscar’s arms coming around his shoulders. His hands briefly brushing his waist.
The last night in Monaco, before Lando departs on the odyssey towards Australia – a journey
that will ultimately consume almost an entire twenty-four hours – is spent on one final stream
with Oscar. 
Most of his things are already packed, and a car will pick him up at four in the morning to
take him to Genoa, where he’ll catch a flight together with Charles and Carlos; something he
is genuinely looking forward to, considering that spending time with Carlos is almost always
a good idea.
Oscar and him are streaming together, playing on their server, with Feinberg and Hax
dropping by briefly before disappearing off to do their own thing again, leaving only the two
of them behind. Of course, none of their viewers know that this is the last stream they’ll ever
do before meeting in person, though plenty of them seem determined to find out, either by
wagering increasingly confident guesses or outright demanding confirmation that the
Melbourne meet-up is actually happening.
Lando can’t shake the feeling that the atmosphere between him and Oscar is a little strange;
not uncomfortable, not awkward, but threaded through with the awareness that whatever
happens in Melbourne, they will never quite return to this version of things again – to the
easy rhythm of their online friendship, to the soft banter that fills the spaces between games,
to this strange stretch of time when they were only this.
And even though Lando wants to be in Oscar’s presence desperately, wants to stand in front
of him and finally look at him properly, to take his measure with his own two eyes rather than
through reflections and shadows and photographs, he cannot help feeling a sort of premature
grief for this era of their friendship. 
What if they discover they don’t get along in real life at all? What if everything suddenly
becomes odd? What if some subtle stiltedness settles over them and retroactively poisons
moments like this one, turning all these late-night calls and streams into relics of something
that only ever worked at a distance?
That night, Lando is so nervous that he can barely focus on anything. He laughs too hard at
things that aren’t objectively that funny, gets distracted every five minutes, and somehow
accomplishes even less than usual despite the fact that he and Oscar had originally intended

to spend the evening grinding one last time before the Formula One season swallows Lando
whole again: gathering resources, collecting diamonds, and working towards Lando’s latest
obsession after he’d watched a YouTube video and decided he now absolutely needed to
acquire every armour trim in the game.
Oscar, of course, humours him, and Lando already knows that Oscar will end up doing most
of the work anyway, considering he is approximately one hundred times faster at everything
related to Minecraft. They’ve beaten the dragon in their world already, and Oscar has
acquired Elytras for both of them so they can fly together across the map, though Lando still
manages to faceplant into the terrain with alarming regularity, forcing Oscar to rescue his
belongings until Lando eventually makes the long trek back from spawn.
Chat, unsurprisingly, adores this dynamic; adores Oscar’s patience, the way he never seems
particularly bothered by the fact that Lando begins half a million different projects, ropes
Oscar into all of them, and then promptly forgets about them half an hour later when a new
idea captures his attention. Every time Lando logs on for the next stream, entire tasks have
mysteriously completed themselves in his absence: resources neatly sorted into chests,
unfinished projects discreetly brought to completion, a fresh set of armour waiting for him
after he’d managed to fall into the void and lose everything.

how small lando’s tolerance for frustration is,

On their last night as online friends, as this unexpected and entirely unforeseen dynamic duo
that has somehow become everyone’s collective fixation over the winter break, Lando
decides that Oscar absolutely has to assist him in killing the Warden; the most powerful mob
in the game, and one that players are generally supposed to avoid rather than actively hunt
down.
Lando, however, has become seized by the peculiar urge to challenge himself. He’s almost
trying to complete a bucket list that exists nowhere except inside his own head; a catalogue of
experiences that have to be ticked off before he can consider himself fully initiated into
Minecraft. Besides, if things somehow go sideways in Melbourne, he thinks, there is a very
real possibility that he will never touch this game again.
Like usual, Oscar indulges him. He tries to prepare him, tries to teach him at least some
semblance of strategy, but Lando has no interest in it. He wants to throw himself into the
Deep Dark and be hit with blindness. He wants to hear his character’s heartbeat thundering in
his ears. He wants the armour trim that has been eluding him for weeks now, always just
barely out of reach.

The entire ordeal is profoundly embarrassing.
Lando screams, dies, runs, dies again, and somehow manages to spawn what feels like an
entire army of Wardens in the process, while Oscar hovers nearby laughing, attempting to
throw him emergency golden apples or explain for the seventeenth time how sneaking works.
Lando, meanwhile, remains committed to the strategy of charging directly at the problem and
hoping for the best.
At some point Oscar casually reveals that he’d already found the armour trim quite a while
ago, while Lando had been busy getting himself repeatedly murdered.
Lando immediately acknowledges defeat, then snatches it out of the air the moment Oscar
throws it to him.
“Twelve down, six to go,” he announces both to himself and chat. “Once I’m back from the
first leg of the season, we’ll tackle the rest.”
Oscar just snorts. “Sure.”
“Don’t you dare finish collecting them without me.”
“Oh, I wouldn’t dare,” Oscar replies, and his voice carries that familiar softness that attentive
viewers have long since christened his Lando Voice. “You’re much too adorable when you
get excited over finding those trims. I’d hate to steal your thunder.”
Reliably, predictably, Lando blushes. And chat, naturally, loses its collective mind.
Their flirting has become considerably more aggressive since the end of December as well. It
spends most of its time balanced delicately on the line between two men who are entirely
comfortable with their sexuality and something that looks suspiciously like unapologetic
coquetry. 
Sometimes Lando finds himself rewatching clipped highlights on Twitter afterwards,
screaming wordlessly into his pillow before inevitably calling Max to complain about the fact
that gauging Oscar might genuinely be the most difficult thing he has ever attempted.
“I can always tell when people are interested in me,” he’d whined to his best friend, who has
now spent the better part of two months listening to the same crisis increase steadily in
intensity. “But if I can’t actually see him–”
“Shut up, you annoying, coy-playing little fuck,” Max had finally erupted. “You’re genuinely
delusional if you don’t think that man wants you. I am sick and tired of watching you twirl
your hair around your fingers, kick your legs, and ask me like a fucking high schooler
whether the hot guy from the other class looked at you across the schoolyard. Yes, he did.
Yes, he wants you. Now do something about it and stop bothering me.”
Do something about it. That’s considerably easier said than done. What exactly is Lando
supposed to do about it?

Threading the needle between not completely losing face the moment he finally beholds
Oscar’s face for the first time and somehow making sure Oscar understands that Lando wants
him, entirely and without reservation, is already going to require every ounce of social
aptitude he possesses; and he isn’t entirely convinced he’ll be able to rely on any of it once
the moment actually arrives.
As their stream finally fizzles out, transitioning into their customary post-stream call after
Oscar has gone through his donos – they are his income, after all, whereas Lando has long
since turned his off, considering he makes enough money elsewhere – Lando leans back in
his chair and slowly spins in a circle while listening to Oscar say goodbye to his viewers.
He’s already logged off, waiting for Oscar to reappear.
“Hi,” Oscar says shortly after the familiar Discord notification announces his return.
“Hi,” Lando replies, unable to suppress the grin spreading across his face. If Oscar has a
Lando Voice, then Lando definitely has an Oscar Grin. “Can you believe that was the last
stream we’ll ever do before the great meet-up?”
“It feels completely surreal,” Oscar admits, and Lando can hear him pacing around his
apartment, like he always does after a stream, trying to bleed off some of the excess energy
from having spent hours folded into the same position. It’s the only time Lando catches
glimpses of the athlete Oscar used to be.
Lando leans further back in his chair, chewing thoughtfully on his lip as he tries to figure out
how to approach this.
The idea has seized hold of him suddenly and completely, and if he’s ever going to do it, then
surely now is the moment; surely now is the time to allow a degree of honesty into their
relationship that he has, so far, carefully denied himself. But first, he needs to test the waters.
He thinks on it long and hard, but he’s suddenly far too nervous to formulate any sort of
strategy.
“Osc, there’s something I want you to know about me,” he blurts out after a moment, his
heart suddenly beating somewhere in the vicinity of his throat, making him sound
considerably squeakier and far less like the image of self-control and solemn honesty he’d
been aiming for.
“Jesus,” Oscar snorts. “What are you dropping on me now? Scared I’m going to cop out?
Banking on it?”
“Don’t be ridiculous,” Lando chides, feeling his heartbeat only accelerate. “It’s actually
something only my closest friends know about me. And my family.” He pauses for a
moment. “It’s something I can only really tell the closest people in my life because it is... in
essence... too volatile to ever be allowed to make its way out of this circle.”
Oscar doesn’t say anything, and Lando can’t tell whether he’s confused or simply trying to
help him keep his train of thought. He knows him like that.

“Which is, uh, me saying that I trust you. Trust you a lot.”
Lando begins chewing on his lip. This conversation is never easy. Though most people
usually look at him afterwards with a forgiving sort of smile, as if to say, oh, Lando, there
was really no need to make this so ceremonial. Nobody is ever particularly surprised.
“Well, I am honoured,” Oscar says carefully, evidently trying to gauge the seriousness of the
conversation. It is a fairly abrupt pivot from their stream, considering Lando has dropped this
on him approximately five seconds after he’d joined the call. “I will keep your secrets.”
“I know that,” Lando says, unable to stop a slightly shaky laugh. “I hope you’ll be able to
keep them better than I kept yours.”
Oscar laughs at that; warm, fond, and entirely free of resentment in a way that makes Lando
realise, then and there, that there is no part of Oscar that still holds his slip-up against him.
“I don’t know where to start,” Lando admits. “Because I’ve been lying to you. And that’s
been shitty of me. But it’s, uh, part of this.”
“Lying to me?” Oscar sounds genuinely puzzled.
“About the nature of my relationship with my, uh, girlfriend.”
“Oh.”
Oscar says only that single word, but Lando hears it anyway; the slight withdrawal, the fact
that Lando has brought him into this conversation, softened him up with all this ceremony
and sincerity, only to start talking about Magui again – a topic that does not exactly rank
among Oscar’s favourites.
“Alright.”
“Magui has been in my life for more than two years now,” Lando says after a moment. “She’s
a good friend of my best mate’s girlfriend, and we brought her in to help with some...
rumours about me.”
He listens anxiously to the silence on the other end of the call. Does Oscar understand
already? Or is he going to have to be more explicit?
Oscar doesn’t do him the favour of voicing whatever is going through his mind, and so Lando
finds himself forced further out onto the plank.
“Very persistent rumours about me,” he continues, and still Oscar says nothing. “Rumours
that could potentially prove career-destroying.”
“I see,” Oscar says. Lando cannot, in a million years, decipher his tone. So he keeps going.
“Remember that conversation we had a while back? About how I was convinced that some
drivers on the grid are, well…” He clears his throat. “Leaning the other way?”

Oscar doesn’t answer immediately, and Lando can feel panic beginning to creep up his spine.
But he’s come too far now, and if he’s being honest with himself, he doesn’t want to walk it
back anyway.
“The reason I’m so sure about that,” Lando says, the words finally spilling out of him like a
tide breaking free, “is that I am... one of them.”
“You’re one of them,” Oscar repeats.
And Lando still cannot read his tone.
“I’m very gay,” Lando says at last. The words come easier once they’ve started. “Extremely
fucking gay. Not interested in women whatsoever. Magui’s on the gayer side as well, though I
