still haven’t entirely figured that woman out.” He laughs nervously. “But, uh, yeah. She helps
me get hook-ups.”
A beat passes. “With men,” he adds helpfully.
Oscar doesn’t say anything for about five seconds. Five seconds that immediately become the
longest and most excruciating five seconds of Lando’s life, during which he feels as though
he could throw up, pass out, or simply lose control of the confines of his body altogether.
Then Oscar clears his throat. “Well, thank you for telling me.”
Lando closes his eyes.
“It means a lot to me that you feel safe enough with me to be honest.”
“Yeah,” Lando says, the word barely making it out of him. “Of course. You’re a good friend.”
“My sister’s gay too,” Oscar says after a moment. “Or bi. Or whatever.”
Oh, God. Lando doesn’t know whether to laugh or cry.
“Which, sorry, is probably a stupid thing to say,” Oscar adds almost immediately. “I didn’t
mean to, uh, diminish what you just told me.”
“You didn’t,” Lando says automatically, though part of him regrets the reassurance the
moment it leaves his mouth. “So who’s gay? H?”
“Yeah,” Oscar says.
A brief silence settles over the call. And Lando immediately knows he’s made it weird.
Oh, God. He should have just kept it to himself. Left it buried in the allusions and
implications between them instead of dragging it out into the open like this.
Because now Oscar is going to start asking himself why Lando told him in the first place.
Whether there had been some ulterior motive behind it.

“I can’t even begin to imagine how hard that must be,” Oscar says after a moment, and Lando
closes his eyes as they begin to burn. “I’ve briefly been in your... world. And I left before
things could permanently take root in me. But it’s not a very... forgiving space for, uh, it.”
“No,” Lando says, only barely managing to bite back a bitter laugh. “Hence the fake
girlfriend.”
“I’m really sorry,” Oscar says. The quiet stretches between them for a moment.
“All is well,” Lando promises him. “It sucks not being able to show... it more openly.
Considering I’m so incredibly possessive and obsessed with physical touch. But I’ve learned
to live with it. It’s not the most important thing in my life, and I’m focusing on the
championship anyway.” He bites his lip. “Which is why I’ve mostly just been getting by on
hook-ups recently.”
“I see,” Oscar says.
And Lando cannot help feeling as though something has shifted between them, something he
can’t quite put his finger on. Not because Oscar seems to have a problem with what he’s told
him – he doesn’t. Not even because he’d technically lied to him.
But because Oscar is now doing that thing. That subtle, overpowering voice-of-reason thing
he always does whenever he wants to gently steer a conversation to its conclusion, usually
after Lando has pushed a little too hard. “You should go to sleep, Lando,” he says, softness
threaded through his voice. “Didn’t you say on stream that your taxi comes at four?”
“Yeah,” Lando replies, his own voice barely above a whisper.
“Well, it’s eleven. You’re downright insufferable on less than six hours of sleep.”
And he sounds exactly like he always does. Deeply indulgent. Soft. Almost outrageously
caring in a way that makes Lando want to punch a wall.
“You’re right,” Lando says. And he feels strangely hollow, even though the conversation has
gone remarkably well. It is, objectively speaking, among the better coming-out experiences
of his life.
It certainly beats Max, who Lando told when they were both seventeen and Lando was still in
the process of accepting the whole thing himself. They’d been absolutely shit-faced,
stumbling back towards some hostel accommodation when Lando had gathered his courage,
and Max had promptly doubled over and vomited into a ditch.
Lando, naturally, had burst into tears. Max had then spent the next five minutes holding him –
 still sporting traces of vomit around his mouth – while Lando sobbed uncontrollably over the
fact that his best friend had immediately emptied his stomach at the revelation.
Only once he’d managed to calm him down had Max explained that he had noticed that
Lando was clearly building towards some sort of confession, and that the surprise of finally

hearing it out loud had simply bypassed every higher cognitive function and gone directly to
his stomach.
And it also beats the countless variations of I could tell, but thank you for finally being
honest.
Oscar has been kind. Understanding. He hasn’t immediately informed Lando that they’d have
to stop being friends. By every conceivable metric, this conversation qualifies as a success.
And still, when the call finally ends and Lando is left sitting alone in his room – for the last
time in a very long while, considering tomorrow begins the long journey towards Australia
and the first leg of the season – he finds himself staring at the dark screen of his phone and
wondering why it feels as though his world is quietly coming apart around him.


II.
 
Something strange happens as soon as Lando touches down in Melbourne: Oscar starts taking
longer and longer to reply to his messages, and when he does, there’s a dryness to them, a
stiltedness that makes Lando violently nauseous.
Lando immediately begins to second-guess himself. Begins to second-guess every single
message he sends. Because when Oscar does reply, he only ever responds to whatever Lando
has said; he doesn’t volunteer anything about himself, about what he’s doing, doesn’t ask
where Lando is, even though they’re currently sharing the same city, the same streets that
Oscar grew up on.
By Friday evening, after two practice sessions during which the only joy Lando manages to
extract is the fact that he’s outperforming his insolent teammate, who continues to ragebait
him at every available opportunity, and with Oscar having shattered his previous record for
ignoring him by a further two hours – leaving Lando hanging for a grand total of seven – he
returns to his hotel suite, slams the door hard enough that the walls tremble in protest, and
promptly calls Max.
His long-suffering best friend picks up almost instantly.
Lando can hear that he’s slightly out of breath, though considering it’s around ten in the
morning in Monaco, he’s probably just stepped off a treadmill somewhere in the middle of a
cardio session. Even so, he appears to have correctly identified that some sort of crisis is
unfolding, judging by the fact that Lando is calling him before he’s even had time to change
out of his McLaren kit.
“What’s up, mate?” he pants.

Lando raises an eyebrow as he drops everything he’s carrying onto the couch in the main
room of the suite. At some point during the day he’d apparently managed to lose his
backpack, though he’s only just noticing now.
“You good?”
“Yeah,” Max says, still slightly breathless. “Bit nauseous. Might’ve overdone it. Whatever.”
His words arrive in a sticky sort of staccato. “Please, shoot. What’s on your mind?”
Now that Max has actually answered, Lando finds himself considerably less eager to bare his
soul. Partly because saying it out loud would make his embarrassment tangible. And partly
because Max suffers from the unfortunate – and, if Lando is being honest, faintly flattering –
 delusion that Lando straight-up pulls. Not that he gets ghosted the second he touches down
in the city of the very person he’s trying to hit.
Of course, this rather perfunctory way of summarising the particular flavour of psychological
torture Lando has been subjected to ever since Oscar seemingly stopped making an effort
doesn’t really do it justice. It doesn’t capture the layers of hurt he’s currently trying to
function through, the way every delayed response seems to excavate a fresh insecurity, but it
is the lingua franca Max and him have always spoken in; the language through which they
have translated every emotional crisis for years.
“I might have fucked up,” Lando says, trudging towards the bathroom and immediately
beginning to peel himself out of the sweat-soaked shirt he’d suffered through on the journey
back from the racetrack in Melbourne’s late-summer heat.
“Oh, God.” Max groans. “I’m terrified already. What happened? Is it Oscar?”
“Well, it isn’t my fault,” Lando immediately says, slipping into his natural defensive posture
– perhaps because he knows Max has legitimate reasons to suspect that Lando might be
partially responsible for any interpersonal disaster.
“What is it?”
Lando starts chewing on his lip as he runs a hand through his curls, immediately getting his
fingers caught in them after a day spent underneath a balaclava and helmet.
“He’s low-key ghosting me,” he admits, and the words feel like confessing a personal failure.
A defeat. Proof that Lando Norris cannot, apparently, escape whatever curse has been placed
upon his love life.
That whatever entity presides over the universe has looked at the man who craves love and
intimacy and affection and devotion more desperately than anyone else and decided that he
should be denied those things at every available opportunity.
“No fucking way,” Max breathes immediately. “Are you taking the piss? Oscar? Ghosting
you?”

“Yeah,” Lando says, pressing both palms against the porcelain rim of the sink as he stares at
himself in the mirror.
He looks paler than usual, which is an impressive achievement for someone with his
complexion. It always manifests the same way; the tan turning faintly ashen, a hint of green
settling beneath his skin. Lando hates how transparent his face is. Hates that he has never
once in his life successfully concealed what he’s feeling.
“He takes an eternity to reply to my texts, and when he does it’s like he’s a completely
different person. Doesn’t engage with me. Doesn’t answer my questions. Doesn’t ask any of
his own.”
Lando hears Max draw a long breath. “That doesn’t sound like him,” he says eventually. The
seriousness in his voice terrifies Lando immediately.
“Yeah,” Lando laughs bitterly. “I’m such a fucking idiot.” A pause. “Because I, uh, came out
to him.”
“You what?” Max’s voice immediately jumps an octave. “Why would you do that?”
“Well, he’s my friend,” Lando says, and instantly hears how stupid and naïve that sounds.
“And I was…” He rubs a hand over his face. “I think I was trying to soft-launch the idea
of…” He trails off. “Man, I don’t know.”
“Oh, God,” Max groans. “You freaked him out.”
“Yeah, I know that now.” Lando continues staring at his reflection. “I am such a fucking
idiot. Why the fuck couldn’t I just keep my giant mouth shut?”
“How did he react in the moment?” Lando sighs.
"That’s what’s tripping me up. Like Oscar would. He was kind about it. Understanding. Even
empathised with the whole closet situation. Brought it up himself, even.”
“But he didn’t–”
“No, he didn’t,” Lando says bitterly. “Said his sister was gay, though. Which is, like... the
worst thing he could possibly say.”
“Why?”
“Because it massively reduces the odds of him being gay himself.”
There is a brief silence. Max sounds genuinely stunned. “What kind of logic is that?”
Lando sighs. “I don’t know. The kind of weird logic my brain is serving me right now.”
Max falls quiet again, evidently trying to think of something useful to say. “I can see how that
might, once again, be your dominant reading of the situation,” he says eventually. “But may I
offer an alternative?”

“Sure,” Lando says, because what else is there to do.
“I think he’s freaking out about meeting you,” Max says. “He made a promise tied to
something that he knew was impossible. But then you actually did it. You pulled off the
impossible, and suddenly he had no choice but to follow through on his end of the bargain.
His own bargain, really.” He pauses. “That was December. March probably felt completely
unreal back then. Meeting you felt unreal. But now you’re actually there. You’re in
Melbourne. You’re, at any given moment, less than ten miles away from him.”
Lando swallows.
“And now he has to do it,” Max says. “Now he has to actually meet you. And maybe that’s
why he’s retreating.”
Lando hates it. Hates that he can feel his reflection beginning to blur as his eyes start to burn.
“But what’s so bad about meeting me?” he asks quietly. “If he really didn’t like me, then why
did he spend so much time with me when I was still in Europe? It can’t have been that much
of a struggle for him, the way he talked to me. The way he engaged with me.”
“Of course not,” Max says with a deep sigh. “I don’t know why he’s like this. I genuinely
don’t. Maybe you did freak him out. Maybe he’s having some sort of crisis. Or maybe he’s
realising that this is very real now. That he’s actually about to meet the guy he’s idolised
since he was, what, fourteen? That’s got to mess with your head.”
“But he should talk to me about it.”
“Maybe he’s afraid you’ll take it as a personal rejection.”
“I fucking am.” Lando can already see the rims of his eyes beginning to redden. God, he’s
such a loser. “You know I am.”
“I’m not defending him,” Max says quickly. “I’m just saying that this doesn’t sound like the
Oscar you’ve spent months talking about.” He pauses. “Don’t do what you always do.”
Lando immediately knows where this is going. 
“Don’t retreat at the first sign of rejection. Don’t disappear into your little woe is me spiral
and convince yourself it’s over before you’ve even asked a single question. You need to
confront him. Ask him what’s wrong. Make him tell you what the problem is.”
Max’s voice turns firmer. “You need to push. Don’t give up now. That’s the worst thing you
could possibly do.”
“But I feel pathetic.” Lando leaves the bathroom, wanders back into the living room of the
suite, and throws himself face-first onto the couch. “Like, he’s supposed to be the fanboy.
Why am I acting like the one who’s–”
“Because you’re in love with him,” Max cuts in. The words land with remarkable little
ceremony. “It’s natural to feel like this.”

Lando groans into a cushion.
“But show him that you care. Show him how much you need him to show up.” Max’s voice
softens slightly. “Maybe that’ll make whatever’s going on in his head right now a little
easier.”
Lando can’t say he likes the advice Max is giving him. It’s much more rational, much less
vindictive than he’d hoped for. Almost suspiciously so. It’s almost not Max.
“Fine,” he says gloomily. “Thank you. I’ll try.”
“Keep me updated.” Max sounds so pitifully earnest that Lando immediately hates
everything even more.
“I will. Thanks, mate.”
“My pleasure.”
After hanging up, he sits there for a moment, exactly where Max left him, staring at his
phone. Almost automatically, he opens Discord and begins to type.
 

landonorris
have i done something to upset you? if yes, please tell me. because i want to make it
right.

 
Then he throws his phone away and disappears into the shower to wash off the sweat and
grime of the day, taking his own sweet time beneath the hot water, nurturing the increasingly
desperate hope that once he steps back out there will be a message waiting for him. Against
all odds.
He even tidies up his hotel room a little afterwards, changing into a white shirt and jeans.
Maybe he’ll go out later. He knows Alex and George might be up for something, and the last
thing he wants is to spend the entire evening sitting in his hotel suite waiting for a text that
never arrives.
When he finally feels brave enough to summon the courage, he walks over to the sofa where
he’d abandoned his phone face-down amongst the cushions and picks it up.
To his utter surprise, there is a message waiting for him.
 

OP81
no. you could never

but about sunday. i can’t make it. i’m sorry
 
Lando stares at the screen for a moment. It almost feels like dreaming, like the world has
shifted half a degree on its axis without registering to anyone else but him. Like gravity is
now fractionally off. Like some ancient and invisible mechanism responsible for keeping the
universe stitched together has suddenly begun to splutter and fail.
He reads the message again. And again. And again. The words do not change.
His fingers move before his thoughts can catch up.
 

landonorris
this is a joke right?

 
And then he waits. Stares at the screen for what has to be fifteen minutes.
There is no reply. Not even the typing indicator makes a brief appearance. Nothing.
And Lando sits there, incredulous and seething and mourning all at once, his insides
simultaneously ablaze with anger and frozen rigid with shock, feeling as though someone has
both reached into his chest and pulled the floor out from underneath him.
Finally, he manages to pull himself free, sends Max a wordless screenshot, and slides his
phone into his pocket. There’s genuinely nothing left for him to do.
Melbourne should have been the highlight of his year, something he’d been looking forward
to from the moment the calendar had turned over and the new season had begun – and instead
it seems to have become his Waterloo.
Yet again, Lando has been defeated by his own stubborn insistence on believing that one day
things will be different.
That somehow, through all the impossibilities of fate, somebody’s red string had wrapped
itself around his little finger; had snagged there and pulled him forward, unseen and unfelt for
most of it, towards a person who had become something to him that he’d once believed to be
impossible.
A person capable of absorbing the full force of his affection without recoiling from it. A
person who seemed endlessly patient with his clinginess. A person who listened to everything
Lando told him with a sort of unwavering attentiveness, as though each thought Lando
voiced was the most important thing he had ever been entrusted with.

But perhaps that relationship had only ever functioned because they were never in the same
room. Never in the same country, never even on the same continent.
Perhaps it only worked because there had always been a medium between them; a screen, a
voice call, a slight reverb in Oscar’s microphone, the invisible distance imposed by the path
between servers and satellites. Because everything they told one another first had to travel
halfway around the world before it arrived.
Maybe that’s the truth of it. Because Lando knows, if he’s being honest, that he cannot
entirely blame Oscar for this.
He had been the one constantly pressing against Oscar’s boundaries, and there is some truth
to the fact that Oscar never seemed particularly capable of saying no to him. 
And Max is right, too. 
Back when Oscar had made that promise, they had both been intoxicated by the Midoffs;
high on victory, high on adrenaline, high on the absurdity of what they’d managed to
accomplish together. March had felt impossibly distant back then. Meeting Lando had
probably felt about as realistic as promising to visit the moon.
And Lando understands now that the promise had been made under a kind of duress. Made
with the knowledge that the ball was already in his court.
Made after Lando had somehow managed to pull off the impossible, despite Oscar spending
most of the tournament trying to prevent exactly that outcome. Oscar had only truly given
him his blessing when it had become the deciding condition of the final.
He never wanted to meet him, Lando realises now. And it has taken him two and a half
months to finally understand it.
Sure, stringing Lando along until the very last possible moment if he’d never planned on
showing up is objectively shitty too – Lando doesn’t deny that – but he cannot help taking the
brunt of the blame upon himself.
He never once stopped to consider what Oscar wanted.
Was much, much too entranced by the idea of finally being able to touch him, of allowing a
sense other than hearing to take stock of the person Lando has become so undeniably
attached to.
That’s one of the character traits he’s less proud of; the fact that he doesn’t always take into
account what other people want. That he’s domineering in the way that people often become
when they’ve spent their entire lives getting what they wish for.
It works in almost every other aspect of his life. It has certainly worked in his career. 
Yet it has never once worked when it comes to love: because you cannot force someone to
love you. God knows Lando wishes he could.

Wishes there was some way to redirect all that yearning, all that wanting, all that desperate
desire to be loved towards himself instead. To make somebody ache for him the way he aches
for love. To make somebody look at him and feel the same inexorable pull that has governed
so much of his own life.
He has to begin admitting something to himself: Oscar might be the single greatest beating
his ego has ever taken.
To have someone come so close to the ideal of love you’ve spent your entire life constructing
in your head, only to be diverted at the very last moment because a different kind of love
resides there – it feels almost biblical in its cruelty. Like a cosmic slap across the face.
To lose a championship because of someone Lando had trusted implicitly, because of
someone whose resentment towards him had apparently been festering beneath the surface
and finally discharged itself into petulance at the worst possible moment – that had already
been difficult enough to swallow.
But to have been this wrong about someone who–
Lando refuses to follow the thought to its logical conclusion. He’s many things. But he is not
a masochist.
And he has always been exceptionally talented at diverting his attention away from the things
inside himself he does not want to take root; the things he does not want trickling down
through the layers of his self-conception until they begin to erode the pillars keeping
everything else upright.
He might be, rather embarrassingly, in love with Oscar.
But he is not going to allow a man who is too cowardly to even show him his face ruin his
season. His comeback.
He drives better when he’s single anyway.


III. 
 
Scoring the first pole of the season, Lando thinks, would probably feel considerably better if
Oscar were somewhere in the garage to witness it. To witness that stellar lap itself.
To watch him shatter the Mercedes’ benchmark by almost four tenths when Lando decides to
gamble on one final run on softs despite already sitting P3, the second row more than
respectable and certainly good enough for the first qualifying session of the year.
But good enough has never been particularly interesting to him. He wants more. He wants to
win.

He wants more than to win. He wants to be untouchable. He wants to dominate.
Wants to make everyone else on the grid look faintly ridiculous for having entertained the
notion that they might be able to compete with him at all.
Because this is his season. He’s coming to collect a title that is long overdue.
A title that already has his name written all over it, even though this is barely the first race
weekend of the year and a thousand things could still happen between now and December.
His performance here matters to him. Not only because it establishes a standard for himself
and for the drivers hoping to challenge him, but because he knows that somewhere, even if he
isn’t here, Oscar is watching.
Oscar hangs over the entire weekend like a dark cloud. He’s watched Lando’s stories, too.
The ones from Friday night after cancelling on him, when Lando had gone out instead,
stubbornly refusing to spend the evening rotting in his hotel room.
Lando derives a particularly petty sort of satisfaction from the fact that every mention of
Oscar on Twitter seems to have devolved into increasingly anxious questions. Is he watching
the race? Has he met Lando yet? What does he think about his favourite driver taking pole on
Australian soil?
People ask him for comments on the season so far, the new regulations, the perennial debate
of Ferrari engines versus Mercedes ones.
Oscar remains entirely silent. He hasn’t streamed since the day of their final stream together,
which is an unusually long absence for him.
If Lando weren’t so furious, he might actually be worried.
Instead, he finds himself indulging in increasingly vindictive fantasies. Oscar sitting
somewhere in the grandstands beneath the merciless Australian sun, wearing the McLaren
merch Lando had sent him, watching the papaya car flash past and realising that he has
fumbled this so catastrophically that there aren’t words for it.
Though he’s probably not at the track. If he were, he could just as easily have accepted
Lando’s offer of paddock passes and spent the weekend hiding in air-conditioned hospitality
suites with complimentary food and drinks.
Oscar never replied to his last message. And ever since then, their Discord chat has remained
silent for the first time in three months.
On Sunday, Lando is at the garage early.
He’d woken before dawn – not by design, but because sleep had been elusive anyway – and
eventually decided there was little point in lying awake staring at the ceiling when he could
just go to the track. Talk to the mechanics, to the strategists. Pretend there were still things
left to prepare.

At some point Jon materialises with breakfast, having apparently reached the stage of their
professional relationship where he can determine Lando’s glycaemic status simply by looking
at his face. Lando doesn’t quite know how to explain that his unhealthy complexion and
general air of defeat have very little to do with blood sugar levels.
Still, he eats. Or at least goes through the motions of eating.
He’s sitting in front of one of the screens, watching simulations of different tyre strategies
scroll endlessly past while he absently chews on something he couldn’t identify if his life
depended on it.
At some point, a group of influencers passes through the garage.
One of McLaren’s marketing executives is shepherding them from station to station, giving
them the exclusive tour experience or whatever the official terminology is, and Lando can
feel their attention settle on him from the opposite end of the garage.
At times he notices phones pointed in his direction. When he glances up from a simulation
Will is running, he can hear breathless giggling from across the room.
Most of them seem more interested in documenting the experience than experiencing it,
filming every square metre of the garage in the hopes of capturing something that signals
exclusivity. The race-winning machinery. The engineers. The driver sitting at the far end of
the room studying data from the first three practice sessions and qualifying: the crowning
glory.
There is one woman, however, who immediately catches his attention. Not because she’s
trying particularly hard to attract it: quite the opposite. She stands slightly apart from the rest
of the group; bony shoulders and large dark eyes made even more striking by bleached hair
and eyebrows.
Lando knows next to nothing about fashion, even though he sometimes pretends he does. But
even he can tell that she’s incredibly... well. Cool.
She’s also the only one who seems genuinely interested in what’s being said. While the others
drift between conversations and photographs, she’s actually listening to the slightly terrified
engineer tasked with explaining the workings of Lando’s car to a group of breathtakingly
beautiful women.
Before they move on, she asks somebody to take a photograph of her next to the car. As she
retrieves her phone afterwards, she glances across the garage. Their eyes meet.
And immediately Lando feels something strange unfurl in his chest: a sudden, inexplicable
feeling of being observed. Seen.
Will eventually has to nudge him with his elbow to redirect his attention towards the data, a
grin already tugging at the corner of his mouth, entirely misreading the situation.

Lando sees her again later. He’s on his way back from the motorhome after a brief pre-race
meeting with Zak and the Brazilian Who Must Not Be Named when he spots her standing in
front of the display celebrating historic McLaren victories.
The thousandth McLaren race start is coming up this season, and there’s an entire exhibition
dedicated to it. Her arms are folded neatly behind her back.
Only now does Lando properly take in what she’s wearing: a cut-up McLaren jersey
reconstructed into something resembling a corset, fragments of his own merchandise woven
into the patchwork. A long white skirt. Black leather boots.
She is standing in front of a display about Bruce McLaren, reading the information plaque
with genuine concentration.
Lando should keep walking, as the drivers’ parade is approaching, and he should be in the
garage.
Instead, he slows. Then stops. Then wanders over until he’s standing beside her.
"Without him, there’d be no me," he says, pointing to Bruce.
She turns towards him immediately. Those large eyes settle on his face. And once again,
there’s something about her expression that he cannot quite decipher. Lando opens his mouth
to say something else about Bruce, instead, an entirely different thought takes hold.
"Sorry," he says. "Do I know you?"
She looks him up and down and then shakes her head, extending her hand for him to take.
“I’m Hattie,” she says, her Australian accent immediately noticeable as he automatically
takes her hand and gives it a proper shake. 
There’s something familiar about her voice – lower than he’d expected – and something
about the cadence of it tugs at him instantly, a recognition so sharp it seems to cut clean
through him. 
“You’d know me as H, though.” She tilts her head ever so slightly. “And I do think you know
my brother very well.”
It is impossible to properly describe the reaction these words have on him: there is a sudden
convergence inside his head; a dozen seemingly unrelated observations rushing together all at
once.
The cut-up jersey. Oscar’s offhand prediction that H would probably take one look at the
merch he’d sent him and turn it into a corset.
The way she’d looked at him from across the garage as though she knew him. Which she
does. Because Oscar has spent the last two months talking about him.

Because somewhere in the endless stream of stories and banter and completely
inconsequential conversations that have carried them through those months, Oscar has told
his sister about him often enough that she recognises him not as Lando Norris, Formula One
driver, but simply as Lando, his brother’s friend.
And then there are her eyes. Brown, and astonishingly captivating. And before he can stop
himself, before he can redirect the thought anywhere more reasonable, Lando finds himself
wondering whether Oscar’s are the same shade.
“You’re... an influencer?” is all he manages, despite the fact that there are about fifty more
important questions trying to claw their way out of him.
“Yeah,” she replies, amusement tugging at the corner of her mouth. “Seems a propensity for
niche internet fame runs in the family.”
Now that she’s disclosed her relation to him, Lando genuinely wonders how he failed to
realise it sooner. Their voices sound incredibly alike. Their accents are almost identical. Even
the slightly sarcastic inflection is exactly the same.
He’s never known how to imagine Oscar, and he certainly doesn’t have much more of a clue
now that he’s standing in front of what he’s fairly certain is his favourite sister; her hair
bleached so aggressively that any trace of its natural colour has long since vanished, robbing
him of yet another avenue towards imagining Oscar. 
She’s much too angular, much too distinctly feminine for him to abstract Oscar from her
entirely – but there is something in the arch of her eyebrows, something faintly sardonic, that
he immediately suspects belongs to him as well. The brown of her eyes has to be hereditary.
Hattie notices him studying her, taking her in, and something in her gaze softens – as though
she understands that he isn’t really looking at her at all. That he’s searching for traces of
somebody else.
“Does your brother know you’re here?” Lando finally asks.
Hattie watches him for another moment before shaking her head.
“Nah,” she says. “Didn’t tell him your team invited me. Seemed... tactless. Considering, uh.”
She grimaces slightly. “Yeah. Everything.”
Something in her tone catches him off guard.
“What do you mean?” he asks. “He could’ve been here. I invited him. He told you about that,
right?”
“Yeah,” Hattie says, adjusting the barrette keeping her impossibly bleached hair tucked
behind her ears. “He told me about that alright.”
“And did he tell you he cancelled on me without an explanation two days ago?” Lando
continues, unable to keep the hurt from bleeding into his voice.

“Yeah,” Hattie repeats. She puffs out her cheeks for a moment, clearly considering how best
to approach this. “Walk with me, Lando.”
She links her arm through his with a naturalness that makes something inside his chest
constrict strangely; a familiarity to the gesture that, despite everything, despite how furious
he still is at her brother, makes him feel as though he’s somehow stepped a little closer to
Oscar as well.
“I want to preface this by saying that there is genuinely nothing my brother wanted more than
to be here,” she says as they begin walking. “To watch the race. To cheer you on. To meet
you, obviously. To come back to Albert Park.”
She glances sideways at him, and she’s almost as tall as he is in her boots. Lando finds
himself completely unable to formulate a response.
“But the truth is that my brother hasn’t been to Albert Park in years,” she continues. “Hasn’t
really been anywhere.”
“What do you mean?”
Hattie furrows her brow, searching for the right words.
“Oh, he’s going to murder me for this,” she mutters. “Actually slime me. He thinks the
correct solution is to swallow it down and stop talking to you before he has to admit the
truth.”
Something ice-cold settles in Lando’s chest. A sharp, immediate panic. He stops walking so
abruptly that Hattie nearly has to stop with him. They haven’t even made it out of the gallery
yet – and they’re standing directly in front of 2019, the year he joined McLaren.
“What are you talking about, Hattie?”
She takes a deep breath, closes her eyes for a moment. Then she looks directly at him, her
hand still resting lightly on his arm.
“Oscar can’t do crowds.”
Lando stares at her. “Can’t do crowds?”
“The official diagnosis is that he’s got a panic disorder,” Hattie continues. “Look, I’m going
to tell you this even though it isn’t really my place, because my brother would sooner bite his
own tongue off than display any sort of weakness in front of you, and me telling you is pretty
much the only way I can salvage what he, in his infinite wisdom and pride, has managed to
fuck up.”
Lando cannot move. Cannot speak. Cannot even seem to draw a proper breath.
It feels immediately wrong to have Hattie standing here telling him something that so
obviously runs contrary to Oscar’s wishes, but at the same time he knows that this is perhaps
the only glimpse he’s ever going to get behind the curtain; the only chance to understand

what Oscar has always been so elusive about, why he is so preternaturally skilled at evading
every question Lando has ever tried to ask.
“At the beginning of the pandemic, he was in a pretty serious car accident,” Hattie says, and
Lando can tell from the way her shoulders instinctively draw up towards her ears that she’s
no longer really standing here beside him. She’s somewhere else entirely. Back there. “He’d
gone out with a few friends from uni. The one driving was drunk, and they ended up on the
wrong side of the road coming back into Melbourne after a day trip.”
“A car accident?” Lando’s mouth feels impossibly dry.
“Yeah,” Hattie says. “It’s why his back is... fucked. It’s not genetic, if that’s what he told you.
It’s a consequence of the accident.”
She shakes her head.
“But that’s almost beside the point. Luckily, nobody died. My brother was hurt the worst, but
he made it through. Spent the first month of the pandemic in a trauma unit while they tried to
put his back back together.”
“Is he...?”
“No.” Hattie immediately shakes her head. “He can walk. He can do almost anything. There
was a lot of rehabilitation involved, and it’s the reason he’s so obsessive about surfing and
working out. His frame takes some of the strain off his back.” She pauses. “He lives a mostly
normal life.”
A beat.
“It’s just that the pandemic really fucked him up. Worse than any of us realised at the time.”
“Fucked him up how?”
“I, uh…” Hattie exhales slowly. “My brother is one of those people who never say anything.
Who thinks asking for help is a weakness. Who would rather crawl into a hole and die than
let someone see him struggling.” There’s something unsteady in her voice now. “I mean, he
almost died.”
Lando says nothing.
“And because of the isolation, and because he was living alone, nobody really realised how
badly he was doing.”
“Badly?” Lando is surprised he can still force the word out.
“He started avoiding going out more and more. At first nobody thought much of it because,
well, we were in a global pandemic. We were all avoiding people. We were all stuck inside.”
“Was that because of the accident?”

“Yeah,” Hattie says after a moment. “At least I think so. I think if the accident had happened
at any other point in his life – if he’d still been going to uni every day, still seeing people
regularly – then maybe it wouldn’t have had the chance to take root the way it did.”
She reaches up and fiddles with her barrette again.
“But by the time the restrictions were lifted, it was already too late. The first time he went
back into the city, just for an afternoon, he had a panic attack.” Her gaze drifts somewhere
over Lando’s shoulder. “It was... pretty harrowing.”
A pause. 
“And out of that came the panic disorder.” She looks back at him. “You know what that is?”
Lando shakes his head.
“It’s when you have a really bad experience once, and afterwards you start subconsciously
avoiding anything that might make it happen again,” Hattie says. “You begin restructuring
your entire life around the avoidance of that fear. Every decision, every routine, everything
becomes about making sure you never end up back there.”
She exhales.
“And pretty soon Oscar realised he couldn’t go out without being terrified that it would
happen again. So he stopped.”
“What do you mean, stopped?”
“He slowly rebuilt his whole life around staying inside. Managed to convince his professors
to let him finish his degree remotely – though, to be fair, he was basically done already
because he did his Master’s on fast-track, the absolute academic overachiever.”
She rolls her eyes fondly. Lando feels another sharp pang. Something else he didn’t know.
Something else he’d always vaguely suspected from the way Oscar seemed to glide around
certain topics whenever they came up.
“He got everyone to deliver everything to him. Groceries. Packages. Whatever he needed.
And he became ridiculously good at Minecraft, then started streaming it too, because he
realised he could actually make a living from it.” She shrugs. “And, frankly, it was the only
career path that accommodated his lifestyle of never leaving his apartment.”
“But…” Lando says after a moment. “He called me from outside. From the ocean.”
“Yeah,” Hattie replies. “There’s a reason he only ever goes out early in the morning or right
before sunset, even though that’s objectively less safe. It’s when the beach near his apartment
is practically empty.”
Lando doesn’t say anything for a while. He can feel Hattie looking at him. “That’s why you
picked up the packages for him.”

“Yeah.” Her answer is soft. “As much as I wish he’d get help, he’s still my brother.” She
pauses. “And, to be honest, I’d kind of held onto the hope that becoming friends with you
would be the thing that finally made him want to.”
“Want to what?”
“Get better.” The words come out almost immediately. “Get professional help. Stop
barricading himself in his apartment. Stop spending every day playing Minecraft and getting
everything delivered to him and only crossing the street to get to the beach.”
Lando looks at her. And he can see exactly how much this hurts – how desperately she misses
him. Not the Oscar who exists now, the one from before. The brother she grew up with. The
brother she remembers.
“When you asked him to come to the race…” Hattie says eventually, shaking her head as
though she still doesn’t quite believe it. “I’ve genuinely never seen him like that.”
Lando swallows, his throat feeling raw.
“It was like…” She searches for the words. “Like the prospect of meeting you had managed
to accomplish something that not even university, or career opportunities, or our mum crying
had been able to accomplish.” She laughs softly, without much humour in it.
“He wanted to.” A pause. “He really, really wanted to.”
The words ache somewhere deep inside Lando.
“Four days ago,” Hattie says, “for the first time in almost twenty-five years of existence, my
brother asked me for help.”
She’s still holding onto his arm, and when a group of mechanics comes striding down the
corridor, Lando automatically guides her towards the side to let them pass.
“We did some... tests,” Hattie says. “We were going to try going into the city. Into crowds.
Into progressively busier places.” She smiles, and there is something deeply sorrowful about
it. “It was awful.”
The words come out almost matter-of-factly.
“And I could see how much it fucking killed him that he couldn’t do it. He nearly passed out
twice. I had to call a taxi and get him back to his apartment before we even made it into the
really bad areas.” She shakes her head. “There was absolutely no chance in hell he was ever
making it to Albert Park.”
Lando doesn’t know what to say. He feels as though something foreign has lodged itself
somewhere inside his chest. Something heavy, something that makes breathing feel strangely
laborious.
“When he texted you on Friday, that was after he’d been basically catatonic for seven hours,”
Hattie continues. “I begged him to tell you the truth. To tell you why he couldn’t make it,

because you were obviously, rightfully going to misinterpret what was happening.”
Her expression darkens.
“But this fucking idiot is too proud for his own good. He still doesn’t want you to know. He’d
genuinely rather lose your friendship than let you see him like this.”
For a moment, Lando just stares at her. Then: “What a fucking moron.”
To his surprise, Hattie gives him a weak smile. “Exactly. And that’s why I’m here.”
“Lando!” Someone calls his name from the other end of the garage. The sound makes him
flinch. 
Right. The parade.
“Wait,” Hattie says, catching him by the wrist before he can move away. She slips her bag
from her shoulder and pulls out a permanent marker.
Then she takes his hand, turns it over, and begins to write on the inside of his wrist, his pulse
fluttering against the tip of her sharpie.
Oscar Piastri.
Beneath it, an address. Apartment complex. Door number.
For a moment, Lando can only stare.
“I can’t just show up if he doesn’t–”
“He wants you to,” Hattie interrupts immediately. The certainty in her voice is almost
startling. “He’s just never going to say it.”


IV.
 
He isn’t even able to summon an ugly, mean sort of triumph from it anymore: winning on
Oscar’s home turf; standing there on the top step of the podium, flanked by George and Kimi
like twin Mercedes pillars, getting to flood the Australian afternoon with the sound of his
own anthem.
The first race win of the season is his, and Lando has to keep reminding himself that it is
supposed to be a herald of greater triumphs yet to come.
In this moment, standing above the crowd while the ceremony unfolds beneath him, feels
right. It feels like a circle closing, like a redemption for everything he suffered through last

season.
Especially because Gabi is nowhere near the podium, having suffered a mechanical DNF that
is almost certainly not his fault but nevertheless fills Lando with a petty sort of glee that he
cannot quite bring himself to feel where Oscar is concerned.
A strange thought occurs to him when he finally gets his hands on the champagne and is
promptly drenched by George and Kimi, while attempting to return the favour and drag his
friend beneath the sticky deluge.
If he’d never joined that godforsaken Minecraft tournament, Oscar probably would’ve posted
about today. 
The thought arrives so suddenly that it almost makes him laugh. Of course, the entire
exercise is futile, Lando would’ve never seen the post – but there still would’ve been a tether
between them.
However tenuous. However one-sided. A thread nonetheless.
In the aftermath of the first victory of the season, Lando finally allows himself to be swept
back into the current of racing, even after climbing out of the cockpit. The old realisation
returns; the one upon which he has built his entire adult life: nothing quiets the incessant
machinery of his thoughts quite like Formula One. Not like the media circus, not like the
relentless sequence of interviews, not like social media obligations and team celebrations and
the endless parade of responsibilities that follow a victory.
He participates gladly. Holds the trophy out whenever he’s asked to. Answers the same ten
questions about his race performance, about his start, about how he managed to keep the
objectively faster Mercedes behind him for the entirety of the race.
It feels good. Winning. 
He’s almost forgotten the rush; to stand indisputably at the summit, to have victory measured
and quantified and rendered incontrovertible by the cold objectivity of numbers. Lando could
grow accustomed to that feeling – to the rush of not merely winning, but knowing that he has
done so on the back of a genuinely exceptional performance.
Maybe there is something to be said for feeling hollowed out. Maybe it takes the absence of
something to fully appreciate how extraordinary it feels to excel at the thing around which he
has built his entire life.
And still, in moments of silence – in the stretches between obligations, in the brief walks
from one station of his day to the next – the thought of Oscar returns.
Whether he watched the race. Lando is almost certain that he did.
And if he watched it, how it made him feel to see Lando dominate like that.
Whether it reminded him of the Midoffs; of the moment Oscar had realised that his coaching
had finally taken root, had found fertile ground in Lando’s peculiar ability to become

outrageously proficient at whatever he truly sets his mind to.
According to Hattie, it kills him that he isn’t here today. And Lando has barely had time to
properly sit with any of it.
Oscar’s affliction. The panic disorder. The fact that coming here had never truly been a
possibility.
Or rather – the fact that it had been. That he’d tried. That for the first time in five years,
Oscar had made a genuine attempt to confront the thing that had held dominion over his life
for so long; had asked his sister for help, had tried to move towards the epicentre of activity,
towards the very place his fractured mind had spent years teaching him to fear as a kind of
pandemonium.
The address on Lando’s wrist is still there – barely legible by now, the ink already beginning
to surrender to sweat and champagne and the constant friction of movement – but he had
taken a picture of it before lowering himself into the car, determined to preserve it.
Now, sitting in the seclusion of his driver’s room, the taste of champagne still lingering on his
tongue and the residue of it still tacky against his skin, he finds himself utterly at a loss as to
what to do with it.
Of course, Hattie has a vested interest in him showing up at her brother’s apartment.
Considering that she, for reasons Lando still struggles to fully comprehend, seems to regard
him as some sort of remedy. A glimmer of possibility. The only thing, apparently, that had
ever managed to coax her brother into pushing against the confines of the life he’d settled
into.
Lando has his full name now, too.
Oscar Piastri.
The initials exactly as he’d imagined them. 
Piastri. A surname that sounds faintly Italian. Is he Italian? Does he speak it?
Lando doesn’t know if he’ll ever find out.
He’s deep in thought, the fresh team kit he’d changed into still clinging unpleasantly to his
skin, when his phone vibrates against the table where he’d abandoned it before the race, not
having checked it once since.
Max, probably. Lando hasn’t told him about Hattie yet. About the revelation her presence
here has brought with it. About finally being able to glimpse the shape of the truth beneath
Oscar’s evasiveness, the things he’d always danced around with such infuriating elegance
whenever Lando ventured too close.
When he picks up the phone, he almost drops it again. 

It’s a Discord notification. And sitting at the top of it is Oscar’s handle.
The message is long. Far longer than the truncated preview allows him to read.
Immediately, Lando feels a wave of dizziness wash through him so abruptly that he has to
brace himself against the edge of the table, his breath leaving him all at once in a sharp rush.
For a moment he simply stands there. Staring.
Then he closes his eyes and tries to gather himself, tries to draw the scattered pieces of his
composure back into something resembling coherence.
Only then does he pick up the phone again and press on the message with trembling fingers.
 

OP81
For years, I’ve celebrated each one of your victories as though they were my own. 
This is something you know, something you’ve caught glimpses of before I could scour
those traces from the internet. I have no explanation for it, considering I had left your
profession before I could ever go pro. 
What was the point of choosing one guy who was slowly rising through the ranks,
someone in whom I could watch the shape of a career that never happened to me unfold
anyway? Why you?
Truth is, I don’t know. I don’t recall the first moment in which I saw you and selected you
as my surrogate, my champion. Back then, I certainly didn’t see any sort of intentionality
in it. It could just as easily have been something that would have subsided as quickly as
it arrived.
But it didn’t. You became better and better.
You made it to F1, you made it into a team that I’d always had a great deal of affection
for – and all the while, I was following you through it all. It felt impossible that the
person I had, one day, decided to follow so devotedly would become as exceptional as
you did.
And the painful thing about it all was knowing, all along, that we’d probably have
gotten along well if I’d stayed in the sport, if our paths had crossed somewhere along
the way. Maybe we could even have briefly shared a team on your way up, though I
don’t delude myself into thinking that I’d ever have made it to F1 myself.
There were times when I genuinely hated the fact that I’d found you back then, that my
stubborn brain had decided to latch onto you.
Because I’m very good at pattern recognition, and I believe some part of me realised
how well we would get along if we ever became friends.

I felt genuine sorrow at not knowing you; at having left that entire world so early, at
following my mother’s wishes, at trying to keep my family together.
I could have had your friendship all along as an avail for persisting, I believed.
So when it was announced that you would, by a stroke of luck, join your friend in that
tournament – a discipline into which I had poured every single ounce of competitiveness
that I’d never found another outlet for – it felt like a sign.
Like there was some truth to it after all. That there was a gravitational pull drawing us
toward one another, if only so that we could finally meet – to put my hypothesis to the
test that we’d get along. 
I would have wagered all ten points that night. I probably would’ve bartered the other
coaches into dropping you if they’d managed to snatch you up instead.
I just needed to have you. To see if I was right. If there was a reason I’d spent years
celebrating your victories, a reason I’d always believed that you and I would get along
so easily.
And then, of course, you know the rest.
You know that in that first call, you completely seized me, captured every inch of my
mind, and reminded me, in all your stubborn exuberance, that of course I’d been right.
You made me give up things about myself that I had always thought I would keep secret
forever.
I wanted you to know me.
Suddenly, my anonymity, my secrecy, my obstinacy became a burden – they became an
obstacle standing between you and the deepest parts of me, between me and the
possibility of truly being known, by you.
I fought it, because I believed I had to. Because I saw myself as entirely without a
chance. Because it felt like overreaching to even entertain the possibility that you might
derive the same joy from my friendship that I did from yours.
I expected you to grow bored of me every day, to drop me, to vanish from my life again.
Because the Lando Norris I’d idolised for years would never have spent his time with
someone like me – a nerdy freak who plays Minecraft for a living and whose closest
friends live halfway across the globe.
But you never did. If anything, you were even kinder, even more captivating than my
imagination had ever managed to make you.
Over the past two months, even after I’d agreed to meet you at Albert Park, you
continued to invest the same effort into me. The same curiosity. The same genuine
interest in understanding me that never once felt invasive or overbearing, but instead

felt like a sincere desire to know me so thoroughly that our friendship might become
something deeper and closer than I ever imagined a Formula One driver of your calibre
would have the time – or inclination – to maintain.
Of course, I know I was an idiot. As though you’re not the person with the richest
emotional life, the most vivid imagination, the greatest capacity for empathy of anyone
I’ve ever met.
Impossibly, you seemed to like me. And, even more impossibly, you seemed to want to
meet me.
And I wanted to meet you, Lando. Believe me. I really wanted to.
But there are things about me that I’ve been deliberately obfuscating, things I cannot tell
you because, frankly, I am too ashamed of them.
You were so brave with me on our last call. But you’re braver than I am, Lando. I am
afraid I will have to insist on my cowardice.
I have nothing, Lando, but the good opinion you hold of me. I am not prepared to
squander that for the slimmest hope of your pity.
You see now that I am unreliable, and cowardly, and weak. You are steadfast, brave, and
selfless.
You live a life in the sun; I merely manage to endure dusk and dawn.
Your victories are witnessed by masses looking up at you. Mine amount to a message on
a loading screen.
I would make myself guilty of an unforgivable overreach if I dared to maintain any claim
upon your friendship. I hope you can forgive me for this, and understand my reasoning.
I am merely correcting my own aggrandizement in regard to the seven points I never
should have wagered on you, and through which I somehow swindled myself into your
friendship.
I will still celebrate your victories as though they are my own. I believe that’s something
I will never tire of. You collect so many of them, after all.
It is still a joy to behold you, and I will forever remember the time I was your friend.
I hope to remain, at least in your memory,
your friend,
Oscar

 

Lando puts the phone face-down on the table in front of him. It lands with a hollow little
sound, while he remains exactly where he is, still and unmoving. He’s read through the entire
message twice already, just to make sure he hasn’t misunderstood it.
There’s a helplessness inside him, an almost impotent rage that rises steadily and ravenously
through him as he repeats Oscar’s words in his head.
This fucking asshole.
Believing he has the right to do this. To break Lando’s heart like this because he thinks he’s
doing the right thing. Because he’s too ashamed to let Lando know the truth.
Well, thanks to powers that seem to elude even Oscar’s meticulous and methodical campaign
of self-sabotage – a meddling sister foremost among them – Lando knows the supposedly
shameful secret Oscar keeps alluding to in his message, as though it is genuinely something
that should diminish him.
As though it is a reason to cast himself out.
Lando turns his hand over and looks at the smudged writing on the inside of his wrist, where
Hattie had left her brother’s address and the entirely unambiguous wish that Lando seek him
out.
Even though he knows Oscar wouldn’t want to see him. Even though he’s made that
abundantly clear in his message.
To his own surprise, Lando doesn’t cry. But he feels a strange hollowness in his chest, a pull
that almost feels as though there’s something trapped inside him, something straining
desperately to get out.
He turns his phone over again. Unlocks the screen. Scrolls through the message once more.
It is abundantly clear that Oscar intended it as a finality; the last thing that would ever be said
between them, the swan song of their almost four-month friendship. And the fact that Lando
knows the reason, knows why Oscar believes he has to do this, only makes it more
outrageous that he genuinely thinks Lando would ever condemn him for it.
Is this really what he thinks of him? After everything? After months of baring his soul to
him? After Lando let him in on the deepest secret he himself harbours?
Lando, who publicly advocates for mental health because his own is fragile too, because his
line of work takes a bite out of it day after day?
This cannot be about Lando. This is about Oscar.
Oscar is punishing himself. Drawing a line through their friendship for reasons Lando cannot
fully comprehend, and there is a part of him that wants to let him. Wants to allow him the
punishment he seems so determined to inflict upon himself for whatever transgression he
believes he has committed.

But Hattie had been right to write that address on his wrist. Had been right to place her trust
in him.
Because if there is even the slightest chance that he can change Oscar’s mind, that he can tell
him Hattie has disclosed everything and that he doesn’t care, that he doesn’t judge him for
any of it, that he isn’t even going to attempt to drag him kicking and screaming towards the
future Hattie so clearly hopes for him, then Lando is going to seize it.
He’s old enough to stomach a slight, old enough to survive a rejection.
Especially when it comes in the form of a letter like this; a letter that carries Oscar’s reluctant
devotion in every single line, unable to conceal it no matter how diligently he tries.
There is an entire undercurrent running through it. One that calls to Lando. One that asks him
not to listen to rational Oscar, the one leading the charge, holding the pen, carefully
constructing his arguments.
Instead, he chooses to listen to the second Oscar. The one lurking beneath the words. The one
meandering through the spaces between sentences, inhabiting the gaps of what is being said.
Lando has always been remarkably recalcitrant when it comes to people telling him what to
do; one of his less endearing qualities.
This time is no different.
He’s going to get into a car and drive to an address. He’s going to climb the stairs and find
the right door. And he’s going to knock.
Oscar can still decide whether he opens it.
On his way out of the park, he texts Max a quick update – partly to keep his hands busy,
partly because he knows his friend is probably waiting for one anyway – giving him the
rudimentary version of what happened with Hattie and what she told him.
There isn’t much Max says in return, except: Good luck. Get your man.
Though Lando isn’t entirely convinced that’s the situation at hand.
All in all, throughout the entirety of his absurdly long message, Oscar only ever referred to
him as a friend. Every reference circled back to their friendship, though there had been one or
two moments where the wording had tripped him up.
I just needed to have you.
I wanted you to know me.
Maybe that’s the second Oscar, too. The one lurking beneath the Oscar who wrote the
message in the first place, carefully arranging every sentence in the hope of slighting Lando
so thoroughly that he would never look back.

The second Oscar underneath it all feels different. Lando has to hold on to that. To the
possibility that he’s not imagining it.
Wherever Lando travels in the world, there is usually a McLaren waiting for him. He hates
being a passenger in any car and only ever takes taxis when circumstances leave him no
alternative, so he’d driven himself here today in a McLaren Spyder – the same model he
owns back home. 
It takes him almost half an hour to get it out of the VIP parking area, even now, nearly three
hours after the race has ended.
Eventually, as he finally makes it out of the park and onto the road, he sends his team a brief
update one-handed. Visiting a friend. Don’t wait up for me.
According to his navigation, Oscar’s apartment is not far from Albert Park at all, and the
drive takes him along the coastline almost the entire way, the sun already beginning its slow
descent towards the horizon, bathing the bay in sheets of molten gold.
The journey takes less than fifteen minutes. He parks his McLaren in a free space beside the
apartment complex his phone assures him is the correct one, and the moment he kills the
engine he becomes aware of how violently his heart is beating, each pulse pressing insistently
against his throat.
There are still people out and about, a handful of late-evening dog walkers drifting along the
pavement, but thankfully they seem far more interested in the car than in the fact that he
himself is, in every conceivable sense of the word, still McLaren-branded.
The team kit is still faintly sticky against his skin. His cap is still on backwards.
He slides his phone into his pocket and crosses the street towards Oscar’s building. There is a
staircase running up the side of it, leading into an open-air corridor that reminds Lando
vaguely of the beach hotels he’s stayed in over the years – which, he supposes, makes perfect
sense considering the ocean sits directly across the road.
He starts making his way up. Seven flights of stairs, no elevator.
And he’s fairly certain the reason he has to stop on almost every landing has less to do with
the climb itself and more to do with the fact that his heart is still beating as though he’s
narrowly escaped death.
At one point an elderly woman emerges from her apartment and gives him a distinctly
puzzled look. Lando has no idea whether she recognises him or simply finds it strange that an
objectively athletic-looking young man is currently bent over a railing, attempting to recover
from a staircase.
A minute later, he finally reaches Oscar’s door. It is inconspicuous enough. 
There is nothing about the exterior of the apartment that feels particularly personalised.
His name is there: Oscar Piastri.

There is a window beside the door as well. The blinds are closed.
Lando stares at it again, stares at the name on the door, at the entirety of it, trying to come to
terms with the fact that over the past months, whenever Oscar called him, whenever he’d
texted him, whenever he’d fallen asleep with his voice still lingering in his ears, he’d been
here.
It feels incredibly strange to know that Oscar’s body has inhabited this space all along, after
having existed as little more than a voice to him for so long, that there are people around him
– the woman from the floor below, the neighbours across the corridor – who know his face,
who know him as Oscar Piastri, a probably somewhat reserved twenty-four-year-old who
only ever leaves his apartment to go to the beach at the other end of the street, who has his
sisters over from time to time, but beyond that?
Lando doesn’t know. Is this the first time he’s had a visitor who isn’t one of them?
He stares at the door for a while longer before finally bringing his knuckles down against it,
rapping against the cheap wood and its peeling finish.
Then he waits. There is no reply. The blinds beside the window shift ever so slightly.
Lando takes a step backwards until the railing catches him and lets his gaze wander over the
entirety of the apartment again, trying to imagine Oscar somewhere behind those walls,
trying to imagine what it must look like inside, the place that has housed so much of him.
He waits another minute before knocking again. Still nothing. This time not even the blinds
move.
For one final moment, Lando looks at the lettering of Oscar’s name on the door and then
abruptly turns around, almost fleeing down the staircase as though the humiliation of having
come all the way here only to be turned away can somehow be outrun.
It was such a stupid fucking idea to come here. Hattie is an optimist. Hattie believes she
knows her brother’s heart.
But perhaps she needs to admit to herself as well that it is, in some fundamental way,
unknowable, that Oscar has chosen isolation again and again and again, and that he will
continue to choose it even when the person standing on his doorstep is the same person he
has spent virtually every waking hour talking to for the better part of four months.
The moment he steps out of the building, Lando makes a beeline for his car on the opposite
side of the street, feeling something inside him gathering force, something worse than
mourning, worse than rejection, something that feels suspiciously like devastation.
Heartbreak.
He has been disappointed before, humiliated before, emotionally dismantled often enough
that he should, by all accounts, have developed some resistance to it by now – but he has
never known a hurt quite like this one, a sharp and all-consuming agony that feels as though

an arrow has pierced his lungs, a knife found its way between his ribs, something vital inside
him punctured beyond repair.
By the time he reaches the car, he feels like a dead man walking, as though everyone passing
him should be able to tell at a glance that he’s bleeding out, that something inside him has
been irreparably damaged.
And then, just as he reaches for the door handle, he catches sight of the sun, red and bleeding
just like him, slowly sinking into the ocean beyond the road, and suddenly, even though only
a minute ago he’d wanted nothing more than to leave this wretched place behind, to take the
first available flight to China and never think about Melbourne again, he finds himself unable
to resist the urge to linger a little longer.
To keep the dying sun company.
And so he steps onto the beach, his gait hindered by the soft sand he keeps sinking into,
sneakers and socks wholly unsuited for it, but he makes it onto the stretch of white shoreline
regardless, now steeped in a deep and satisfying orange.
He makes it all the way to the water’s edge, where he collapses into the sand without the
slightest regard for the fact that he’s getting it everywhere now, that the sticky residue of
champagne on his skin and fine grains of sand are a combination he’s going to despise later.
But he doesn’t care.
He props his arms on his knees and stares straight out at the ocean, which is ablaze as well,
painted orange and flecked with veins of blood-red, while his eyes begin to burn and he feels
his face growing wet, feels it finally spill over after having wrapped himself in stoicism for
the entirety of the day.
He can finally cry now. He can finally mourn the person he thought singular in understanding
him. Singular in enduring him.
Turns out not even Oscar could remain in his orbit for very long before growing tired of him,
tired of his relentless demands for closeness, for intimacy, for the way he keeps pressing
against boundaries until they splinter.
The tears spill freely down his face now, and Lando presses the back of his hand against his
mouth in a futile attempt to stop the shaky breaths threatening to escape him, every inhale
feeling like drawing shards of glass deep into his lungs.
Out in the water, directly ahead of him, there is a lone figure.
A wave rises behind him, gathering itself slowly before rearing up high enough to briefly
swallow the sun, towering over its dying shape, and for a moment the surfer becomes nothing
more than a silhouette cut from darkness against the blood-red horizon, carving gracefully
through the face of the wave and leaving behind a trail of white sea froth.

Then the wave folds over itself. The figure dives from the board into the water. And Lando
loses sight of him completely.
When the wave dissolves into a chaotic perturbation of water retreating back into the ocean,
the surfer emerges from it as though spat back out by the sea itself, water streaming from him
in rivulets, his dark wetsuit clinging to every line of his body, a faded green surfboard tucked
beneath one arm.
He’s close enough now for Lando to see his face. And the surfer sees him, too.
He freezes. Staring at Lando as though he is some cruel hallucination conjured from salt
water and sunset light, from sand and grief and the long shadows cast by the dying sun.
Lando cannot move. The surfer takes another step out of the water, then another. Until he
stands no more than three metres away.
He’s got wet hair, dark and plastered against his pale forehead. His eyes really are brown, a
shade somehow even lovelier in his face than it had been in his sister’s. And then Lando
notices everything else all at once – the strong line of his jaw, the rounded shape of his nose,
the constellation of moles scattered across his neck, the curve of his mouth.
Oh, Lando thinks. He’s exactly my type.
And he is. There is a softness to him that had always been there in his voice, a gentleness
Lando had somehow learned by heart long before he ever saw his face. It lingers in the way
he’s built, in the broad curve of his shoulders, in the narrower line of his waist, in the easy
strength with which he carries the surfboard tucked beneath his arm.
And his face–
His face is softer than Hattie’s, less angular, though the resemblance between them is
unmistakable now that Lando knows to look for it.
But Lando does not recognise him because he resembles his sister. Lando recognises him
because of the way he is looking at him: as though he doesn’t know whether he wants to
throw himself straight back into the ocean or cross the remaining distance between them, as
though every instinct inside him is pulling in opposite directions.
His eyes move relentlessly across Lando’s face, drinking him in with an almost desperate
intensity, lingering on the tears still wet on his cheeks, the redness around his eyes, the bitten
raw shape of his mouth.
Lando doesn’t move. He simply stares up at him.
And eventually Oscar seems to emerge from whatever paralysis has seized him. He takes one
step. Then another. Then a third.
Then he lowers the surfboard into the sand beside them and sits down next to Lando so that
both of them are facing the ocean.

Lando can feel him looking at him from the side. There is an expression on Oscar’s face that
seems suspended somewhere between paralysed disbelief and genuine fear.
His arm is almost touching Lando’s. Lando can feel the cold dampness radiating from him.
Can smell the salt clinging to his skin.
And when he finally turns his head and meets Oscar’s eyes, he finds them still fixed on him,
still searching his face again and again and again, as though he cannot quite convince himself
that this is real. As though he cannot get enough.
Cannot get enough of the man he has spent years looking at through screens, through
photographs, through broadcasts and interviews and grainy clips on the internet.
And now he’s here. Now he’s here, tear-streaked and red-eyed and heartbreakingly human,
sitting on Oscar’s beach while the sun dies behind them.
“Hi,” Oscar says finally, and Lando almost faints at the sound of his voice in real life,
stripped of the slight distortion of Discord, of distance, arriving wholly unmediated into the
evening air between them.
“Hi,” Lando replies, and against his will – even though he’s still a little bit cross with him –
he feels the corners of his mouth lift ever so slightly at the familiarity of it, at the fact that
after all of this, after heartbreak and panicked, misdirected letters, they are still greeting each
other exactly the way they always do.
“How did you...?” Oscar doesn’t even finish the sentence. The words simply trail off between
them.
Lando turns his wrist upwards and shows it to him – the smudged writing, faded now but still
legible.
For a moment Oscar only stares at it. Then something seems to give way inside him. As
though the impulse arrives before he can stop it, before he can think better of it.
He reaches out and brushes his fingertips over the fading ink of his own name, his own
address, and Lando feels a jolt run through him at the contact, sharp enough that it almost
startles him.
Oscar seems to feel it too. His hand retreats immediately.
“I don’t...” He shakes his head. “I don’t understand.”
He looks at Lando again, still caught somewhere between desperation and disbelief, as
though he genuinely cannot comprehend the fact that he’d done everything in his power to
stop this from happening and Lando has shown up anyway.
“Your sister,” Lando says after a moment. “She... told me everything.”
The reaction is immediate. There is genuine terror in his eyes. Betrayal and shame and panic
chase each other across Oscar’s face so quickly that Lando almost cannot keep up with them.

He manages to hold Lando’s gaze for another second before looking away entirely, turning
towards the other side as though he physically cannot bear to be seen.
“I...” Lando sees his throat work. Sees him swallow against the neoprene clinging to his skin.
Oscar seems to feel the constriction too, because he reaches for the zipper of his wetsuit and
pulls it down slightly, dragging in a deep breath that sounds almost painful.
He still doesn’t look at him.
“I’m so sorry that she ambushed you like that,” he says. “Believe me, she did so entirely
without my–”
“I know,” Lando interrupts gently. “Like I said. She told me everything.”
Oscar turns back towards him. The distress in his face is almost unbearable now that Lando
can actually see it: he’s only known this face for a handful of minutes, but he already feels as
though he can read it; the tight crease between his brows, the strain around his eyes, the way
his mouth keeps threatening to turn downward.
“I’m sorry,” Oscar manages. The words seem physically difficult for him. “I’m so–”
“What are you apologising for?”
“Misleading you,” Oscar breathes. “Telling you I was going to meet you when–”
God. Lando cannot stop looking at him. Cannot get enough of it.
The voice he knows – knows so intimately that he could probably identify it in a crowded
stadium from a hundred metres away – is suddenly coming from an actual person, from an
actual mouth, and every time Oscar speaks Lando finds his eyes dragged helplessly back to
it. To the shape of his lips. To the slight hesitation before certain words. To the visible
evidence that Oscar has been real all along.
“The only thing you need to apologise for,” Lando says, turning fully towards Oscar so that
he’s facing him now, “is thinking I’d ever fucking think differently of you if you’d been
honest with me.” He shakes his head slightly, disbelief making his voice brittle around the
edges. “Why did you think I’d think differently of you?”
Oscar is quiet for a moment. “All I am,” he says eventually, his voice threaded through with
bitterness, “is this. This husk of who I used to be. Unable to break from pattern, unable to
move beyond my apartment and this beach without–”
His voice catches. He stops. Tries again.
“I’ve become little more than a mind and a voice over the past few years. And then you came
along and somehow managed to make me feel like more than that again, even though this is
all you’ve ever known of me too. You wanted to meet me. You made it your personal mission
to excavate me.” His mouth twists slightly. “And I was stupid enough to think I could do it.
That wanting to meet you badly enough would somehow be enough for me to–” His hand
lifts briefly towards his temple. “To get rid of whatever the fuck is wrong with me.”

The bitterness in his voice deepens.
“But it can’t be bargained with. It can’t be reasoned out of existence. It doesn’t care what I
want.” He laughs again, softer this time. “If anything, it becomes more vicious whenever it
realises I desire something.”
The last sentence lands between them and remains there.
Lando feels his eyes burning again. Feels the tears threatening all over.
And Oscar notices immediately. His gaze snaps back to him, confusion and alarm flashing
across his face in equal measure, as though he cannot quite process what he’s seeing.
As though the sight of Lando Norris sitting on a beach in front of him, eyes shining with
tears, is somehow more incomprehensible than the fact that he’s here at all. Because he’s
crying. Over him. Because of him.
“And it didn’t help that all you talked about was... how important physical contact is for
you,” Oscar continues eventually, and now his voice really does sound thin, strained around
the edges, like an animal caught in a trap and exhausting itself trying to escape. “How...” 
He breaks off again, derailed by yet another thought before he can finish the first. “Lando, I
really fucking wanted to be there today. I wanted to see you win. I wanted to celebrate your
victory with you in person for once.”
Lando blinks. He’s still caught on the first part of it, still reeling from that brief glimpse
behind the curtain, from the sudden appearance of the second Oscar, the Oscar that has
always existed beneath the surface current of every conversation they’ve ever had.
He knows he’s still crying, so whatever absolution he’s attempting probably loses some of its
dignity in the process, but he turns towards him anyway. “I forgive you,” he says. “H told me.
She told me the lengths you went to trying to–”
“I will murder her,” Oscar interrupts, almost matter-of-factly. “This traitor. How did she
even–”
“I’m really glad she told me,” Lando cuts in, his voice unexpectedly firm. “Because you
never would have. You would’ve written me this... this letter and then disappeared. Gone
completely no-contact. You incredibly stubborn and moronic asshole.”
Oscar’s teeth sink into his lower lip and Lando can barely drag his attention away from it,
from the way every emotion seems to move openly across his face, from how expressive he
is, how transparent, how much of what he feels is written there for anyone willing to look.
Something Lando has been deprived of for months.
“I’m sorry,” Oscar repeats. “With all your talk about physicality being a deal-breaker in
your... relationships, I thought the last thing you’d want was being friends with someone who
can’t leave the house. You lead this life, Lando. This life of excitement and noise and crowds
and movement, and I never would’ve fit into it.” He laughs weakly. “I didn’t want to watch

the realisation dawn on you that our personalities might be... twin flames or whatever... but
the rest of our lives would never fit together.”
“That’s not something you get to decide for me, Osc.” Lando looks at him.
The sun is bleeding its last orange light into Oscar’s face and, god, he’s beautiful. The wet
strands of hair beginning to dry into salty streaks against his forehead.
The startling fairness of his skin, the softness of his features. The impossible kindness in his
eyes, the slightly uneven shape of his ears. The elegant front teeth.
All the details that make up a face, and somehow none of them feel incidental.
Lando feels something tear inside his chest at the sudden resurgence of that hunger, the one
he has carried for the longest time now, ever since the first allusion to the breadth of Oscar’s
