chest in that first picture he’d ever sent him, the familiar shape of his shoulders, the
broadness of his frame.
Oscar’s neck looks so biteable, so broad and sturdy, and Lando is suddenly overcome by the
absurd, overwhelming urge to climb straight into his lap, to sink his teeth into the reality of
him, to make up for months of distance and yearning by holding onto him hard enough that
he cannot possibly disappear again.
He wants to consume the space between them, wants to tear through every remaining layer of
separation. Wants, with a desperation that almost frightens him, to finally have proof that
Oscar is real.
He wrestles the urge back down, but only barely.
“I understand that now,” Oscar finally says, his eyes fixed on Lando the entire time, and
Lando wonders whether he saw any of what had just been running through his mind. He
might have, because Lando sees him swallow, sees his pupils slightly dilated – but that could
just as easily be an effect of the fact that the sun is gone now.
“Will you allow me to remain your friend, then?” Lando asks.
“For as long as you’ll have me,” Oscar replies, and there’s a soft smile on his lips.
God, Lando loves the way he smiles, just as self-ironic as he’d always imagined it would be.
He wants to tear the snark right off his mouth with his teeth, wants to sink into it, fill his
mouth with the entirety of him, have Oscar choke on the taste of it, on the reality of it.
“We should go back,” Oscar says after a moment. “The beach is about to become
annoyingly... crowded. And loud.”
“To your apartment?”
“Yeah,” Oscar says. “I can’t, uh, really go anywhere else.”
Lando nods. “Yeah. I’d love to.”

Oscar gets to his feet rather quickly, holding out a hand for Lando, who lets himself be pulled
up. Oscar’s fingers brush over his wrist, over the hammering pulse there, and Lando feels his
skin burn at the simplest touch.
God, how is he supposed to survive this?
For a moment they simply stand there in front of each other, almost the same height, Oscar
slightly taller, and Lando takes him in, the entirety of him; and before he can stop himself,
before he can even pretend at restraint, he wraps his arms around him and pulls him closer.
After a moment of obvious surprise, Oscar returns the embrace, his arms coming together
behind Lando’s waist, much firmer than he’d expected, much more decisive for all of Oscar’s
constant self-effacement. Lando buries his face in the crook of his neck, clad in neoprene,
breathing him in.
Mostly salt water. The lingering scent of neoprene. But also something else; something
distinctly, undeniably Oscar. It sends a shiver through him.
He feels solid beneath Lando’s embrace, the shape of muscle beneath the wetsuit wrapping
around Lando’s much leaner frame, but the softness of him is no less undeniable for it. Their
embrace lasts almost half a minute, during which Lando tries desperately to rein in his
breathing, his heartbeat, the urge to press himself deeper and deeper into this man.
He’s vaguely mortified by how wildly his pulse seems to be racing, at least until he feels
Oscar’s heartbeat against the side of his face and realises it’s going just as fast.
When he finally pulls away, he looks up at him and finds an expression on Oscar’s face that
he cannot quite put into words.
The crease between his brows again. A look of concentration. A look of agony.
For a moment they simply stare at each other, breathless, before Oscar takes a step back and
bends to retrieve his surfboard.
“You smell like victory champagne,” he says, his voice faintly amused.
“Yeah,” Lando replies, flippantly. “A side effect of winning.”
Oscar turns towards him, grinning, one hand resting on his surfboard. “You had a great race.”
“You watched it?” Lando asks, and immediately feels his heart climb into his throat.
“Of course,” Oscar says, jerking his head in a silent motion for Lando to follow him – as
though Lando doesn’t already know where he lives.
Which means he must have written the message immediately afterwards. Not a DM this time
that Lando would never read, but a message he knew Lando would.
They make their way back across the beach and towards the street, where Lando’s McLaren,
still parked exactly where he’d left it, has attracted a sizeable crowd.

Oscar slows. Looks at the car. Then at Lando. “This yours?”
“Yeah,” Lando says.
He almost asks him if he wants to take it for a drive, but he doesn’t know how Oscar feels
about cars anymore, doesn’t know whether the crash has stolen that from him too.
“Well, not mine mine. But for as long as I’m in Australia, it’s at my disposal.”
“It’s breathtaking,” Oscar says, and there’s something almost raw in the admission. His eyes
roam over the entire thing; the sweeping line of the bodywork, the low-slung cockpit, the
impossible elegance of it.
Lando sees the hunger immediately. Recognises it with painful ease.
“You want it?”
Oscar stares at him. “What?”
“You want it?” Lando repeats. “The car. I’ll buy it off the lease and give it to you.”
Oscar scoffs. “Don’t be ridiculous.”
But his eyes never leave it, and Lando is already making a mental note to call the dealership
later and set everything in motion. Even if Oscar never drives it, even if it just sits
somewhere, and he only ever looks at it.
“I’m not,” Lando says with a shrug.
“Lando, that thing costs three hundred thousand quid.”
“I get an employee discount,” Lando quips.
That finally earns him a snort. “Let’s go,” Oscar says, shaking his head. “Before they notice
you.”
They cross the street and Oscar takes a detour towards a sort of storage room where roughly a
hundred surfboards are chained up.
Lando leans against the doorframe, a grin tugging at the corner of his mouth as he watches
Oscar chain his up as well. His frame is so broad that Lando cannot help but drift into a brief
daydream about Oscar pressing him against the dirty wall and caging him there with nothing
but the breadth of his shoulders and the span of his arms.
Oscar turns around and catches him grinning. “What?” he asks, faintly embarrassed.
“You’re so delightfully Australian,” Lando says after a moment, electing to voice the least
embarrassing and most socially acceptable thought from the myriad currently ricocheting
around his head.

“Oh, come on.” He snorts and brushes past Lando through the doorway, and Lando follows
him back towards the stairs.
On the stairwell they encounter Tangerine, who truly is the largest beast Lando has ever seen,
meowing loudly and refusing to let anyone pass until Oscar scoops her into his arms and
placates her with scratches beneath her chin and affectionate strokes across her face.
Lando feels his throat go dry as he watches the cat curl herself against Oscar’s chest.
Once, he had been jealous of a dolphin. Now he’s jealous of a cat. He has truly reached the
nadir of his existence.
Oscar sets Tangerine back on the floor and she saunters off, entirely satisfied with the tribute
she demanded, before he turns back to Lando, who is still staring at him, which seems to
embarrass him even more. 
God, he blushes a lot. It’s there every time Oscar turns around and discovers Lando already
looking at him. The colour creeps into the tips of his ears, and Lando almost loses his mind
entirely.
He follows behind Oscar on the climb to the seventh floor, and all the while his eyes keep
returning to him against his better judgement; the shape of his shoulders, the way his frame
narrows at the waist, the thickness of his thighs, the suggestion of muscle beneath it all.
Never in a million years – not even in his most delusional moments – had Lando imagined
that the man he’d fallen in love with through nothing but the cadence of his voice and the
shape of his attention would also happen to be someone he would have absolutely attempted
to chat up if he’d spotted him across a club somewhere.
He’s almost aggressively Lando’s type. Almost insultingly good-looking, built: and
apparently entirely unaware of it. Shy and awkward. Nerdy.
Lando is genuinely relieved when they finally step into Oscar’s apartment, if only because it
gives him something else to look at besides Oscar’s back.
It’s more spacious than he expected, a kitchen and living room bleeding seamlessly into one
another, an en suite and a normal bathroom, a study – from where he streams – and a
bedroom.
Lando is amused by the relative mess. It looks exactly like the apartment of a twenty-four-
year-old who lives alone; clothes draped over the backs of chairs, dishes in the sink, the bed
unmade, picture frames leaning against the walls instead of hanging from them.
An AC unit is running, which is what had moved the blinds by the door, Lando now realises,
and Oscar has a genuinely spectacular view of the ocean through a sliding door that leads out
onto the balcony.
Oscar looks mortifyingly embarrassed by the state of the apartment. He immediately begins
rushing through it, attempting to restore order at impossible speed, shoving a cereal box into

a kitchen cabinet before opening the dishwasher to load the dirty dishes, only to realise in
real time that it’s still full of clean plates.
This seems to send him into even greater panic.
“Uh,” he says, turning around to Lando, who has slowly wandered into the main room after
peeking into the streaming room. That one is by far the worst. The sight elicits an immediate
grin.
As someone who has spent most of his adult life either in hotel rooms or places cleaned by
other people, Lando has very little personal experience with the specific horror of
unexpectedly having someone over and suddenly seeing every mess through their eyes.
He finds it impossibly endearing.
“Do you want to take a shower?”
“Do I stink?” Lando asks, grinning as he leans against the doorframe and watches Oscar
hurriedly gather clothes from every available surface.
There’s a lot of yellow and green from the Australian team. A surprising amount of McLaren
papaya too.
“No,” Oscar says immediately, sounding genuinely alarmed. “I just meant because of the
champagne and the... the sand and–”
“I’m pulling your leg,” Lando says. “I’d love to. But I don’t have any fresh clothes.”
“No worries,” Oscar says quickly. “You can have some of mine.”
The mere idea of wearing Oscar’s clothes makes Lando’s knees go slightly weak, forcing him
to lean a little harder against the frame of the door.
“Oh, yeah,” he says. “Please.”
Lando follows Oscar into his bedroom, where he immediately begins rummaging through his
closet in search of the freshest shirt and shorts available, while Lando takes the opportunity to
absorb the room itself.
The window faces the ocean, though there’s no balcony attached to it, and Oscar’s bed sits
directly in front of it so that he can sleep with the window open and the sound of the sea
pouring into the room.
His bed is unmade, of course. Something about that makes something tighten low in Lando’s
stomach, the sight of the rumpled sheets. The evidence of Oscar existing here.
There are books on the nightstand too, which surprises him at first, though only briefly. Then
he remembers his message, the precision of it. The carefulness of the language. The
vocabulary that had startled him more than once.

So Oscar reads, huh?
A laptop lies abandoned on the bed. Maybe that’s where he watched the race.
Oscar finally turns around after rummaging through his closet for a while.
“Do you want my uni shirt, or a baggy green, or one of your own McLaren tees?”
“My own shirt is boring,” Lando says. “What’s a baggy green?”
“Cricket,” Oscar replies, pulling out a dark green shirt, and Lando immediately likes the
colour.
“Yeah,” he says. “That.”
“Australia colours?” Oscar tilts his head. “Even though you’re English?”
“I have no loyalty to my country’s cricket team,” Lando grins.
Oscar laughs softly and tosses him the shirt along with a pair of black shorts. “I hope they
fit.”
He then escorts him to the bathroom, which is in slightly tidier state than the rest of the
apartment, hands him a fresh towel and then more or less flees the room, closing the door
behind him the moment Lando starts taking off his shirt. His cheeks have been growing
steadily pinker over the past few minutes.
Lando strips out of his clothes and throws them into the washer like Oscar instructed him to
before stepping beneath the spray of the shower, watching the sand disappear down the drain.
He tries not to wash the address off his wrist, even though it serves no purpose anymore,
considering he’s already standing at the place it led him to.
He uses Oscar’s body wash and shampoo, which seem to be utterly ordinary supermarket
products, but somehow smell better to Lando than any five-hundred-pound luxury brand that
has ever arrived in a PR box. His curls are probably going to suffer for it, considering Oscar
has straight hair, like he once told him – but one shower is hardly going to ruin them.
When he finally steps back out – having only once wondered how many times Oscar might
have jerked off in here, which he considers a victory all things considered – he slips into the
clothes Oscar gave him.
They’re a little too large. The Australian team shirt hangs off his frame, the sleeves reaching
farther down his arms than they should, but he can’t exactly afford to be picky.
He studies himself in the slightly fogged-up mirror. Oscar’s clothes. Oscar’s colours – the
dark green looks surprisingly good against his tan skin. 
A small, irrational part of him is almost disappointed that the shirt appears freshly washed.
But he can’t exactly ask Oscar for something he’d already worn. That would be an

extraordinarily strange request and would betray the almost insulting degree to which Lando
is down bad for him.
Before tossing his jeans into the washer as well, he fishes his phone out of the pocket. Max
has texted him.
 

Max
Did you find him?

 
Then, an hour later.
 

Max
I’m going to choose to see it as a good sign that you still haven’t texted me.

 
Max
But I would appreciate a reply. At some point.

 
Max
Lando???

 
Lando grins to himself as he starts typing out a response, his heartbeat fluttering at the mere
recollection of their first meeting, which had happened barely half an hour ago and already
feels like a decisive marker in the chronology of his life going forward.
 

Lando
Yeah, I found him. I’m currently in his apartment. 
Max, I’m so fucked. He’s djdkdj hnnng. hot. You know how I could barely keep it
together when I knew almost nothing about him. Now I’ve talked to him for half an hour
and I need to climb him like a tree. 
And literally I have no idea whether I’m completely delusional about all of this.

 
He finishes typing the message and slides the phone back into the pocket of Oscar’s shorts
before opening the bathroom door and stepping back out into the apartment.
Lando hasn’t been in the bathroom for very long, but Oscar seems to have somehow
managed to restore a semblance of order to the entire apartment in the span of fifteen
minutes; the windows are open, a fresh sea breeze sauntering through the rooms and stirring
the leaves of the two plants that Oscar appears to be systematically tormenting through
overwatering, judging by the yellowing leaves.
Every surface has mysteriously been cleared of whatever had previously occupied it, the door
to the streaming room is closed, and the clothes that had been strewn across half the
apartment have somehow vanished as well.
Lando wanders through the living room on quiet feet when he cannot immediately find
Oscar, and eventually realises he’s in the bedroom.
When he appears in the doorway, he catches a glimpse of it. Oscar has gotten rid of the
wetsuit and is changing into normal clothes.
He’s standing with his back to the door and doesn’t notice Lando immediately. Lando only
sees it for a second; Oscar’s bare back, the raised red scar running the length of his spine
before ending in a perpendicular line near the base of it. 
His surgery scars, Lando realises with a start. Much more pronounced than he’d imagined.
Oscar turns around at precisely that moment and finds Lando standing there in the doorway.
For the briefest second, something like panic flashes across his face at the realisation that
Lando might have seen it, the way the scar bisects the entirety of his back.
Then he smooths the expression away. Or perhaps he simply forgets about it, because his
eyes have settled on Lando instead, standing there in Australia’s colours.
Lando watches him stare, for a number of seconds that borders on the obscene. And for the
first time, Lando feels genuinely certain that the hunger he keeps seeing in himself exists in
Oscar too.
The way Oscar takes him in, the way his gaze travels over him. The way he seems unable to
stop looking despite the fact that the shirt is far too large and hangs loosely from Lando’s
frame.
Lando sees his throat work as he swallows. Almost immediately, that familiar flush returns to
his cheeks.
“Green looks good on you.”
Only then does Lando notice that Oscar is wearing one of McLaren’s team kits. “Orange
looks even better on you.”

For a moment they simply look at each other, watching one another furtively, as though both
of them are waiting for some shift in the other’s posture, some crack in composure, as though
one of them might suddenly pounce or inadvertently betray something that would demand an
immediate response from the other.
“I’m going to wash the sand off as well,” Oscar says after a moment. “I’ll be back in a
second.”
With that, he more or less flees the room again, brushing past Lando and stirring the loose
fabric of the oversized shirt as he goes, his drying curls spilling messily across his forehead.
A second later, Lando hears the bathroom door click shut behind him, and the moment the
shower starts running, he knows his brief window for snooping has begun.
The first thing he gravitates towards are the books on Oscar’s nightstand. There are only
three of them.
Two non-fiction books about aerospace engineering – which immediately makes Lando still.
Is that a clue? – and, rather unexpectedly, Persuasion by Jane Austen. It’s the one sitting on
top of the stack, a pair of horn-rimmed specs next to it.
Lando picks it up. It looks well-read, the spine softened from use, and for a moment he finds
himself imagining Oscar propped against the headboard of this very bed, reading glasses on,
turning the pages of what Lando assumes is, at its core, a love story. The image does strange
things to him.
After that, he drifts towards the other side of the room, where a collection of photographs has
been pinned to a corkboard he hadn’t noticed before.
The board is crowded with reminders, notes, prescriptions for painkillers – strong ones,
Lando recognises them immediately – and a birthday card from someone named Edie.
But it’s the photographs that hold his attention.
There’s a picture of a small boy, drowning in a helmet and sitting in a kart, the number 81 on
the front plate. Another of Oscar, no older than twelve, on a podium flanked by two boys who
look years older and twice his size.
As the photographs progress, he gets older too. His features begin settling into themselves.
There are pictures with his parents; one with all three sisters lined up together somewhere on
holiday; Oscar the tallest and oldest, then a girl who looks startlingly like him – Hattie – and
then, Lando assumes, E and M. 
A picture of Hattie with a rabbit in her lap. Oscar sprawled across a sofa with a dog curled
beside him. Basil, probably.
There are photographs from university too; a fresh-faced eighteen-year-old Oscar standing
shoulder-to-shoulder with a girl and a boy around his age. Friends, Lando assumes.

And then there is Albert Park. Oscar standing beside his father, both of them smiling at the
camera while an orange-and-blue car blurs past in the background.
Lando freezes. The realisation arrives all at once. His MCL34. It is his car. This is their first
photograph. 
Lando stares at it for longer than any of the others. If he has the timeline right, then the
accident happened sometime in early 2020. Which means that after this photograph was
taken, Oscar never came back to Albert Park again.
He carefully takes the photo off the board before continuing his exploration.
There’s a desk, one he clearly doesn’t use for streaming but which is instead dominated by a
bookcase overflowing with textbooks – mathematics, statistics, physics, and an alarming
amount of engineering. There are notes as well, covered in a messy handwriting that is barely
legible to Lando; and tucked away in one of the drawers are even more photographs, some
that apparently never made it onto the wall, including several of the boy and the girl from the
university picture.
In one, Oscar is wearing safety goggles in what appears to be some sort of laboratory, holding
something with an absurdly long pair of tongs that looks moments away from exploding.
There’s another photograph of the boy asleep in Oscar’s lap in one of the university
courtyards while Oscar reads through a textbook. He looks so young there, his face still
closer to the kid on the podium than the man he is now. Lando’s attention snags on a detail he
almost misses: Oscar’s hand buried in the boy’s hair.
The next picture is even more revealing.
It was taken at a party, and Oscar has his arms wrapped around the other boy from behind, his
chin resting on his shoulder as they both smile into the camera.
Lando’s heart immediately begins to beat faster. He puts the photographs back into the
drawer a little too quickly and slides it shut.
Hadn’t Oscar once said he dated someone from his lab? What if Lando had misinterpreted it?
What if it had been a boy? But then why had Oscar never said anything?
Lando had heard about the high-school girlfriend and had automatically assigned the other
person Oscar had dated – however briefly and prosaically – the same pronouns, even though,
now that he thinks about it, none had ever actually been mentioned.
After that, he wanders back into the living room, where one of the frames turns out, upon
closer inspection, to be a Master’s diploma from the University of Melbourne in Engineering,
and Lando cannot quite suppress the small smile that curls at his mouth.
He knew it. At this point it could hardly have been anything else, not with all the clues Oscar
had already scattered in front of him over the months.

The remaining frames contain photographs of waves. One captures a lone figure carving
through the face of one, and after a moment Lando realises it is probably Oscar. Only he
never hung any of them up.
Lando steps out onto the balcony, the door still standing open behind him, the last light of the
day slowly draining from the sky while the ocean stretches before him as a vast black
expanse.
He closes his eyes and draws in a deep breath, filling his lungs with salt air and the smell of
tar slowly cooling after a day spent baking beneath the Australian sun.
Now that darkness is settling in properly, he can make out the gathering on the beach that
Oscar had been alluding to. Music drifts across the water, accompanied by lights and the
distant murmur of a crowd.
“They do this every year after the Grand Prix,” Oscar says from somewhere behind him.
Lando startles slightly at the sound of his voice and turns around to find him standing in the
doorway, one shoulder resting against the frame. His hair has fallen over his forehead again,
darker than it looked in the photographs Lando had spent the past minutes familiarising
himself with in Oscar’s absence.
“They wander over from the park and have some massive cookout or party or whatever down
there.”
“It’s nice.” Lando doesn’t turn back towards the ocean. Instead, he keeps looking at Oscar
standing there on the threshold of his own balcony.
Oscar gives him a strange look. “You really are the life of the party, aren’t you?” he says. “I
bet if you went down there, they’d completely lose their minds.”
Lando lifts one shoulder in a shrug. “I do like attention,” he admits after a moment. “You
know that about me.”
Oscar nods towards the photograph still clutched in Lando’s hand. “What’s that?”
Lando holds it up.
“Our first picture together,” he says with a grin. “Look. That’s my car in the background.”
Oscar laughs, barely even glancing at the photograph. “I know,” he says. “That’s why it’s on
my wall.”
Then he tilts his head slightly. “You snooped?”
“Thoroughly,” Lando replies. He wants to ask about the photographs in the drawer. About the
boy. About Oscar’s hand in his hair and his arm wrapped around his shoulders. About what
any of it means.

“Didn’t expect anything less from you,” Oscar says after a moment, still looking at Lando
standing on his balcony as though the sight remains too unfamiliar to quite believe. “Look,
uh–”
“Can I stay over for the night?” Lando asks in that exact moment, and he hates how needy he
sounds, how pathetic he is for even asking, but–
“Oh, my god,” Oscar says, blinking rapidly. “I was literally about to ask you the same thing,
but I didn’t want to overstep. I don’t know what your obligations look like after a race win.
And you’re due in China already for next week’s race.”
“I already told my team I’m visiting a friend,” Lando replies. “They know not to expect me
tonight. I don’t have any obligations. I already filmed all my McLaren stuff, and they usually
let me do whatever I want on a Sunday evening, especially if I win.”
“And you’re sure you want to spend your race-win evening with me?”
Lando is almost certain he catches the implication buried underneath it, subtle enough that it
could be denied if challenged. Maybe emphasising, during his coming out, how many hook-
ups he was getting had not been the wisest strategic choice. At the time he’d been
overcorrecting, terrified that Oscar would think he was hitting on him.
Lando rolls his eyes. “You owe me your life story,” he tells him. “All the things you kept
secret because you were too scared I’d find out. Your studies. Your friends. Your karting
career. All the years in between. Why you graduated with honours. I’m afraid I need to know
all of that now that I have your full name as well, Oscar Piastri.”
“Jack,” Oscar says.
“Huh?”
“My full name is actually Oscar Jack Piastri.”
For a moment, Lando can do nothing but stare at him, feeling his jaw physically drop.
“You’re joking.”
“I’m not.”
Oscar is still looking at him, his arms folded across his chest, only making Lando realise how
broad he actually is. There’s a smile tugging at the corners of his mouth, something almost
smug about it, a slight purse of the lips that seems entirely too pleased with itself.
“You know what?” Lando says.
“What?”
“I see it now.”
Oscar furrows his brow slightly. “What?”

“The Jack part of you,” Lando replies, stretching against the railing like a cat in heat. God.
Jesus Christ. He needs to get a grip. “At first I thought that was the worst fuckboy name I’d
ever heard, completely inappropriate for someone as kind and understated as you.” He points
at him accusingly. “But then you just grinned like that.”
Oscar is blushing again. Too much direct attention from Lando, too much scrutiny, too much
commentary on something intrinsically his.
He’s always been bad at receiving it, usually changing the subject before the spotlight can
linger for too long, but now he doesn’t seem capable of switching gears quite as quickly as he
normally would.
“I’m more of an Oscar than a Jack,” he concedes after a moment, hastily averting his gaze
while Lando remains standing there on the balcony, bathed in the soft light spilling out from
the apartment behind him. Beyond Lando’s shoulder, the waning moon is beginning to rise
from the darkness of the ocean, pale and faintly yellow against the night sky.
“You definitely have a Jack side, though,” Lando says after a moment, still watching him.
Oscar remains leaning in the doorway, absent-mindedly brushing a thumb across his upper lip
as he looks back at Lando. “I do?”
For a moment, Lando wants to ask him about the boy in the photographs tucked away in the
drawer, the ones Oscar never put up on the wall, though the image of Oscar’s hand buried in
his hair while reading through a textbook feels far too soft to belong entirely to the Jack side
as well.
“All ripped and shit,” Lando says, attempting nonchalance. “Oscar’s a scrawny nerd who
plays Minecraft.”
“Yeah, well,” Oscar replies. “It’s not that I particularly enjoy working out. I just don’t enjoy
waking up in the middle of the night and writhing in pain.”
Lando immediately winces. “I’m sorry. That was–”
But Oscar shakes his head. “No, don’t worry about it.”
“If it’s any consolation, you’re fucking hot.” Of course Lando somehow manages to select
the single most catastrophically stupid conversational option available to him.
Oscar, however, appears to disagree. The colour in his cheeks deepens almost immediately,
spreading across his face and into the little bit of his ears visible through his hair.
God. God. Lando wants to repeatedly introduce his forehead to the railing behind him. He
genuinely cannot do this anymore. The way Oscar reacts to him.
He knows he reacted like this before as well, back when they had only been voices on
Discord calls, but now all Lando can think about is the fact that Oscar must always blush like
that. Every time he’d disappear for a moment and return a minute later with his voice a little
rougher than before. All the blushes Lando never got to see. All the expressions he missed.

Christ. He wants to make up for lost time as quickly as possible.
“Don’t,” Oscar says. “You don’t have to do that.”
“What?”
Oscar makes a strange gesture with his hand, something vaguely indicating the space
between them. “I don’t know, like–”
“I was paying you a genuine compliment, you muppet.” Lando bites his lower lip around a
grin. “I tend to do that with my friends. It’s my love language.”
Oscar gives him a strange look then, as though he disagrees with at least one part of that
statement. “Well, uh, you’re not so bad yourself.”
Lando laughs. “You don’t have to return it. It’s not a swap meet.”
“But you are,” Oscar insists, and the sincerity in his voice almost wipes the grin straight off
Lando’s face.
The way Oscar looks at him then is faintly disarming; slightly enraptured, as though Lando
Norris leaning against his balcony remains a sight he cannot quite reconcile with reality.
Lando tilts his head. A considerable part of him wants nothing more than to close the
distance between them, grab Oscar by the collar of his McLaren shirt, and drag his mouth
against his own.
But he knows that would be a bridge too far. A violation of the natural chronology of things.
Oscar seems to catch something shifting in his expression because he uncrosses his arms and
abruptly turns back towards the apartment. “Should we order food?”
“Gladly,” Lando replies, following him inside and pulling the balcony door mostly shut
behind him.
They settle on pizza, which turns out not to be much of a debate at all, and spend the half
hour it takes for the delivery driver to make it out to Oscar’s part of the city standing in the
kitchen.
Lando is leaning over the island while Oscar occupies his now-familiar position against the
cabinets, his arms folded across his chest again as though the gesture serves as some form of
protection.
Lando is paging through a stack of photographs Oscar grudgingly produced from somewhere,
documenting his karting career, while Oscar watches and provides occasional commentary on
whatever image Lando happens to be looking at.
“So the eighty-one in your name has always been a reference to your karting days?” Lando
asks.

“But I do also like it because it’s a perfect square number,” Oscar says with a grin. “It’s a
good number. Four’s a good number too.”
“Because it’s also a perfect square?”
Lando is still studying the photographs, Oscar rapidly aging through them all while somehow
remaining much too small amidst competitors who are taller and broader and stronger, and he
feels an absurdly protective instinct stir inside him at the sight of the little boy with flaxen
hair and a grin that looks more like a grimace.
“Yeah,” Oscar replies. “Among other things.”
“You’re really into numerology, aren’t you?”
Oscar visibly winces. “I’m into maths. Numerology is esoteric bullshit. You may as well
believe in zodiac signs.”
“I do believe in zodiac signs,” Lando replies, looking up at him with a grin, half baiting him
and half completely serious.
Oscar sighs deeply. “I know.”
There’s a note of resignation in it that immediately makes Lando grin, as though some
substantial part of Oscar still cannot quite fathom how he ended up friends with someone like
Lando, how a person so fundamentally different from his usual orbit of acquaintances
managed to become this important to him.
Lando places the last of the karting photographs onto the pile beside them, a strange
heaviness settling in his chest at the thought that Oscar never really got much further than
this. Then he looks up at him, gathering what feels like an unreasonable amount of courage.
“I, uh, saw the photos on the board in your room,” he says eventually. “The boy and the girl
standing next to you in front of your university. Who are they?”
A strange expression flickers across Oscar’s face. “Uh, that would be Martha and Nicolas,”
he says. “They were my best friends.”
“Were?”
Oscar winces. “It’s complicated. Stupid drama.”
“Love triangle?”
Oscar snorts. “Something like that.”
He turns the glass of water in his hands, one finger tracing the rim slowly and absent-
mindedly. Lando finds himself inexplicably hypnotised by it. Oscar glances up, and Lando
attempts what he hopes is an encouraging grin.

“What happened?” he presses. “Come on. You have to tell me. I missed out on all the good
university gossip and drama because all I ever knew was racing.”
Oscar snorts again. “It’s not that good.”
He sighs.
“We were this sort of dynamic trio in school. We all went to the same elite STEM prep school
to get into engineering programmes early, so we all started university at seventeen. I came to
that school later. Nicky and Martha were already friends. Then I arrived and managed to fuck
everything up.”
“How?”
Oscar shrugs. “I don’t know. I kind of got between them.”
“Did they both want you?” Lando tries to conceal his grin behind his hand, considering Oscar
looks genuinely mortified.
“Yeah,” he admits after a moment.
“So you dated Martha?”
“Yes.”
“And you dated Nicky too?”
“Yeah,” Oscar repeats.
Lando stares at him.
“So you’re...”
“Yeah.”
Oscar rubs a hand across the back of his neck, as though trying to ease some of the
awkwardness currently consuming him. His gaze drops to the glass again, avoiding Lando’s
entirely while Lando continues watching him from across the kitchen island.
“I never really put a label on it,” he says after a moment. “But yeah, I guess.”
“Why didn’t you say anything?” Lando asks. “Back when I–”
“Because it would’ve completely undermined what you were telling me,” Oscar replies.
“That was your… moment. And besides, I’d never really defined it that way before. It
would’ve felt wrong to stumble into trying to define it when you were being so clear and
precise about what you were telling me.”
“You’re such an idiot,” Lando says fondly. Predictably, his heart is attempting to beat its way
straight out of his chest.

A considerable part of him wants to text Max underneath the table immediately, if only so
somebody else can share in the revelation with him, though of course it doesn’t mean…
doesn’t mean that–
“What happened to Nicky and Martha?” Lando asks after a moment. “You said they were
your friends. Past tense.”
“It was a strange time in my life,” Oscar admits. “Feelings got hurt, and I didn’t manage the
inherent, uh, explosiveness of a situation like that particularly well. Turns out, you probably
shouldn’t date both of your friends at the same time. Even when they insist they’re okay with
it, they very much are not.”
Lando finally breaks into a grin. “Well, I find it admirable that you first had to test that theory
to arrive at the conclusion.”
“Thanks,” Oscar says, and for a moment his eyes flick to Lando’s lip, which he’s been
chewing on absent-mindedly. “I’m a slow learner.”
“You most definitely are not,” Lando scoffs.
“I am... in these things,” Oscar says after a moment. “We’ve talked about this before. The
whole... dating thing. I dislike it.”
“Right,” Lando says, clearing his throat. “You said you’d rather do it the organic way. Like
falling in love with your best friend.” He tilts his head. “Did you mean Nicky?”
Oscar looks at him, utterly puzzled. “Yeah,” he says eventually, but he sounds strange. “I
guess.”
Lando starts worrying more aggressively at his lower lip, trying not to reveal just how much
he dislikes that answer. “So where are they now?”
“Martha’s doing her PhD at MIT. She went into aerospace engineering. And Nicky went to
work for, well, Williams.”
“Oh.” Lando turns the photograph over in his hands. “Chances are I crossed paths with him
in the paddock?”
“No, he’s back at the factory.” Oscar scrunches his nose slightly. “We don’t keep in touch.”
“Ended on bad terms?”
“Pretty sure I broke his heart.”
Lando raises his eyebrows. “So your middle name isn’t that misleading after all. You’re a
fuckboy?”
Oscar snorts. “I should hope not. He just wanted more. I was more content keeping it... uh,
physical. So he gave me an ultimatum. No more sex unless I agreed to show up for the rest of
it as well.” He sets the glass down beside him with a sharp clatter that makes Lando jump.

“Wow,” he says, suddenly finding his mouth dry. “I didn’t think you’d be the type for–”
“I’m not anymore,” Oscar cuts in quickly. “The whole accident... changed me completely. It’s
part of the reason we drifted apart. Our friendship had already run its course before the crash,
and I think Martha felt guilty. She was the one driving. She’d had a little too much to drink.
We all had, to be honest. But when I... stopped emerging from my apartment, they eventually
stopped trying to coax me out.” He pauses. “I think we were all a little relieved. There was
too much hurt there.”
“I see,” Lando says quietly. “So your outlook on relationships changed because of that?”
“I’m not sure,” Oscar admits. “I’m a very different person now. I used to be... very normal. I
always liked Minecraft, but I liked a lot of other things too. Now I’m quite... insular.”
“You’re not,” Lando immediately counters. “You’re so much more than that. Your entire
apartment is proof of it.”
Oscar gives him a strange look. “Yeah,” he says. “But it’s all inside my apartment, isn’t it?”
Lando turns the photographs over absent-mindedly, each of them another glimpse into an
Oscar who might have been his rival one day, had things unfolded only a little differently. He
looks over at him, finding Oscar staring out into the night beyond the window, his arms
folded across his chest. The line of his jaw stands out against the pale of his skin, and Lando
realises that he is hurting. That he is ashamed.
This, then, is why he had sidestepped every question Lando had ever thrown his way. Every
question that had merely asked for a little more; for a glimpse into his life. Oscar had evaded
them all with quiet, unwavering determination, intent on keeping this part of himself hidden.
The fact that, over the past four years, these four walls had come to constitute the entirety of
his world, while Lando had made the entire whole world his.
Lando doesn’t know what to say. He doesn’t know how to make this any better, how to ease
some measure of the shame that seems so profoundly corrosive, eating away at Oscar’s sense
of self until it has left it brittle, fragile, liable to splinter beneath the slightest pressure.
Before Lando can sift through his repertoire of encouragement for something – anything – to
offer him, the intercom buzzes at the door, making both of them start. Oscar turns almost
immediately and leaves the kitchen without looking back, heading to buzz the delivery driver
into the building. Lando remains where he is, quietly arranging the photographs back into a
neat stack before sliding them into the clear plastic sleeve Oscar had unearthed for him at
Lando’s eager insistence on seeing a few remnants of his karting days.
When Oscar returns, the heaviness has gone from his features, and Lando realises that he
must have left it at the door with surprising ease. Not that he is, by any means, suddenly
alright now, but Lando understands what he is doing: he doesn’t want the one evening he gets
with Lando before the season carries him away again to dissolve into brooding. Lando
decides to let the subject rest, especially because Oscar begins asking about the race, pivoting
the conversation with that same effortless deftness he has always had.

They take almost two hours to finish the food they ordered, both of them sitting on the carpet
beside the couch, the balcony door still open, the sounds of the gathering on the beach
drifting lazily into the apartment. Oscar is leaning back against the sofa, one arm draped
across a bent knee, listening as Lando recounts the race, the little battles on track, his
predictions about Mercedes and how difficult they’re going to be to beat over the course of
the season.
It is strange to watch Oscar listen to him for the first time.
Before, whenever Lando talked – whenever Oscar coaxed him into talking – he had spent the
entire conversation gesticulating at a phone, interrupted only by the occasional dry quip from
Oscar every few minutes. Now, for the first time, Lando gets to watch him listening. The
little smiles that flicker across his face whenever Lando slips a joke into the story. The way
he scarcely takes his eyes off him, looking over with an expression that borders on
enrapturement, sometimes for the better part of a minute at a time.
The look in Oscar’s eyes is difficult to put into words. There is a quiet fondness to it, one that
settles over his face whenever he looks at Lando, sometimes absently worrying at his lower
lip as he listens, only tearing his gaze away when he seems to remember that people are, in
fact, expected to break eye contact every now and then. Lando loves the way he laughs. It is
understated, almost noiseless, but so utterly genuine that his shoulders shake with it before he
inevitably looks back at Lando again, the tenderness in his eyes almost unbearable to
withstand.
Lando conducts himself with almost painful restraint on the opposite side of the coffee table.
He remains exactly where he is, like a good friend should, entertaining Oscar like a good
friend should, carefully steering the conversation around anything that might tip them into
more dangerous territory, instead of simply crawling across the carpet, settling himself in
Oscar’s lap, taking his hands and guiding them beneath the green cotton of his Australia shirt,
onto the bare skin of his waist.
It’s well past midnight by the time they finally clear away the mess they have left behind, and
Lando feels the exhaustion settling heavily over him.
No wonder. It has been an eventful day: he has won a race, cried his eyes out, met the person
he is devastatingly in love with, and now he is sitting in that very person’s apartment,
pretending that what exists between them is friendship. It wears on a man, that.
Oscar insists that Lando take the bed while he sleeps on the couch.
“No,” Lando immediately protests, absently plucking at the collar of his shirt while Oscar
stands opposite him in the narrow strip of space between the kitchen island and the cabinets
where they have come to a halt. Oscar is close, and Lando tries very hard not to let his eyes
drift back to his arms, which somehow look even broader with them folded across his chest.
“Let me take the couch.”
Or even better, crawl into bed with me, he adds silently.
“Absolutely not,” Oscar snorts. “What kind of host would I be?”

“You think I’m too spoiled to sleep on the couch?” Lando tilts his head as he takes another
step towards him.
Oscar doesn’t move. He only looks down at Lando, though his eyelids flutter ever so slightly
as Lando closes what little distance remains between them.
The unmistakable movement of Oscar’s throat as he swallows against the skin of his neck
makes something inside Lando tighten painfully. He wants to fist his hands in the front of
Oscar’s McLaren shirt, tear the stupid number four off his chest along with the fabric, sink
his teeth into the softness of his skin, into the muscle wrapped around those impossible arms.
It is suddenly far too warm in here. Lando feels it in the sweat beginning to gather at the
small of his back, in the growing dryness of his throat, in the heat radiating from his cheeks
despite the fact that the night outside is only growing cooler by the minute.
He sees it in Oscar, too. The flush across his cheeks. The colour climbing into the tips of his
ears. The brief, almost absent-minded sweep of his tongue across lips that seem every bit as
dry as Lando’s own.
What are we doing? Lando wants to ask. Why are we discussing sleeping arrangements when
we both know that the only way either of us finds acceptable is spending the night in one
another?
“I’ll get some sheets,” Oscar says, his voice little more than a hoarse murmur before he
abruptly turns away, leaving behind nothing but the faint breeze of his passing brushing
against Lando’s overheated skin.
Lando never manages to change his mind. He tries – tries with an almost embarrassing
degree of determination – but Oscar never yields.
So Lando ends up leaning in the bedroom doorway instead, watching Oscar pull fresh sheets
over the mattress, when all Lando really wants is to sleep in the ones Oscar has already used,
if he cannot have Oscar beside him.
The atmosphere shifts almost imperceptibly, and then all at once. Somehow the banter no
longer comes as effortlessly as it always has; it falters, stagnates between them before either
of them can find another opening to slip back into it.
Lando keeps catching his gaze wandering over Oscar instead – the curve of his neck, the
softness of his freshly washed hair, the long line of his legs beneath his shorts, his bare feet
against the wooden floor. He looks like summer. Like a surfer between tides, sun-warmed
and temporarily ashore, which, Lando supposes, is exactly what he is.
In turn, Lando feels Oscar looking at him too.
He catches him watching from the corner of his eye, his gaze snagging on the bracelets
around Lando’s wrists, lingering at his throat, at the mole on the side of his face, as though
Oscar is silently committing him to memory in exactly the same way Lando has spent the
better part of the evening memorising him.

With any other man, Lando realises, he would have fucked him twice by now.
He isn’t stupid. He recognises the tension for what it is; the inevitable consequence of two
people spending an evening together, growing steadily more tired while every boundary
between them is worn thinner by the constant abrasion of simply occupying the same space
after months of being denied it.
The novelty of finally meeting has begun to ebb away. Lando can close his eyes now and
summon the imprint of Oscar’s face with frightening ease, and what remains once that
astonishment has settled is everything that had always existed underneath it, everything that
circumstance alone had kept safely beyond reach because there had never been any
possibility of following that road to its natural conclusion.
He knows, too, that part of the thickening air, of the strange paucity of words between them,
comes from the knowledge that they met beneath the final embers of the setting sun, and that
the evening is steadily drawing itself closed.
Soon they will have to go to bed. Tomorrow morning Lando will return to his life, while
Oscar remains here.
Neither of them can say when Lando will be back. Or what seeing one another in the flesh
will do to the shape of whatever it is they have painstakingly constructed over these past
months.
There is a very real possibility that this is the only chance Lando will ever have to know him
like this; to feel the undeniable reality of him, to have his skin beneath his hands instead of
merely his voice in his headphones, to discover the cadence of his laboured breathing spilling
against Lando’s sweaty skin instead of through compressed audio, to learn the absolute
corporality of him – the way he occupies space, the way he moves through it, the way his
body answers every impulse of his mind.
The thought makes him almost light-headed with wanting. For a moment he has to close his
eyes as Oscar turns back towards him, finished making the bed, absently running a hand
through his hair.
Oscar brushes past him, and for a moment Lando considers catching him by the wrist,
stopping him, telling him exactly what he wants. But he doesn’t – and the silence stretches
between them, growing longer and heavier with every passing second.
Half an hour later, Oscar switches off the light in his bedroom. Lando is already sitting on the
bed, one leg folded beneath the other, and in the dim light spilling in from the kitchen Oscar
turns back towards him.
“Well,” he says, one shoulder resting against the doorframe. “Sleep well, Lando.”
His voice sounds genuinely raw now.
“Oscar,” Lando breathes, just as Oscar shifts to leave the doorway, to close the door behind
him, to retreat once more to the safety of the living room.

Oscar freezes immediately. “Yeah?”
“Can you sit down here for a moment?” Lando asks. “I want to... say something.”
For a moment he is certain Oscar is going to refuse. His entire body draws taut, and even in
the sparse backlight Lando can see him sink his teeth into his lower lip. But Oscar has never
really been capable of denying him anything.
So he steps away from the doorway instead.
Lando shuffles backwards until his shoulders rest against the headboard, then pats the empty
space beside him. After only the briefest hesitation, Oscar crosses the room and sits down on
the other side of the bed, leaning back against the headboard as well, until they are shoulder
to shoulder, both of them staring straight ahead.
“What is it?” Oscar asks, his voice almost breaking into a croak. The desperation threaded
through it is so overwhelming that Lando feels the heat rise inside him until it borders on
nausea.
“Why did your sister send me here, Oscar?” he finally manages to ask, the words resisting
him every step of the way, balking in his throat before they can make it out.
“I don’t know.”
“What did you tell your sister about me?” Lando tries again, searching for a different angle.
“What made her think I had the power to... to–”
Oscar doesn’t answer. When Lando finally glances sideways, he finds naked agony written
across Oscar’s face. Moonlight spills through the open window, washing his features in a
pale, almost ghostly light.
“I wish she hadn’t,” Oscar says at last. “I wish she’d minded her own business.”
Something inside Lando twists so violently it almost hurts. “So you wish I weren’t here.”
Oscar still doesn’t look at him. 
“I wish I weren’t this,” he says, the words sounding as though he has to force each one free.
“I wish we’d met at the race. I wish I’d been there to cheer you on from the garage. I wish I
could have–”
“Why are you like this?” Lando tries – tries so desperately – not to let the tears gather in his
eyes again. “I don’t give a shit about what–”
“But I do.” Oscar’s words burst out of him so suddenly that they almost make Lando flinch.
“I fucking do, Lando. I hate being this. I want to be–”
“What?”
“I want to be someone worthy of you.” 

His voice sounds strange, constricted, and Lando doesn’t dare look at him, afraid he’ll find
something in Oscar’s face he isn’t prepared to witness.
“I can’t...” Oscar swallows. “I can’t be this fucking pathetic and still think I have even the
slightest claim to someone like you.”
Lando feels it; the weight of the words. The confession buried beneath them. God. They’re
almost there.
“Oscar,” he says quietly. “Oscar, listen to me.”
Oscar doesn’t move. Neither does Lando. Both of them remain staring at the wall ahead,
crowded with fragments of Oscar’s life.
“Look at me,” Lando says. “Then tell me what you see.”
Oscar doesn’t. He keeps his eyes fixed ahead, his jaw drawn so tight that Lando can almost
see the bone beneath the pale stretch of skin.
“Look at me.”
Only after another long moment does Oscar relent. He turns.
His eyes immediately settle on Lando, drinking him in where he sits beside him against the
headboard, and for a while neither of them speaks. They simply look at one another, their
heads resting against the wood, the silence between them suddenly more articulate than either
of them has managed to be all evening.
“What do you see?” Lando asks again.
Oscar’s gaze drifts slowly across his face. “I see...” He exhales softly. “Someone I was never
supposed to see. Not like this.”
“Like what?”
“In my room.” His voice has fallen to little more than a whisper. “You aren’t supposed to be
here. My message was supposed to make sure of that.”
“Why?” Lando asks, unable to look away from him. “Why do you insist on that?”
“Because–” Oscar begins the sentence, only to discover that he cannot finish it. The words
falter and die somewhere between his chest and his mouth.
He keeps looking at Lando. Lando keeps looking back.
“Oscar,” he says. His thoughts return, unbidden, to that moment almost four months ago now,
when Oscar had first surrendered this very sound now slipping so effortlessly from Lando’s
lips. I’ve got your name now, he’d thought back then, long before he’d understood the gravity
of it. Soon, I’ll get the rest of you, too.

“Lando.” 
He drinks in the way Oscar says his name. It scrapes him open.
Look at me, he wants to plead. Look at me and see the truth written all over my face. You
think I cried on that fucking beach because the sunset moved me? Do you really think that?
Fuck it, Lando thinks.
Oscar would sooner turn to stone than make the first move; Lando understands that now.
Some part of him remains convinced that Lando has no rightful place in his life, not after
Oscar relinquished his own for the sake of his family, not after he retreated from the world so
completely.
And yet the world came looking for him.
Lando leans in. His mouth brushes Oscar’s lips, only just catching them before diverging
across the corner of his mouth and the line of his jaw. He doesn’t steady him with a hand,
doesn’t guide the kiss or perfect the angle, which is why it ends up little more than the
faintest graze.
His breath catches instantly. A violent jolt races through him the moment his lips so much as
touch Oscar’s.
For one suspended instant he cannot move. 
Oscar is utterly motionless, exactly as he had been a heartbeat before, before Lando’s
restraint finally gave way beneath the accumulated weight of months spent wanting him.
For a single, endless moment, Oscar looks like a deer caught in headlights.
Then he lurches to his feet, almost stumbling in his haste to put as much distance between
them as possible, and before Lando can force so much as an apology past the tightness in his
throat, Oscar is gone. The bedroom door swings shut behind him.
“Fuck,” Lando whispers to himself, pressing his fist against his mouth as he feels the heat of
shame surge up inside him.
God, this is so quintessentially him. Overstepping. Wanting too much. Being too hungry, too
clingy–
Even for Oscar.
Even though all he wants is to curl up beneath the sheets and cry himself to sleep, to let the
ache seep into his bones until it becomes a permanent fixture of the way he has always
wanted too much, he instinctively knows he cannot allow this to fester. He cannot let the
night settle over it and carve tomorrow morning into something shaped entirely by shame.
He has to fix this now. Apologise. Beg. Explain himself.

Lando all but tumbles out of bed as he tangles himself in the sheets, then stumbles across the
room and reaches for the door, wrenching it open to find the living room, the couch where
Oscar–
Oscar is already there. Right in front of him. On his way back to the bedroom. Back to him.
For a suspended moment they do nothing but stare at one another, half-formed apologies
stranded on both of their lips, until Oscar suddenly catches Lando by the collar of his shirt
and pulls him forward, straight into the breadth of his chest, one arm wrapping firmly around
Lando’s waist as his mouth finds Lando’s.
He kisses him less than he folds into him, immediately backing Lando against the wall,
catching one of Lando’s legs as his hand slips beneath the hem of his shorts, his fingertips
finding the feverish heat of his skin.
He yanks Lando’s leg up, lifting it higher as he crowds him against the wall of the corridor
beside the bedroom door, closing the last remnants of distance between them. The feeling of
Oscar’s hand against the bare skin of his thigh as he crashes into him, his mouth hot and
impossibly soft against Lando’s, draws the smallest, most fractured of sounds from
somewhere deep inside him the moment he tastes Oscar, the warmth of him blooming across
his tongue.
Oscar’s other hand has found the nape of Lando’s neck, having travelled there from the
moment he first caught him by the collar of his shirt. His thumb disappears into the curls at
the base of Lando’s neck, brushing gently through them while the rest of his hand steadies
him, subtly tilting his head back so that Oscar can reach him more completely, claiming the
angle with an almost desperate certainty. Lando’s lips part helplessly beneath the unabashed
insistence of it all, yielding without thought as Oscar presses further into the kiss, licking
inside him; every movement carrying the accumulated gravity of months spent wanting what
had seemed forever beyond reach.
Lando does not think he has ever been kissed like this before.
There is a singularity to Oscar’s attention, an almost frightening certainty in the way he
moves against him, in the way he holds him there, every touch so deliberate that it borders on
reverence, and yet threaded through it all is a barely contained urgency, a tremor running
beneath the surface that betrays how much restraint it is costing him. Even as he crashes into
Lando like the tide finally reclaiming the shore, he is still holding something back, and that
restraint somehow makes the hunger pouring out of him feel all the more overwhelming.
Lando slides a little lower against the wall, his knees threatening to give beneath the force of
finally having Oscar in his arms, and Oscar follows the movement instinctively, never once
breaking away from his mouth. His lips remain fastened to Lando’s as though the thought of
letting go has become physically impossible.
Lando does not want him to.
He wraps both arms around Oscar’s back, feeling the muscles shift beneath the thin cotton of
his shirt, but even that is nowhere near enough. He needs to know the shape of him properly.

Needs to feel the warmth of his skin beneath his palms, to convince himself, at last, that the
man he has spent months reaching for is no longer only a voice carried to him through a
headset, but real, and solid. 
Oscar’s hand travels higher beneath the hem of Lando’s shorts, slowly riding the fabric up
until his palm finds the curve of Lando’s hip and then the fullness of his arse, holding him
there as he lifts him higher once more, higher than before, until Oscar has to reach up to kiss
him. His mouth slips free of Lando’s lips only to wander over the side of his face, along the
line of his jaw, before descending to his throat. He scarcely leaves a trail of distinct kisses
there; instead, he seems to taste the path to Lando’s neck, his mouth gliding over his skin
until Lando feels the edge of Oscar’s teeth catch against him.
Every brush of them sends a violent tremor through him.
Each fleeting graze convulses through his body like a surge of adrenaline, making him feel as
though he is attempting an overtake on a rain-soaked circuit, only infinitely worse, infinitely
more consuming, every nerve in him suddenly strung so impossibly tight. 
Lando sags forward against him, and Oscar catches him without hesitation, the steady
pressure of his mouth against Lando’s throat never relenting as he presses another trail of
kisses there. Lando’s head falls back almost involuntarily, and something utterly helpless
escapes him, a sound so broken and unguarded that he would be mortified by it anywhere
else.
His fingers tighten convulsively in the fabric of Oscar’s shirt, feeling the hard line of muscle
drawn taut beneath it, every part of Oscar straining simply to keep him exactly where he is.
The moment that involuntary, unmistakable sound leaves Lando’s lips and spills into the
heated air between them, Oscar goes rigid.
Lando feels it instantly.
He feels Oscar’s breathing hitch, feels it quicken against his skin, feels the hand cradling the
back of his neck tighten almost imperceptibly, not as a conscious decision but as something
entirely instinctive, a reflex born of finally hearing what this is doing to Lando, of realising
that Lando is not suffering through the silence of wanting him, but giving voice to it in the
only way his body still can.
“Fuck, Osc. Please.” It is all Lando can force past his lips before the plea dissolves into
another broken moan, and he no longer even knows what he is begging for.
Oscar’s mouth is still against the side of his throat. “You need to stop making those sounds,”
he manages to croak into his skin. “Otherwise I’m going to–”
Lando feels Oscar’s grip tighten against the curve of his arse, his thumb pressing more firmly
into the yielding skin beneath it.
“I can’t fucking stop,” Lando barely manages, his fingers threatening to tear through the
fabric of Oscar’s McLaren shirt just to reach the warmth of the skin whose promise he can

already feel beneath the thin cotton. “Have you got any idea how many times I’ve touched
myself thinking about you? At this point it’s just my body reacting to the completely
embarrassing conditioning I’ve inflicted on myself.”
That does it. Oscar tears himself away from Lando’s neck, bringing their faces level again.
They are so close that Lando almost goes cross-eyed trying to look at him.
Oscar is in an absolutely disastrous state. His pupils have blown so wide that the warmth of
his brown eyes has almost disappeared into black, and the flush spread across his cheeks
makes him look as though he has been slapped right across the face. Damp strands of hair
cling to his forehead, his lips are parted around uneven breaths, and only now does Lando
notice the faint crescents of teeth pressed into them, marks he must have left there without
even realising.
“You what?” His voice is raw. “You did what?”
“I wanked,” Lando repeats, letting his gaze drift slowly across Oscar’s face. “To you. More
times than I can count.”
“Fuck.” Oscar buries his face in Lando’s shoulder for a moment, drawing one long,
shuddering breath. “Say that again,” he murmurs. “Please.”
When he finally lifts his head again, Lando catches the small crease between his eyebrows,

Please don’t send this to Lando or OP, and don’t tag either of them. We’re all just having
a bit of fun over here. Sleep well, my sweets. See you at the next one. <3



Chapter End Notes

I honestly don’t know what to say in this author’s note. I’ve been writing on here for
almost a year now, and never in all that time (or even before that) have I experienced
support like this for something I wrote. The amount of love that Zero Cycle received - a
fic I genuinely thought would maybe be of interest to a dozen people because of how
inherently niche it is - and I have never been happier to be so wrong.
Writing Oscar and Lando falling in love over 100k words without ever even meeting is
not something I thought would gather any sort of audience. But the way you guys rooted
for them through everything meant the world to me.
I really hope you enjoyed the last chapter - them finally meeting, and everything that
came after. I don’t think I’ve ever written two people who are so utterly obsessed with
one another, haha, and that was such a fun dynamic to explore.
One last thing: many of you theorized that, with his engineering degree and the fact that
he and Lando got along so well, Oscar would eventually become his race engineer. And
that is absolutely something I entertain myself - and something I genuinely believe
happens a few years down the line, once Oscar grows more comfortable with returning
to the world and takes all the necessary steps to earn such a high position within the
McLaren ecosystem. Or maybe he’s perfectly content staying a revered MCSR player.
But considering they literally get distressed when the other isn’t in the room, I do
believe the end goal for them is actually working together and collecting WDC after
WDC together. <3
What remains now is simply to thank you. Thank you for your incredible support, for
the art you created, the edits you made, for talking about my fic, for sending me your
thoughts on Tumblr, and for all the love you showed it beyond that. I will never be able
to repay that. This has been such a wonderful experience for me.

My next fic is going to be another Landoscar non-AU, so if you’re interested in that -
stay tuned.

End Notes
